lessons.title: What Operations Research Is
lessons.content:
Imagine your family has 5,000 taka for Eid shopping. Your little sister wants a dress, your father needs a panjabi, your mother wants a sari, and everyone wants sweets. You cannot buy everything. So you sit down, list what each thing costs, think about how happy each one makes the family, and try to find the plan that makes the most people happiest without going over 5,000. Without knowing it, you just did operations research. You had a goal (most happiness), choices (what to buy), and limits (money). Operations research, or OR, is the science of doing exactly this, but carefully, with math, for problems far too big to do in your head.

What it is: Operations research is the use of mathematical models and careful analysis to make better decisions, usually the best decision, when resources are limited. The resources can be money, time, machines, trucks, workers, warehouse space or anything else that runs out. The key word is best. OR is not about finding a plan that works; it is about finding the plan that is cheapest, fastest, most profitable or least risky among all plans that work. In America it is often called operations research, in Britain operational research, and today it overlaps with what business schools call management science and what tech companies call optimisation or decision science.

Why we need it: Guessing is expensive. A garments factory in Gazipur that guesses how many shirts and trousers to sew might leave machines idle while orders pile up. A courier company in Dhaka that lets riders choose their own routes might burn twice the fuel it needs. A hospital that guesses how many nurses to put on the night shift might either waste salary or leave patients waiting. When the problem is small, common sense is enough. When there are hundreds of products, thousands of customers and dozens of rules, common sense quietly gives a bad answer and nobody even notices how much money was lost. OR replaces the guess with a plan you can prove is good.

How big the problems get: Here is a tiny example that shows why we cannot just try everything. A delivery rider has 10 shops to visit. How many different orders could he visit them in? The first stop can be any of 10, the second any of the remaining 9, and so on, so the count is 10 x 9 x 8 x ... x 1 = 10 factorial = 3,628,800 orders. With 20 shops it becomes 20 factorial, about 2.43 x 10^18 orders. A computer that checks one billion orders per second would need about 77 years to check them all. Real delivery companies have thousands of stops a day. So OR is not just about writing the problem as math; it is about clever methods that find the best answer without checking every possibility.

Where it came from: OR was born in Britain in the late 1930s, when scientists were asked to help the military use the new radar system well. The radar machines worked, but the operations around them, like who reports to whom and how fast, did not. During World War II, teams of scientists, such as the group led by physicist Patrick Blackett, studied real data to answer practical questions. One famous finding was that bigger ship convoys lost a smaller fraction of their ships to submarines than small convoys, because the number of escort ships needed grows more slowly than the number of ships protected. Another was that anti-submarine bombs set to explode at a shallower depth hit far more submarines. These were not new weapons, just smarter decisions based on numbers.

After the war: In 1947, the American mathematician George Dantzig, who was planning schedules and supplies for the US Air Force, invented the simplex method for solving linear programs. A little earlier, in 1939, the Soviet mathematician Leonid Kantorovich had written about similar planning problems, and he later shared the 1975 Nobel Prize in economics with Tjalling Koopmans for this work. Once computers arrived, OR spread to factories, oil refineries, airlines and banks. Today airlines use it to build crew schedules, delivery companies to plan routes, and ride sharing apps to match drivers with riders.

The OR approach, step 1, define the problem: Every OR study follows roughly the same five steps. First, define the problem clearly. What exactly are we deciding? What does best mean: lowest cost, highest profit, shortest waiting time? What are the hard limits we cannot break, like 120 sewing hours a day, and what are soft wishes? This step sounds easy, but many projects fail here because the team solves the wrong problem very well.

Step 2, build a model: A model is a simplified picture of reality written in math. We choose decision variables (the things we control, like x = number of shirts), an objective function (the thing to maximise or minimise, like profit = 200x + 300y), and constraints (the limits, like 2x + 3y <= 120 hours). A good model keeps what matters and throws away what does not. A map of Dhaka does not show every brick, and that is exactly why it is useful.

Step 3, solve the model: Then we use a method to find the best values of the variables. For linear programs we use the graphical method or the simplex method. For special shapes like transportation or assignment we have faster special methods. For problems with randomness we may use formulas from queuing theory or switch to simulation. For very hard problems we may accept a near-best answer from a heuristic.

Steps 4 and 5, validate and implement: A solution is only as good as the model. So we check it: does the plan make sense to the people who actually run the factory? If we test it on last month's data, does it beat what they really did? Then we put it into practice, train people, and keep watching, because prices, demand and rules change. Many OR models run every day, re-solving with fresh data each morning.

Deterministic and stochastic models: In a deterministic model, all the numbers are known for sure, like the profit per shirt and the hours each one needs. Linear programming, transportation, assignment and CPM scheduling are deterministic. In a stochastic model, some numbers are random, like how many customers will arrive at a bank in the next hour or how long a task will really take. Queuing theory, PERT, inventory with uncertain demand and decision analysis handle randomness. Real life is always a little random, so choosing a deterministic model is itself a simplification you should be aware of.

Optimisation, simulation and heuristics: OR has three big families of tools. Optimisation finds the provably best answer to a model, like the simplex method does for linear programs. Simulation builds a computer copy of a system, like a bank with random arrivals, and runs it thousands of times to see what happens; that is the topic of Simulation & Modeling (deep-cse-6-5). Heuristics are smart rules of thumb that find good, not guaranteed best, answers quickly when the problem is too hard for exact methods, like planning routes for 5,000 deliveries. A good OR person knows when each family fits.

A tiny model to feel it: A tea stall near a university sells plain tea for 10 taka and milk tea for 15 taka. Plain tea uses 1 spoon of sugar and milk tea uses 2. The stall has 100 spoons of sugar a day and can make at most 70 cups in total. How many of each should it make? Decision variables: p = plain teas, m = milk teas. Objective: maximise 10p + 15m. Constraints: p + 2m <= 100 (sugar), p + m <= 70 (cups), p, m >= 0. In lesson 03 you will see that the best plan is p = 40, m = 30, earning 400 + 450 = 850 taka. Making only milk tea would give m = 50 cups, inside the cup limit, but it earns only 750 taka, less than 850. The model found a mix you might not have guessed.

Where OR is used today, part 1: Airlines decide which plane flies which route and which pilots fly together, under rest-time rules. Garments factories decide which line sews which order to meet shipping dates. Supermarket chains decide how much stock each branch holds. Power companies decide which power plants to run each hour at the lowest fuel cost while meeting demand. Hospitals schedule doctors, nurses and operating theatres.

Where OR is used today, part 2: Mobile financial services face a neat OR problem. An agent shop must keep enough cash for people who want to cash out and enough e-money balance for people who want to cash in. Too little and customers are turned away; too much and money sits idle. Deciding how much to keep and how often to rebalance is an inventory problem (lessons 18 and 19). Ride sharing apps solve matching problems every few seconds. Food delivery apps solve routing problems. Cricket teams even use data and optimisation to pick batting orders and field placements.

Real-life example 1, a rice mill in Naogaon: A rice mill buys paddy from several farmer groups and sells rice to wholesalers in Dhaka, Rajshahi and Bogura. The owner must decide how much paddy to buy from each source, how much rice to send to each city, and how many trucks to rent. Each source has a price and a limit, each city has a demand and a selling price, and each road has a transport cost. Written as a model, this is a mix of linear programming (lesson 02) and the transportation problem (lessons 09 and 10). The owner who uses it can earn more from the same paddy simply by sending the right amount to the right place.

Real-life example 2, a city hospital's emergency room: Patients arrive at random, some needing a quick check and some needing a long treatment. The manager wants to know: how many doctors do we need at night so that the average wait stays under 20 minutes? Queuing theory (lessons 20 and 21) gives formulas for average wait based on the arrival rate and service rate. If the formulas say two doctors give a 45-minute wait and three give an 8-minute wait, the decision becomes clear and can be defended to the hospital board with numbers instead of feelings.

What OR cannot do: OR is only as good as its model and data. If the profit numbers are wrong, the best plan for the model is not the best plan for reality. Some things are hard to put into numbers, like staff morale or a customer's loyalty, and a model that ignores them can give an answer that looks great on paper but fails on the floor. And for some problems, finding the exact best answer is so hard (we will meet NP-hard problems in lesson 12) that we must settle for very good answers. A good OR analyst says clearly what the model includes and what it leaves out.

Course map: Lessons 02 to 08 build linear programming: formulating models, the graphical method, standard form, the simplex method and its special cases, duality and sensitivity analysis. Lessons 09 to 11 cover transportation and assignment problems. Lesson 12 adds integer variables. Lessons 13 to 16 are about networks and projects: shortest paths, spanning trees, maximum flow, CPM and PERT. Lesson 17 is dynamic programming. Lessons 18 and 19 are inventory, 20 and 21 queues, 22 game theory, 23 decision analysis, 24 nonlinear optimisation and heuristics, and 25 brings everything together in a capstone.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think OR is just linear programming; it is a whole toolbox. Another mistake is jumping to solving before the problem is clearly defined. A third is trusting the model blindly instead of checking it against reality. Exams usually ask you to define OR, list the phases of an OR study, explain the difference between deterministic and stochastic models, name application areas, and describe the components of a model: decision variables, objective function and constraints.

Recap: Operations research uses math to find the best decision when resources are limited. It began with military operations in World War II and grew with Dantzig's simplex method in 1947. An OR study defines the problem, builds a model, solves it, validates it and implements it. Models can be deterministic or stochastic, and we solve them by optimisation, simulation or heuristics. Next lesson, you will learn the most important skill in the whole course: turning a word problem into a linear program.
key_points: OR uses mathematical models to find the best decision when resources like money, time and machines are limited.
It started with British military radar and convoy studies in WWII; Dantzig invented the simplex method in 1947.
An OR study has five phases: define the problem, build a model, solve it, validate it, implement it.
A model has decision variables, an objective function to maximise or minimise, and constraints.
Deterministic models use known numbers (LP, CPM); stochastic models include randomness (queues, PERT).
Tools fall into three families: exact optimisation, simulation, and heuristics for very hard problems.
Trying every option fails fast: 20 delivery stops already have about 2.43 x 10^18 possible orders.
A model is a simplification; its answer is only as good as its assumptions and data.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a decision around you, ask three questions out loud: what am I choosing, what am I trying to make best, and what limits me? Those three answers are the skeleton of every OR model in this course.
lessons.task: Pick one real decision from your week, like planning a study timetable or buying groceries with a fixed budget. On paper, write the decision variables, the objective and at least three constraints with real numbers. Then try three different plans by hand and see which one scores best on your objective.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of operations research?
options: To collect as much data as possible
To find the best decision when resources are limited
quiz.explain: OR is about choosing the best plan (cheapest, fastest, most profitable) under limits on resources.

quiz.q: Who invented the simplex method, and around when?
quiz.explain: George Dantzig developed the simplex method in 1947 while working on US Air Force planning.

quiz.q: Which of these is a stochastic model?
options: A queue at a bank where customers arrive at random
A product-mix linear program with fixed profits
An assignment of 4 jobs to 4 workers with known costs
A CPM network with fixed activity times
quiz.explain: Random arrivals make the queue model stochastic; the others use known, fixed numbers.

quiz.q: A delivery rider has 10 shops to visit. How many visiting orders are possible?
quiz.explain: The number of orders is 10 factorial = 10 x 9 x ... x 1 = 3,628,800.

quiz.q: Which list gives the correct order of phases in an OR study?
options: Build a model, implement, define, solve, validate
Define the problem, build a model, solve, validate, implement
quiz.explain: You first define the problem, then model it, solve it, check it against reality, and finally put it into use.

lessons.title: Formulating Linear Programs
lessons.content:
Before you can solve a problem, you have to say it clearly. A doctor cannot treat you until you describe where it hurts. In the same way, no method in this course can help until a messy real situation, full of words like "we want to earn more but the machines are busy", is written as a precise math model. This step is called formulation, and most OR teachers will tell you it is the hardest and most important skill in the subject. The simplex method can be done by a computer; deciding what to put into it cannot.

What a linear program is: A linear program (LP) is an optimisation model where the objective and every constraint are linear, meaning each variable appears only multiplied by a fixed number and added up, like 3x + 5y. No x squared, no x times y, no square roots. The word program here is old-fashioned and means plan, not computer code. An LP has four parts: decision variables, an objective function, constraints, and non-negativity conditions.

Decision variables: These are the quantities you control and want the model to choose. Always define them in words with units, for example x = number of shirt batches made per day. Never write x = shirts; is it shirts per day, per week, in hundreds? A vague variable leads to a model where the units do not match and the answer is nonsense.

Objective function: This is the single number you want to make as big or as small as possible, written in terms of the variables. Maximise profit, minimise cost, minimise time, maximise people served. It has to be one number. If the manager says "we want high profit and low pollution", you either pick one as the objective and turn the other into a constraint (pollution at most 50 units), or combine them with weights. Linear programming optimises one goal at a time.

Constraints: These are the limits. Each one is a linear expression compared with a number using <=, >= or =. Resource limits are usually <= (hours used must not exceed hours available). Requirements are usually >= (protein must be at least 20 kg). Exact balances are = (everything produced must be shipped). Non-negativity says the variables cannot be negative, x >= 0, y >= 0, because you cannot sew minus 3 shirts. Forgetting non-negativity is one of the most common exam mistakes.

Example 1, product mix in a Gazipur garments factory: The factory sews shirts and jackets in batches. A batch of shirts earns 3,000 taka profit and a batch of jackets earns 5,000 taka. Shirts are cut on Line A, which has 4 hours a day, and each shirt batch needs 1 hour there. Jackets are cut on Line B, which has 12 hours a day, and each jacket batch needs 2 hours there. Both go through the shared finishing section, which has 18 hours a day; a shirt batch needs 3 hours and a jacket batch 2 hours. How many batches of each should be made per day?

Building the model step by step: Variables: x = shirt batches per day, y = jacket batches per day. Objective in thousand taka: maximise Z = 3x + 5y. Line A: 1x <= 4. Line B: 2y <= 12. Finishing: 3x + 2y <= 18. Non-negativity: x >= 0, y >= 0. That is the whole model. Check one plan by hand: x = 2, y = 6 uses 2 of 4 hours on Line A, 12 of 12 on Line B and 3(2) + 2(6) = 18 of 18 in finishing, so it is feasible, and earns 3(2) + 5(6) = 36 thousand taka. In the next lessons you will prove that 36 is the best possible. We will use this factory again and again, so remember it.

Units check: A quick way to catch errors is to read each constraint aloud with units. "Hours per batch times batches per day, summed, is at most hours per day." Hours per batch x batches = hours, so both sides are hours. Good. If one side ends up in taka and the other in hours, you mixed something up. Do this for every constraint, every time.

Example 2, a cattle-feed blend: A feed mill in Bogura mixes maize and soybean meal into a 100 kg bag. Imagine maize costs 30 taka per kg and has 9% protein; soybean meal costs 60 taka per kg and has 44% protein. The bag must contain at least 20% protein, which is 20 kg of protein. Variables: x = kg of maize, y = kg of soybean meal in one bag. Minimise cost C = 30x + 60y. Constraints: x + y = 100 (the bag weight), 0.09x + 0.44y >= 20 (protein), x, y >= 0. Solving later gives about 68.57 kg maize and 31.43 kg soybean meal, costing about 3,942.86 taka. Notice the mix uses just enough of the expensive ingredient to hit the protein target, not more.

Why the protein constraint looks like that: Each kg of maize brings 0.09 kg protein and each kg of soybean meal brings 0.44 kg. So the protein in the bag is 0.09x + 0.44y kg, and it must be at least 20. A common mistake is writing 9x + 44y >= 20, mixing percentages and kilograms. Another is writing the requirement as a percentage of a bag whose weight is itself a variable; then you get (0.09x + 0.44y) / (x + y) >= 0.20, which is not linear, but multiplying both sides by the positive x + y gives 0.09x + 0.44y >= 0.20(x + y), which is linear again. This trick appears often in blending problems.

Example 3, staff scheduling for a call centre: A mobile operator's call centre runs 24 hours in six 4-hour periods. It needs at least 4, 8, 10, 7, 12 and 4 agents in periods 1 to 6. Each agent works one 8-hour shift, which means two back-to-back periods, and shifts can start at the beginning of any period. Variables: x1 to x6 = agents who start in period 1 to 6. Period 2 is covered by those who started in period 1 or 2, so x1 + x2 >= 8. Writing all six: x6 + x1 >= 4, x1 + x2 >= 8, x2 + x3 >= 10, x3 + x4 >= 7, x4 + x5 >= 12, x5 + x6 >= 4. Minimise x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6.

Solving the scheduling model: The best answer turns out to be 26 agents, for example 0, 8, 2, 5, 7 and 4 starting in periods 1 to 6. Here is a neat check that 26 cannot be beaten: take the three constraints x2 + x3 >= 10, x4 + x5 >= 12 and x6 + x1 >= 4; they cover every variable exactly once, so the total is at least 10 + 12 + 4 = 26. Without a model, a manager would usually hire for the peak in each period separately and end up with far more people.

Example 4, choosing projects with a budget: A rice-mill owner has 10 lakh taka and four possible upgrades: a dryer, a husker, a solar panel and a truck, each with a cost and an expected yearly gain. Here the variables are yes or no: build it or not. That is not quite an LP, because you cannot buy 0.37 of a truck. It is an integer program, and we will solve problems like this in lesson 12. The lesson for now is to notice when a variable must be whole or yes/no, and say so in the model.

The four LP assumptions, part 1: An LP is only a correct model if four assumptions hold well enough. Proportionality: if one batch uses 3 hours, two batches use 6 hours and earn twice the profit; no setup costs, no bulk discounts. Additivity: the total is the sum of the parts; making shirts does not change how long jackets take. If these fail, for example the profit per batch drops when you flood the market, the true model is nonlinear (lesson 24).

The four LP assumptions, part 2: Divisibility: variables can take fractional values like 2.5 batches. That is fine for kg of feed or hours of work, and often fine for large counts where rounding hardly matters, but not for 3 trucks versus 4 trucks; then you need integer programming. Certainty: every number in the model (profits, hours, capacities) is known exactly. It never is, which is why lesson 08 studies sensitivity analysis: how much can a number change before the best plan changes?

General form: With n variables and m constraints, an LP looks like this. Maximise Z = c1 x1 + c2 x2 + ... + cn xn, subject to a11 x1 + a12 x2 + ... + a1n xn <= b1, and so on for all m rows, and every xj >= 0. In matrix form, which you know from Linear Algebra (deep-cse-2-5): maximise c^T x subject to A x <= b, x >= 0. The c's are objective coefficients (profit or cost per unit), the a's are technological coefficients (how much resource one unit uses), and the b's are right-hand sides (how much resource exists).

Real-life example 1, a tea garden in Sylhet: The garden decides how much green tea and black tea to process each week. Each type needs different hours on the withering, rolling and drying machines, and each sells at a different price. Fresh leaf is limited, and the buyer has a contract for at least 2,000 kg of black tea. Variables: kg of each tea. Objective: maximise revenue minus leaf cost. Constraints: machine hours on each machine, leaf available, and black tea >= 2,000. The model is small, but writing it down often reveals that one machine is the real bottleneck, a fact the manager can act on without solving anything.

Real-life example 2, a school canteen menu: A school in Chattogram must plan a weekly lunch menu from rice, dal, egg, vegetables and fish so that each child gets at least the required protein, energy and iron, while the cost per child stays as low as possible. This is the classic diet problem, one of the first LPs ever solved in the 1940s. A pure cost-minimising answer may say "dal every single day"; real menus add variety constraints like "fish at least twice a week" and "no item more than three times". Adding such constraints is part of good formulation.

Common formulation mistakes: Defining variables vaguely, without units. Forgetting non-negativity. Writing >= when the story says "at most", or <= when it says "at least". Mixing units (percent with kg, minutes with hours). Writing two objectives. Adding a constraint for something that is already implied by another. Using an LP when the story clearly needs whole numbers or yes/no choices. Making a constraint that depends on another variable's value in a non-linear way, like profit per batch that changes with the number of batches.

What exams ask: Formulation questions are almost guaranteed. A typical question gives a paragraph about a factory, diet, advertising budget, investment or staffing and asks you to "formulate as an LP; do not solve". Marks are given for clear variable definitions, the correct objective with max or min, every constraint with the right sign, and non-negativity. A good habit is to write the data in a small table first: products as columns, resources as rows, with usage per unit inside and availability at the right.

Recap: An LP has decision variables, one linear objective, linear constraints and non-negativity. Define variables with units, read each constraint aloud to check units, and choose <=, >= or = from the story's words. The model is correct only when proportionality, additivity, divisibility and certainty roughly hold. Our running example is the garments factory: maximise 3x + 5y subject to x <= 4, 2y <= 12, 3x + 2y <= 18, x, y >= 0. In lesson 03 you will solve it by drawing.
key_points: An LP has decision variables, one linear objective (max or min), linear constraints and non-negativity.
Define every variable in words with units, like x = shirt batches per day.
Resource limits are usually <=, requirements >=, exact balances =.
Running example: maximise Z = 3x + 5y with x <= 4, 2y <= 12, 3x + 2y <= 18, x, y >= 0; the plan (2, 6) earns 36.
Ratio constraints like protein share >= 20% become linear after multiplying by the positive total.
The call-centre shift model needs at least 26 agents, and three disjoint constraints prove it.
LP assumes proportionality, additivity, divisibility and certainty; when these fail use IP, NLP or sensitivity analysis.
Matrix form: maximise c^T x subject to A x <= b, x >= 0.
lessons.tip: Before writing any equation, draw a small table: activities as columns, resources as rows, usage per unit in the cells, availability on the right, profit or cost at the bottom. The LP almost writes itself from that table.
lessons.task: A bakery in Mirpur makes cakes and loaves. A cake earns 80 taka and needs 0.5 kg flour and 20 minutes of oven time; a loaf earns 30 taka and needs 0.3 kg flour and 10 minutes. There are 40 kg of flour and 16 hours of oven time a day, and at least 20 loaves must be made for a regular customer. Write the full LP with variable definitions, units and non-negativity. Then check whether the plan of 30 cakes and 60 loaves is feasible.

quiz.q: In the garments LP (max 3x + 5y, x <= 4, 2y <= 12, 3x + 2y <= 18), how much finishing time does the plan x = 2, y = 6 use?
quiz.explain: Finishing uses 3x + 2y = 3(2) + 2(6) = 6 + 12 = 18 hours, exactly the 18 available.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a linear constraint?
quiz.explain: x times y multiplies two variables, so it is nonlinear; the others only add variables times constants.

quiz.q: A story says protein must be at least 20% of a bag whose weight x + y is a variable. Which is the correct linear form?
quiz.explain: Multiplying the ratio (0.09x + 0.44y)/(x + y) >= 0.20 by the positive total x + y keeps the direction and makes it linear.

quiz.q: Which LP assumption is broken if you cannot make half a truck?
quiz.explain: Divisibility assumes variables can be fractional; whole-number needs call for integer programming.

quiz.q: Why do we add x >= 0 and y >= 0?
options: Because negative production makes no sense
Because the simplex needs integer values
quiz.explain: You cannot produce a negative number of items, and forgetting these conditions can give meaningless answers.

lessons.title: The Graphical Method
lessons.content:
Think of a field in your village with fences on some sides. You are allowed to stand anywhere inside the fences, and you want to stand at the spot that is highest above sea level. If the ground slopes evenly in one direction, like a tilted plate, where would the highest spot be? Not in the middle. It would be pushed against the fences, at one of the corners. That picture is the whole idea of the graphical method for linear programs. The fences are the constraints, the field is the set of allowed plans, the tilt is the objective, and the best plan sits at a corner.

What it is: The graphical method solves a linear program with two decision variables by drawing it on an x-y graph. It only works for two variables (three if you are very good at drawing in 3D), so real problems need the simplex method. But it is worth learning carefully because it shows, with your own eyes, every idea the simplex method uses: feasible region, corner points, binding constraints, and the special cases like unbounded or infeasible problems.

Step 1, turn each constraint into a line: Take a constraint like 3x + 2y <= 18. Replace the <= with = to get the boundary line 3x + 2y = 18. The easiest way to draw it is to find where it meets the axes. Put x = 0: 2y = 18, so y = 9; that gives the point (0, 9). Put y = 0: 3x = 18, so x = 6; that gives (6, 0). Join these two points with a straight line. Constraints like x <= 4 are vertical lines at x = 4, and 2y <= 12 means y <= 6, a horizontal line at y = 6.

Step 2, pick the correct side: Each line splits the plane into two halves, and the inequality keeps one half. Test the origin (0, 0) if the line does not pass through it. For 3x + 2y <= 18: 3(0) + 2(0) = 0, and 0 <= 18 is true, so the side containing the origin is allowed. For a constraint like 2x + y >= 10: 0 >= 10 is false, so the allowed side is the one away from the origin. Shade or arrow the allowed side of every line. Non-negativity x >= 0 and y >= 0 keep us in the top-right quarter of the graph.

Step 3, find the feasible region: The feasible region is the area that is on the allowed side of every constraint at once. Every point inside it is a plan that breaks no rule. For our garments factory (maximise Z = 3x + 5y with x <= 4, 2y <= 12, 3x + 2y <= 18, x, y >= 0), the region is a five-sided shape with corners at (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 3), (2, 6) and (0, 6). For an LP, the feasible region is always convex: if you pick any two points in it and join them with a straight line, the whole line stays inside. No dents, no holes.

Finding corner points exactly: Corners are where two boundary lines cross, so solve the two equations together. The corner (4, 3) is where x = 4 meets 3x + 2y = 18: substitute x = 4 to get 12 + 2y = 18, so y = 3. The corner (2, 6) is where y = 6 meets 3x + 2y = 18: 3x + 12 = 18, so x = 2. Never read corners off a rough sketch; the drawing tells you which lines meet, but the algebra gives the exact numbers.

Step 4, method A, corner point enumeration: The fundamental theorem of linear programming says that if an LP has an optimal solution, at least one corner point of the feasible region is optimal. So evaluate Z at every corner. Z(0, 0) = 0. Z(4, 0) = 12. Z(4, 3) = 12 + 15 = 27. Z(2, 6) = 6 + 30 = 36. Z(0, 6) = 30. The largest is 36 at (2, 6). The factory should make 2 batches of shirts and 6 batches of jackets for a profit of 36 thousand taka a day. That matches the plan we checked by hand in lesson 02, and now we know it is the best.

Step 4, method B, the iso-profit line: An iso-profit line is a line on which every point gives the same profit. For Z = 3x + 5y, draw 3x + 5y = 15, which passes through (5, 0) and (0, 3). Every point on it earns 15. Now slide this line parallel to itself, away from the origin, because moving away increases Z. Keep sliding until it is just about to leave the feasible region. The last point it touches is the optimum, here (2, 6). For minimisation you slide toward the origin instead, and the line is called an iso-cost line. This method is faster when there are many corners, and it shows why the answer is a corner: a sliding straight edge always last touches a corner or a whole edge.

Binding and non-binding constraints: At the optimum (2, 6), check how much of each resource is used. Line B: 2(6) = 12 of 12 hours, fully used. Finishing: 3(2) + 2(6) = 18 of 18, fully used. Line A: 2 of 4 hours, with 2 hours left over. Constraints that are exactly satisfied at the optimum are called binding (or tight); here Line B and finishing. Line A is non-binding, with a slack of 2 hours. This tells the manager something valuable: buying more Line A time is useless, but more finishing time or Line B time could raise profit. Lesson 07 will put an exact price on that.

A minimisation example: A dairy farmer mixes two feeds. Feed X costs 40 taka per kg and feed Y 30 taka per kg. The cow needs at least 10 units of protein and 15 units of energy a day. Each kg of X gives 2 units of protein and 1 unit of energy; each kg of Y gives 1 unit of protein and 3 units of energy. Minimise C = 40x + 30y subject to 2x + y >= 10, x + 3y >= 15, x, y >= 0. The feasible region is above both lines and is open toward the top right, which is fine because we are minimising.

Solving the minimisation: The corners are where the region touches the axes and where the two lines cross. 2x + y = 10 meets the y-axis at (0, 10). x + 3y = 15 meets the x-axis at (15, 0). The crossing: from the first, y = 10 - 2x; substitute into the second: x + 30 - 6x = 15, so x = 3 and y = 4. Costs: C(0, 10) = 300, C(3, 4) = 120 + 120 = 240, C(15, 0) = 600. The cheapest is 3 kg of X and 4 kg of Y for 240 taka a day. Check: protein 2(3) + 4 = 10, energy 3 + 12 = 15, both exactly met.

Special case 1, infeasible: Sometimes the constraints contradict each other, like x + y <= 4 and x + y >= 6. No point can satisfy both, so the feasible region is empty and the LP has no solution at all. In real life this means the requirements are impossible with the resources given; the fix is not mathematical, it is a conversation with the manager about which rule to relax.

Special case 2, unbounded: Maximise Z = x + y subject to x - y <= 2, x, y >= 0. The region stretches forever upward: (0, 100), (0, 1000) and so on are all feasible, and Z grows without limit. An unbounded LP almost always means you forgot a constraint, like a market limit or a resource. No real factory makes infinite profit. Note that an unbounded region does not always mean an unbounded LP; the feed problem above has an open region but a finite minimum.

Special case 3, alternative optima: If the objective line is parallel to a binding constraint, the best value is reached along a whole edge, not just one corner. Change the factory's objective to Z = 3x + 2y. Then Z(4, 3) = 12 + 6 = 18 and Z(2, 6) = 6 + 12 = 18: both corners tie, and every point on the edge between them, like (3, 4.5), also gives 18. The manager gets a choice of equally good plans and can pick using some other reason, like fewer jacket batches if jackets are harder to ship.

Special case 4, redundant constraints: A constraint that does not touch the feasible region at all, like x + y <= 20 in the factory problem, is redundant: the other constraints already keep x + y at most 8. Removing it changes nothing. Redundant constraints are harmless but they make models bigger, and in the simplex method they can cause degeneracy (lesson 06).

Why the optimum is at a corner: Here is the intuition. The objective is linear, so moving in any straight direction changes Z at a constant rate. If you are at an interior point, you can move in the direction that increases Z until you hit a boundary. On the boundary, you can slide along the edge in the improving direction until you hit a corner. At a corner you might stop. So you never need to look inside the region or in the middle of edges; checking corners is enough. This is exactly what the simplex method exploits.

Real-life example 1, the tea stall from lesson 01: Maximise 10p + 15m with p + 2m <= 100 (sugar) and p + m <= 70 (cups). The lines meet where p + 2m = 100 and p + m = 70; subtracting gives m = 30, then p = 40. Corners: (0, 0) gives 0, (70, 0) gives 700, (40, 30) gives 400 + 450 = 850, (0, 50) gives 750. So 40 plain and 30 milk teas earn the most, 850 taka. Both sugar and cups are binding, so the owner should know that more sugar alone or more cups alone will help only partly.

Real-life example 2, an advertising budget: A new mobile shop in Rajshahi has 60,000 taka for ads on Facebook (x thousand taka) and a local FM radio (y thousand taka). It wants to reach as many people as possible. Each thousand taka on Facebook reaches about 2,000 people, on radio 1,500. The radio station sells at least 10 thousand taka of slots, and the owner wants Facebook to be at most twice radio. Constraints: x + y <= 60, y >= 10, x <= 2y. Drawing these gives a four-cornered region, and the corner where x = 2y meets x + y = 60, namely (40, 20), reaches 2,000(40) + 1,500(20) = 110,000 people, more than any other corner. A two-variable picture makes the reasoning easy to explain to the owner.

Common mistakes: Shading the wrong side of a line, especially for >= constraints; always test a point. Reading corner values off the drawing instead of solving equations. Forgetting the axes as boundaries. Thinking the optimum can be strictly inside the region; for an LP it cannot be only there. Calling a problem unbounded just because the region is open, without checking the objective direction. Missing alternative optima when the objective is parallel to a binding edge.

What exams ask: Solve a two-variable LP graphically, show the feasible region, list corner points, state the optimum and optimal value, identify binding constraints and slack, and recognise special cases (infeasible, unbounded, alternative optima, redundant). Some questions give a small region and ask why the optimum is at a vertex, or ask you to find the range of a profit coefficient that keeps the same corner optimal, which is a preview of sensitivity analysis.

Recap: Draw each constraint as a line, shade the allowed side, and the overlap is the convex feasible region. The optimum of an LP is at a corner, found by checking all corners or by sliding an iso-profit line. At the optimum, binding constraints are fully used and non-binding ones have slack. Watch for infeasible, unbounded, alternative optimum and redundant cases. For our factory the best plan is (2, 6) with Z = 36. With more than two variables we cannot draw, so in lesson 04 we turn the LP into equations that a computer can walk through corner by corner.
key_points: Draw each constraint as a line, test a point to choose the allowed side; the overlap is the feasible region.
The feasible region of an LP is convex, and an optimum (if one exists) occurs at a corner point.
Find corners exactly by solving pairs of boundary equations, not by reading the sketch.
Iso-profit lines slide away from the origin for max, toward it for min; the last touch is optimal.
Binding constraints are fully used at the optimum; non-binding ones have slack (Line A has 2 spare hours).
Special cases: infeasible (empty region), unbounded (Z grows forever), alternative optima (objective parallel to a binding edge), redundant constraints.
Feed example: minimise 40x + 30y with 2x + y >= 10, x + 3y >= 15 gives (3, 4) at 240 taka.
lessons.tip: Use graph paper and a ruler, and always label each line with its constraint. Then check every corner by algebra. Neat drawings earn marks, but exact algebra earns the answer.
lessons.task: On graph paper, solve: maximise Z = 4x + 3y subject to x + y <= 8, 2x + y <= 10, x, y >= 0. Draw the region, find all corners by solving equations, evaluate Z at each, and name the binding constraints at the optimum. Then change the objective to Z = 2x + 2y and see what special case appears.

quiz.q: For max Z = 3x + 5y with x <= 4, 2y <= 12, 3x + 2y <= 18, x, y >= 0, what is the value of Z at the corner (4, 3)?
At the optimum (2, 6) of that problem, which constraint is non-binding?
quiz.explain: x = 2 uses only 2 of 4 hours on Line A, leaving slack of 2; the other two are used fully.

quiz.q: What does an empty feasible region mean?
options: The optimum is at the origin
quiz.explain: If no point satisfies all constraints at once, the LP has no feasible solution.

quiz.q: When does an LP have alternative optimal solutions?
options: When there are only two variables
When the objective line is parallel to a binding edge of the optimal face
quiz.explain: Then the iso-profit line touches a whole edge at the best value, so every point on that edge is optimal.

quiz.q: For min C = 40x + 30y with 2x + y >= 10, x + 3y >= 15, x, y >= 0, what is the minimum cost?
quiz.explain: The corners (0, 10), (3, 4), (15, 0) cost 300, 240 and 600, so the minimum is 240 at (3, 4).

lessons.title: Standard Form and Basic Solutions
lessons.content:
Computers are great at solving equations but bad at looking at pictures. In lesson 03 we found the best corner by drawing, but a real LP with 200 variables cannot be drawn. So we need a way to describe corners using only equations, so that a computer can jump from one corner to the next. This lesson builds that bridge. We first rewrite every LP in one tidy shape called standard form, then learn that every corner of the feasible region is a special solution of those equations, called a basic feasible solution. Once you understand this, the simplex method in lesson 05 is just careful bookkeeping.

Why one standard shape: Real LPs come in many flavours: some maximise, some minimise, some have <=, some >=, some =, and some variables can be negative. If an algorithm had to handle every flavour separately, it would be messy and error-prone. So we convert everything into one form first. Different textbooks use slightly different standard forms; in this course we use: maximise (or minimise) the objective, every constraint is an equation with a non-negative right-hand side, and every variable is non-negative.

Slack variables: A <= constraint says the left side is at most the right side. The difference is the unused amount, and we give it a name. For Line A in the garments factory, x <= 4 becomes x + s1 = 4 with s1 >= 0. If x = 2, then s1 = 2: two hours of Line A are left over. So a slack variable is literally the leftover resource. Doing this for all three constraints: x + s1 = 4, 2y + s2 = 12, 3x + 2y + s3 = 18, with x, y, s1, s2, s3 >= 0. Slack variables earn nothing, so the objective becomes Z = 3x + 5y + 0s1 + 0s2 + 0s3.

Surplus variables: A >= constraint says the left side is at least the right side, so the extra is the amount by which we exceed the requirement. In the feed problem of lesson 03, 2x + y >= 10 becomes 2x + y - e1 = 10 with e1 >= 0. If x = 3 and y = 4, then 6 + 4 - e1 = 10, so e1 = 0: protein is exactly at the minimum. If x = 5 and y = 4, e1 = 4: four units of protein more than needed. The surplus is subtracted because the left side is bigger than the right.

Negative right-hand sides: If a constraint looks like x - 3y <= -6, multiply both sides by -1 and flip the direction: -x + 3y >= 6. Now the right side is positive and you add a surplus. The rule is simple: multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses its direction. Standard form wants b >= 0 because the simplex method starts from a solution where the slacks equal the b's, and a negative slack would be infeasible.

Turning min into max and back: Minimising C is the same as maximising -C. The best plan is the same; only the sign of the value flips. For example, minimising C = 40x + 30y is the same as maximising -40x - 30y, and if the maximum of that is -240, the minimum cost is 240. Some textbooks run the simplex directly for minimisation with a reversed rule for choosing the entering variable; both ways give the same answer. Choose one and be consistent.

Free and negative variables: Sometimes a variable can really be negative, like a change in stock level or a temperature. Such a variable is called free or unrestricted. Standard form wants all variables >= 0, so we write a free variable as the difference of two non-negative ones: x = x' - x'' with x', x'' >= 0. If x = -3, we can use x' = 0 and x'' = 3. If a variable must be <= 0, substitute x = -x' with x' >= 0. These tricks keep the algorithm simple at the cost of one extra variable.

A full conversion example: Minimise C = 2x1 - x2 subject to x1 + x2 >= 3, x1 - x2 <= 5, x1 >= 0, x2 free. Step 1, replace x2 = x2' - x2''. Step 2, add surplus e1 to the first and slack s2 to the second. Step 3, if you prefer max, flip the objective. Result: maximise -2x1 + x2' - x2'' subject to x1 + x2' - x2'' - e1 = 3, x1 - x2' + x2'' + s2 = 5, all variables >= 0. Every LP, however strange, can be converted like this.

Counting equations and unknowns: After adding slacks, the garments LP has m = 3 equations and n = 5 variables (x, y, s1, s2, s3). With more unknowns than equations, there are infinitely many solutions. From Linear Algebra (deep-cse-2-5) you know that if you fix n - m = 2 of the variables, the remaining 3 equations in 3 unknowns usually have exactly one solution. The question is: which two do we fix, and to what value? The answer that matters for LP: fix them to zero.

Basic solutions: Choose m variables to be basic and set the other n - m to zero; the zero ones are called non-basic. Then solve the m equations for the basic variables. The result is a basic solution. If all basic variables also come out >= 0, it is a basic feasible solution (BFS). The set of basic variables is called the basis. In our example, picking basis {s1, s2, s3} means x = y = 0, and then s1 = 4, s2 = 12, s3 = 18. All non-negative, so it is a BFS: the factory makes nothing and all hours are unused. Geometrically, that is the corner (0, 0).

Listing all basic solutions for the garments LP: With n = 5 and m = 3, the number of ways to choose the basis is C(5, 3) = 10. Working them out: basis {x, y, s1} gives x = 2, y = 6, s1 = 2, which is the corner (2, 6), feasible. {x, y, s2} gives (4, 3) with s2 = 6, feasible. {x, s2, s3} gives (4, 0), feasible. {y, s1, s3} gives (0, 6), feasible. {s1, s2, s3} gives (0, 0), feasible. That is five feasible ones, exactly the five corners we drew in lesson 03.

The infeasible and impossible ones: Basis {x, y, s3} gives x = 4, y = 6 and s3 = -6, because 3(4) + 2(6) = 24 is more than 18; negative slack means it breaks finishing, so it is a basic solution but not feasible. Geometrically it is where the lines x = 4 and y = 6 cross, outside the region. Similarly {x, s1, s2} gives x = 6, s1 = -2 and {y, s1, s2} gives y = 9, s2 = -6, both infeasible. Two bases, {x, s1, s3} and {y, s2, s3}, have no solution at all: with y = 0 and s2 = 0 the second equation says 0 = 12, impossible. Those correspond to parallel lines that never meet.

The big theorem: Every corner (extreme point) of the feasible region corresponds to a basic feasible solution, and every basic feasible solution is a corner. Combine this with lesson 03's result that an optimum, if it exists, is at a corner, and you get: to solve an LP, it is enough to search among basic feasible solutions. Pictures are no longer needed; we only need algebra on a set of equations.

Why not just try every basis: With 5 variables and 3 equations, 10 bases is nothing. But a modest real LP with 100 decision variables and 50 constraints has 150 variables after adding slacks, and the number of bases is C(150, 50), about 2 x 10^40. Even checking a trillion per second would take far longer than the age of the universe. We need a smarter way: start at one BFS and only move to a neighbouring BFS that is better. That smarter way is the simplex method.

Adjacent basic feasible solutions: Two BFSs are adjacent (neighbours) if their bases differ in exactly one variable. For example, {s1, s2, s3} (the corner (0, 0)) and {y, s1, s3} (the corner (0, 6)) share s1 and s3; y entered the basis and s2 left. Geometrically, adjacent corners are joined by an edge of the feasible region. Moving between neighbours means one variable enters the basis and one leaves. That swap is called a pivot, and it is the single step the simplex method repeats.

Degenerate basic solutions: Sometimes a basic variable comes out exactly zero. Then more than n - m variables are zero, and the same corner can be described by more than one basis. This is called degeneracy. It happens when more lines than necessary pass through one corner, for example if we added a redundant constraint x + y <= 8 to the factory: it passes through (2, 6), so three lines meet there instead of two. Degeneracy is mostly harmless but can make the simplex method pivot without improving; lesson 06 explains how to handle it.

Real-life example 1, slack as information: A Narayanganj knitwear factory runs its LP every week. The manager does not only read the production plan; she reads the slack values. If dyeing has a slack of 0 hours and knitting a slack of 30 hours, she knows dyeing is the bottleneck. When a buyer asks for a rush order, she knows immediately which machine will cause trouble. In practice, slack and surplus values are as useful as the plan itself.

Real-life example 2, a free variable in cash planning: A small shop plans its bank balance over three months. The balance at the end of a month can be positive (savings) or negative (overdraft from the bank, which costs interest). In the LP, the balance is a free variable. The modeller writes balance = saving - overdraft, both non-negative, and puts an interest cost only on overdraft. The model then automatically prefers saving and only uses overdraft when forced. The free-variable trick has turned into a meaningful business split.

Common mistakes: Adding a slack to a >= constraint instead of subtracting a surplus. Forgetting to flip the inequality when multiplying by -1. Leaving a negative right-hand side. Thinking every basic solution is feasible; it is feasible only if all basic variables are >= 0. Counting the number of basic solutions as C(n, m) and forgetting that some of those are infeasible or do not exist. Mixing up the number of basic variables (always m, the number of equations) with the number of decision variables.

What exams ask: Convert a given LP to standard form, showing slack, surplus and free-variable substitutions. Find all basic solutions of a small system, classify each as feasible or infeasible and degenerate or not, and find the optimum by comparing the objective at the feasible ones. Explain the relation between corner points and basic feasible solutions. State how many basic variables a system has (m) and the maximum number of basic solutions, C(n, m).

Recap: Standard form makes every constraint an equation with b >= 0 and every variable non-negative, using slack (leftover), surplus (excess), sign flips and the x = x' - x'' trick. With m equations and n variables, a basic solution sets n - m variables to zero and solves for the m basic ones; it is a BFS if they are non-negative. Every corner is a BFS and vice versa. For the garments LP, 5 of the 10 possible bases give the 5 corners. Since checking all bases is hopeless for big problems, lesson 05's simplex method walks from one BFS to a better neighbour until no neighbour is better.
key_points: Standard form: equations with non-negative right-hand sides and all variables >= 0.
Slack variables (added to <=) measure leftover resource; surplus variables (subtracted from >=) measure excess over a requirement.
Minimising C equals maximising -C; a free variable becomes x' - x'' with both parts >= 0.
With m equations and n variables, a basic solution sets n - m variables to zero and solves for m basic variables.
A basic feasible solution has all basic variables >= 0, and BFSs are exactly the corners of the feasible region.
Garments LP: C(5, 3) = 10 bases; 5 are feasible corners, 3 are infeasible, 2 have no solution.
Adjacent BFSs differ by one swap (one enters, one leaves): that pivot is the step simplex repeats.
Trying all bases is hopeless at scale: 150 variables and 50 equations give about 2 x 10^40 bases.
lessons.tip: When you add a slack or surplus, write one short sentence saying what it means in the story, like s3 = unused finishing hours. It turns abstract algebra into something you can check with common sense.
lessons.task: For the system x + y + s1 = 8, 2x + y + s2 = 10 with all variables >= 0, list all C(4, 2) = 6 bases. For each, set the other two variables to zero, solve, and mark it feasible or infeasible. Match each feasible one with a corner of the region you drew in lesson 03's task.

quiz.q: How is the constraint 2x + y >= 10 written in standard form?
quiz.explain: For a >= constraint we subtract a non-negative surplus variable to make it an equation.

quiz.q: The garments LP in standard form has 3 equations and 5 variables. How many variables are basic in each basic solution?
quiz.explain: The number of basic variables always equals the number of equations, m = 3; the other n - m = 2 are set to zero.

quiz.q: Basis {x, y, s3} gives x = 4, y = 6, s3 = -6. What is this solution?
options: A basic solution that is infeasible
quiz.explain: It solves the equations but s3 is negative, so it breaks the finishing constraint and lies outside the region.

quiz.q: How do you handle a variable x that may be positive or negative?
options: Replace it with x' - x'' where x', x'' >= 0
quiz.explain: Any real number can be written as the difference of two non-negative numbers, keeping standard form.

quiz.q: What is the geometric meaning of a basic feasible solution?
options: A point strictly inside the region
A corner point of the feasible region
quiz.explain: The extreme points of the feasible region are exactly the basic feasible solutions.

lessons.title: The Simplex Method
lessons.content:
Imagine you are standing on a hill in thick fog at night. You cannot see the top, but you can feel the ground under your feet. A simple rule will get you to the top of a smooth hill: feel which direction goes up most steeply, walk that way until the ground stops rising, then feel again. When no direction goes up, you are at the top. The simplex method works exactly like this, except that it walks along the edges of the feasible region, from corner to corner, and each step is a little algebra instead of a footstep. George Dantzig invented it in 1947, and it remains one of the most used algorithms in the world.

What it is: The simplex method is an algorithm that solves linear programs by starting at a basic feasible solution (a corner), checking whether any neighbouring corner gives a better objective, moving to the best-looking neighbour if so, and stopping when no neighbour improves. Lesson 04 showed that corners are basic feasible solutions and neighbours differ by swapping one basic variable. So each step of simplex is: choose a variable to enter the basis, choose one to leave, and update the equations. The whole thing is kept in a table called the simplex tableau.

Why it works: Because the feasible region is convex and the objective is linear, a corner that is at least as good as all its neighbours is the best corner overall. There are no false hilltops in an LP. So the simple local rule of "go to a better neighbour" is guaranteed to finish at the global optimum, as long as we do not go in circles (lesson 06 handles that).

Our problem again: Maximise Z = 3x + 5y subject to x <= 4, 2y <= 12, 3x + 2y <= 18, x, y >= 0. In standard form: x + s1 = 4, 2y + s2 = 12, 3x + 2y + s3 = 18. We also write the objective as an equation: Z - 3x - 5y = 0. This Z-row is how the tableau keeps track of the objective.

Step 1, the starting tableau: Start at the corner (0, 0), where the slacks are basic: s1 = 4, s2 = 12, s3 = 18, and x = y = 0. Write one row per basic variable, with columns x, y, s1, s2, s3 and the right-hand side (RHS). Row s1: 1, 0, 1, 0, 0 with RHS 4. Row s2: 0, 2, 0, 1, 0 with RHS 12. Row s3: 3, 2, 0, 0, 1 with RHS 18. Z-row: -3, -5, 0, 0, 0 with RHS 0. Notice that each basic variable has a column of the identity matrix: a 1 in its own row and 0 everywhere else, including the Z-row. That is what makes reading the current solution easy: each basic variable equals its row's RHS.

Step 2, the optimality test and entering variable: The Z-row numbers under the non-basic variables tell you what happens if that variable increases from zero. A negative number means Z goes up. Under x we have -3: each unit of x adds 3 to Z. Under y we have -5: each unit of y adds 5. If no Z-row number is negative, the current corner is optimal and we stop. Otherwise, the usual rule (Dantzig's rule) picks the most negative one. Here that is -5, so y enters the basis. The y column is called the pivot column.

Step 3, the minimum ratio test and leaving variable: How far can y increase? Every constraint row limits it. For each row with a positive number in the pivot column, divide the RHS by that number. Row s1 has 0 under y, so it does not limit y; skip it. Row s2: 12 / 2 = 6. Row s3: 18 / 2 = 9. The smallest ratio is 6, from row s2. That means when y reaches 6, s2 drops to zero, and any further increase would make s2 negative, which is infeasible. So s2 leaves the basis. The number at the crossing of the pivot column and pivot row, 2, is the pivot element.

Why only positive entries count: If the pivot column number in a row is zero, increasing y does not change that row's basic variable at all. If it is negative, increasing y actually increases that basic variable, so it never hits zero. Only positive entries create a limit. If no row has a positive entry in the pivot column, y can grow forever and Z goes to infinity: the LP is unbounded. That is how simplex detects unboundedness.

Step 4, pivoting: Now make the y column look like an identity column with the 1 in row s2's place, using row operations from Linear Algebra (deep-cse-2-5). First divide the pivot row by the pivot element 2: new row y is 0, 1, 0, 1/2, 0 with RHS 6. Then, for every other row, subtract a multiple of the new row so that its y entry becomes zero. Row s1 already has 0, so it stays. Row s3 has 2 under y, so subtract 2 times the new y row: 3, 0, 0, -1, 1 with RHS 18 - 12 = 6. The Z-row has -5, so add 5 times the new y row: -3, 0, 0, 5/2, 0 with RHS 0 + 30 = 30.

Reading the second tableau: The basis is now {s1, y, s3}. Reading the RHS: s1 = 4, y = 6, s3 = 6, and the non-basic x = s2 = 0. Z = 30. Geometrically we moved from (0, 0) to (0, 6), along the y-axis edge, and profit rose from 0 to 30. The finishing slack s3 = 6 means 6 hours of finishing are still free. Good: the tableau tells the same story as the picture.

Iteration 2, entering and leaving: The Z-row is -3, 0, 0, 5/2, 0. There is still a negative number, -3 under x, so x enters. Ratio test on the x column: row s1 has 1, ratio 4 / 1 = 4. Row y has 0, skip. Row s3 has 3, ratio 6 / 3 = 2. The smallest is 2, so s3 leaves, and the pivot element is 3.

Iteration 2, pivoting: Divide row s3 by 3 to make the new row x: 1, 0, 0, -1/3, 1/3 with RHS 2. Row s1 has 1 under x, so subtract the new x row: 0, 0, 1, 1/3, -1/3 with RHS 4 - 2 = 2. Row y has 0, unchanged: 0, 1, 0, 1/2, 0 with RHS 6. Z-row has -3, so add 3 times the new x row: 0, 0, 0, 5/2 - 1, 1, which is 0, 0, 0, 3/2, 1, with RHS 30 + 6 = 36.

The final tableau: Z-row: 0, 0, 0, 3/2, 1 with RHS 36. No negative numbers remain, so this is optimal. Reading off: x = 2, y = 6, s1 = 2, s2 = s3 = 0, Z = 36. Exactly the answer the graph gave in lesson 03, but found without any drawing. The path was (0, 0) with Z = 0, then (0, 6) with Z = 30, then (2, 6) with Z = 36: two pivots, three corners visited out of five.

Hidden treasure in the final Z-row: The numbers under the slack columns, 0 for s1, 3/2 for s2 and 1 for s3, are not random. They are the shadow prices: how much Z would rise if we had one more unit of that resource. One more Line B hour is worth 1.5 thousand taka, one more finishing hour 1 thousand taka, and one more Line A hour nothing, because Line A already has 2 spare hours. Lesson 07 on duality explains exactly why. For now, notice that the final tableau answers not only "what is the best plan?" but also "which resources are worth buying?".

Summary of the algorithm: 1. Put the LP in standard form with slacks and find a starting BFS (all slacks basic when all constraints are <= with b >= 0). 2. If no Z-row entry is negative, stop: optimal. 3. Choose the entering variable: most negative Z-row entry. 4. Ratio test: for rows with positive pivot-column entry, RHS divided by that entry; smallest ratio gives the leaving variable. If none are positive, the LP is unbounded. 5. Pivot: divide the pivot row by the pivot element, eliminate the pivot column from all other rows including Z. 6. Go back to step 2.

Minimisation with simplex: Two common approaches. You can maximise -C instead and use the same rules. Or you can keep minimising and flip the optimality rule: choose the most positive Z-row entry to enter, and stop when all entries are <= 0. Both give the same plan. Be careful that minimisation problems usually have >= constraints, which do not give an easy starting basis; lesson 06 introduces artificial variables to fix that.

How many steps does it take: In practice, simplex usually needs a number of pivots that is a small multiple of the number of constraints, which is why it solves LPs with thousands of constraints quickly. In theory, cleverly built examples can force it to visit an exponential number of corners; lesson 06 mentions this and the faster-in-theory alternatives. Modern solvers also use a matrix version called the revised simplex method, which avoids updating the whole table at each step.

Real-life example 1, a Dhaka furniture workshop: A workshop makes chairs, tables and shelves, with three variables and four constraints (wood, carpentry hours, polishing hours, a market limit on tables). It cannot be drawn, but the simplex tableau handles it the same way: start with all slacks basic, let the product with the most negative Z-row entry enter, ratio-test, pivot, repeat. After three pivots the owner learns to make no shelves at all, because they use too much polishing time for their profit, and the final Z-row shows that one more polishing hour is worth 400 taka. That number tells him whether hiring an extra polisher at 300 taka an hour pays off: it does.

Real-life example 2, an electricity dispatch decision: A power grid operator must decide how many megawatts each power plant produces in an hour to meet demand at the lowest fuel cost, while respecting each plant's maximum output and transmission line limits. This is a linear program with many variables, solved again and again through the day by simplex-based software. The shadow price of the demand constraint, read from the final tableau, is the cost of one more megawatt of demand in that hour, which is used in setting electricity prices in many markets.

Common mistakes: Choosing the leaving variable by the largest ratio instead of the smallest. Including rows with zero or negative pivot-column entries in the ratio test. Forgetting to update the Z-row during a pivot. Arithmetic slips with fractions; keep them as fractions, not rounded decimals. Reading the answer from the wrong column: decision variables that are non-basic are zero, even if their column has numbers in it. Stopping when the Z-row has a negative entry left.

What exams ask: Solve a two- or three-variable LP by simplex showing every tableau, entering and leaving variables, pivot element and ratios. Read the optimal solution, the value of slacks and the shadow prices from the final tableau. Explain why the ratio test uses the minimum and only positive entries. Explain how simplex detects optimality and unboundedness. Sometimes they ask you to match each tableau with the corner it represents on a graph.

Recap: Simplex walks from corner to better neighbouring corner. In each iteration: pick the most negative Z-row entry to enter, use the minimum ratio test (positive entries only) to pick the leaving variable, then pivot. Stop when the Z-row has no negative entries. For the garments LP it went (0, 0) to (0, 6) to (2, 6), finishing at Z = 36, and the final Z-row gives shadow prices 0, 1.5 and 1. Next, lesson 06 deals with what happens when the start is not easy or the walk gets strange.
key_points: Simplex moves from one basic feasible solution to a better adjacent one until no neighbour improves.
Optimality test (max): stop when no Z-row entry is negative.
Entering variable: most negative Z-row entry (Dantzig's rule).
Leaving variable: minimum ratio RHS / pivot-column entry over rows with positive entries; no positive entry means unbounded.
Pivot: divide the pivot row by the pivot element, then clear the pivot column in every other row including Z.
Garments LP: (0,0) Z=0 to (0,6) Z=30 to (2,6) Z=36 in two pivots.
Final Z-row under slacks gives shadow prices: 0, 3/2 and 1 for Line A, Line B and finishing.
For minimisation, maximise -C or flip the entering and stopping rules.
lessons.tip: Keep every tableau entry as a fraction and double-check each new row by plugging the current solution back into the original constraints. One arithmetic slip early ruins every tableau after it.
lessons.task: Solve by simplex: maximise Z = 10p + 15m subject to p + 2m <= 100 and p + m <= 70, p, m >= 0 (the tea stall). Write every tableau, the entering and leaving variables and the ratios. Check that you reach p = 40, m = 30, Z = 850, and read the two shadow prices from the final Z-row.

quiz.q: In the first garments tableau the Z-row is -3, -5, 0, 0, 0. Which variable enters?
quiz.explain: The most negative entry is -5 under y, so y enters (each unit of y adds 5 to Z).

quiz.q: With y entering, the ratios are row s1: none, row s2: 12/2, row s3: 18/2. Which variable leaves?
quiz.explain: The minimum ratio is 6 from row s2, so s2 hits zero first and leaves the basis.

quiz.q: When does simplex conclude an LP is unbounded?
options: When all Z-row entries are positive
When the entering column has no positive entry in any constraint row
When a slack variable is basic
quiz.explain: No positive entry means no constraint stops the entering variable, so Z can grow forever.

quiz.q: What is the final Z-row entry under s3 (finishing) in the garments LP, and what does it mean?
options: 3/2, the value of one more Line B hour
1, one more finishing hour adds 1 thousand taka to profit
quiz.explain: The final Z-row under a slack gives that resource's shadow price; finishing's is 1.

quiz.q: Why is the minimum ratio used in the ratio test?
options: To keep all basic variables non-negative after the pivot
To make the pivot element as large as possible
To maximise the objective in one step
quiz.explain: The smallest ratio is the first basic variable to hit zero; going further would make it negative and infeasible.

lessons.title: Artificial Variables and Special Cases in Simplex
lessons.content:
The simplex method in lesson 05 had an easy start: we stood at the origin, where all slacks were basic, and walked uphill. But what if the origin is not allowed? A cow that needs at least 10 units of protein cannot eat zero kg of feed. If the starting corner is not feasible, the walk cannot even begin. This lesson shows the trick that fixes the start, artificial variables, and then the strange things that can happen along the walk: infeasible problems, unbounded problems, ties, ties that cause going round in circles, and many equally good answers. Finally we peek at how fast simplex really is and what the alternatives are.

The starting problem: For a <= constraint with b >= 0, the slack gives a ready-made basic variable equal to b. For a >= constraint like 2x + y >= 10, standard form gives 2x + y - e1 = 10. If we set x = y = 0, then e1 = -10, which is negative and infeasible. For an = constraint like x + y = 100 there is no slack at all. In both cases there is no obvious variable with a +1 coefficient that can start in the basis.

Artificial variables: The fix is to add a temporary helper variable, called an artificial variable, to each >= and = row: 2x + y - e1 + a1 = 10. Now a1 = 10 is a valid starting basic variable. But a1 has no real meaning; it is like a scaffolding pole around a building under construction. Any solution where an artificial variable is still positive does not satisfy the original constraint. So we must push all artificial variables to zero before the answer counts. Two methods do this: the Big-M method and the two-phase method.

The Big-M method: Give each artificial variable a huge penalty M in the objective, so the algorithm hates keeping them. For a minimisation, add + M a1 + M a2 to the cost; for a maximisation, subtract M from the profit. M is not a specific number, just "bigger than anything else in the problem". The simplex method then naturally drives artificials out of the basis because they are so expensive. If at the end an artificial variable is still positive, the original problem is infeasible.

Big-M worked, setting up: Use the feed problem from lesson 03: minimise C = 40x + 30y subject to 2x + y >= 10, x + 3y >= 15. Standard form with artificials: 2x + y - e1 + a1 = 10 and x + 3y - e2 + a2 = 15. We maximise -C = -40x - 30y - M a1 - M a2. Writing the Z-row as Z + 40x + 30y + M a1 + M a2 = 0, the basic variables a1 and a2 do not yet have zeros in the Z-row, so we subtract M times each constraint row. The Z-row becomes: x: 40 - 3M, y: 30 - 4M, e1: M, e2: M, a1: 0, a2: 0, RHS: -25M.

Big-M worked, iteration 1: Since M is huge, the most negative entry is 30 - 4M under y, so y enters. Ratios: row a1 gives 10 / 1 = 10, row a2 gives 15 / 3 = 5. The minimum is 5, so a2 leaves: the first scaffolding pole is removed. After pivoting, y = 5, a1 = 5, and the x entry in the Z-row is 30 - (5/3)M, still very negative.

Big-M worked, iteration 2: x enters. Ratios: row a1 gives 5 / (5/3) = 3, row y gives 5 / (1/3) = 15. The minimum is 3, so a1 leaves. After pivoting, x = 3, y = 4, both artificials are out, and the Z-row is x: 0, y: 0, e1: 18, e2: 4, a1: M - 18, a2: M - 4, RHS: -240. No entry is negative, so we are optimal: -C = -240, so the minimum cost is 240 taka at x = 3, y = 4, exactly what the graph gave. The 18 and 4 under the surplus columns are again shadow prices: one more unit of required protein would cost 18 taka, one more unit of energy 4 taka. Check: 18 x 10 + 4 x 15 = 240.

The two-phase method: Big-M has a practical problem: computers do not like mixing a huge M with ordinary numbers, because rounding errors appear. The two-phase method avoids M. Phase 1: ignore the real objective and minimise the sum of artificial variables, W = a1 + a2. If the minimum W is 0, all artificials are zero and we have found a genuine basic feasible solution. If the minimum W is above 0, the original LP is infeasible; stop. Phase 2: drop the artificial columns, put back the real objective, and continue simplex from the feasible basis found in phase 1. Solvers use this idea.

Special case 1, infeasibility in the tableau: If Big-M ends with an artificial variable still basic at a positive value, or Phase 1 ends with W > 0, the LP has no feasible solution. For example, x + y <= 4 and x + y >= 6 together: the artificial for the second row can never be pushed below 2. The algorithm does not just fail; it tells you the minimum violation, which is useful when explaining to a manager how far the requirements are from possible.

Special case 2, unboundedness in the tableau: Maximise Z = x + y subject to x - y <= 2. After x enters (ratio 2 / 1 = 2), the tableau row is x - y + s1 = 2 and the Z-row is 0 under x, -2 under y, 1 under s1, with RHS 2. Now y enters, but its only entry in the constraint rows is -1. No positive entry means no ratio, so nothing stops y from growing: if y increases by t, then x = 2 + t stays feasible and Z = 2 + 2t grows forever. The LP is unbounded, and simplex reports it.

Special case 3, alternative optima in the tableau: Change the garments objective to Z = 3x + 2y. Simplex goes from (0, 0) to (4, 0) and then to (4, 3) with Z = 18. In the final Z-row, the non-basic slack s1 has a 0 entry. A zero under a non-basic variable means bringing it into the basis would change Z by zero per unit, so there is another corner just as good. Pivoting s1 in leads to (2, 6), also with Z = 18. Every point on the edge between them is optimal. In the tableau, the rule is: at optimality, a zero Z-row entry for a non-basic variable signals alternative optima.

Special case 4, degeneracy: Add the redundant constraint x + y <= 8 to the garments LP. In the second iteration, x enters and the ratio test gives row s1: 4, row s3: 6 / 3 = 2 and row s4: 2 / 1 = 2, a tie between s3 and s4. Whichever leaves, the other stays basic with value 0. A basic variable at zero is a degenerate BFS. It happens because three lines pass through the corner (2, 6). Degeneracy itself is harmless here: Z still reaches 36. But in the next iteration the ratio for that row could be 0, so simplex might pivot without moving, changing the basis but not the corner.

Cycling and Bland's rule: In rare degenerate cases, simplex can pivot through a sequence of bases at the same corner and come back to where it started, looping forever. This is called cycling. Real problems almost never cycle, but a guaranteed fix exists: Bland's rule. Number the variables; among all variables with a negative Z-row entry, choose the one with the smallest index to enter; among tied rows in the ratio test, choose the basic variable with the smallest index to leave. With Bland's rule, simplex always terminates. Solvers often use small random perturbations instead, which work well in practice.

Revised simplex: The tableau updates every number at every pivot, which wastes work when the matrix is large and mostly zeros. The revised simplex method stores only the basis inverse B^-1 (or a factorisation of B) and computes what it needs: the reduced costs to choose the entering variable, one column for the ratio test, and the new values of the basic variables, x_B = B^-1 b. The idea is identical; it is just smarter bookkeeping, and every serious LP solver uses a version of it.

How fast is simplex really: In practice, simplex is very fast. But in 1972 Victor Klee and George Minty built a family of LPs, squashed cubes, where Dantzig's rule visits all 2^n corners of an n-dimensional cube. With n = 50, that is about 10^15 pivots. So in the worst case, simplex is exponential. Later research on smoothed analysis (Spielman and Teng, around 2001) helped explain why such bad cases essentially never show up in real data.

Polynomial-time alternatives: In 1979 Leonid Khachiyan showed that LP can be solved in polynomial time using the ellipsoid method, a theoretical breakthrough that was too slow in practice. In 1984 Narendra Karmarkar introduced an interior-point method that is polynomial and also practical. Instead of walking along edges, interior-point methods move through the inside of the feasible region toward the optimum. Today's commercial solvers offer both simplex and interior-point methods, and pick based on the problem; for very large sparse LPs, interior point is often faster, while simplex is better for re-solving after small changes.

Real-life example 1, a minimum-order contract: A pharma distributor in Dhaka must deliver at least 500 cartons a week to a hospital chain (a >= constraint) and exactly 200 cartons to a government tender (an = constraint), while minimising transport cost. Neither constraint gives a free starting basis, so the solver adds artificial variables and runs a Phase 1. One week the warehouse stock is only 650 cartons. Phase 1 ends with W = 50: the solver reports that the requirements are 50 cartons more than possible. The manager now knows exactly how much to borrow from another warehouse.

Real-life example 2, an unbounded model in a startup: A new e-commerce team builds an LP to choose how much to spend on each ad channel, maximising expected sales. The solver returns "unbounded". The team is excited for a second, then realises they forgot the total budget constraint and the fact that each channel's audience is limited. Unboundedness is almost always a modelling error, and simplex is helpfully telling them exactly which variable can grow without limit.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to make the Z-row entries of artificial variables zero before the first iteration (subtract M times the rows). Treating M as a small number. Declaring optimality while an artificial is still basic and positive, which actually means infeasible. Confusing a tie in the ratio test (degeneracy) with a zero Z-row entry (alternative optima). Saying simplex is polynomial; it is not in the worst case, though it is fast in practice.

What exams ask: Solve a small LP with >= or = constraints by Big-M or two-phase, showing artificial variables. Identify infeasible, unbounded, alternative optimum and degenerate cases from a given tableau and explain the signs. State Bland's rule. Explain the difference between Big-M and two-phase. Short notes on revised simplex, Klee-Minty, ellipsoid and Karmarkar's interior-point method.

Recap: Artificial variables give a starting basis for >= and = constraints. Big-M penalises them heavily; two-phase first minimises their sum and then optimises the real objective. The feed LP solved by Big-M gives x = 3, y = 4, C = 240, with shadow prices 18 and 4. In the tableau, positive artificials at the end mean infeasible, a pivot column with no positive entry means unbounded, a zero reduced cost for a non-basic variable means alternative optima, and a zero basic variable means degeneracy, which Bland's rule makes safe. Simplex is exponential in the worst case but fast in practice; interior-point methods are polynomial. Next, lesson 07 reveals the twin of every LP: its dual.
key_points: >= and = constraints have no ready starting basic variable, so artificial variables are added temporarily.
Big-M gives artificials a huge penalty; two-phase first minimises the sum of artificials, then optimises the real objective.
Feed LP by Big-M: y enters (a2 leaves), x enters (a1 leaves), optimum x = 3, y = 4, C = 240; shadow prices 18 and 4.
An artificial left positive at the end (or Phase 1 W > 0) means the LP is infeasible.
No positive entry in the pivot column means unbounded; a zero reduced cost for a non-basic variable at optimum means alternative optima.
A tie in the ratio test gives a degenerate BFS (a basic variable at 0); Bland's rule prevents cycling.
Revised simplex keeps only B^-1 or a factorisation, which is how real solvers work.
Simplex is exponential in the worst case (Klee-Minty, 1972); ellipsoid (1979) and interior point (Karmarkar, 1984) are polynomial.
lessons.tip: When reading any final tableau, run a four-item checklist: any artificial still positive? any zero under a non-basic variable? any basic variable equal to zero? any column with no positive entry? Those four questions catch every special case.
lessons.task: Solve by Big-M or two-phase: minimise C = 3x + 2y subject to x + y >= 4, x + 3y >= 6, x, y >= 0. Show the artificial variables and every tableau. Then check your answer by drawing the region and testing the corners.

quiz.q: Why do we add artificial variables?
options: To provide a starting basic feasible solution for >= or = constraints
quiz.explain: Surplus variables enter with -1, so they cannot start in the basis; artificials give an initial basis.

quiz.q: Phase 1 of the two-phase method ends with W = 3 > 0. What does this mean?
