quiz.explain: If the artificials cannot all be driven to zero, no solution satisfies the original constraints.

quiz.q: At an optimal tableau, a non-basic variable has a 0 in the Z-row. What does it indicate?
quiz.explain: Bringing that variable in changes Z by zero, so another optimal corner exists.

quiz.q: What does a tie in the minimum ratio test lead to?
quiz.explain: One of the tied variables leaves; the other stays basic at value 0, which is degeneracy.

quiz.q: Which method first solved LP in polynomial time in practice-friendly form, in 1984?
quiz.explain: Khachiyan's ellipsoid method (1979) was polynomial but slow; Karmarkar's 1984 interior-point method was polynomial and practical.

lessons.title: Duality
lessons.content:
Every coin has two sides. The garments factory owner looks at her factory and asks, "how many shirts and jackets should I make to earn the most?" Now imagine a rich businessman who wants to rent the whole factory's machine hours for a day. He asks a different question: "what is the lowest rent per hour I can offer for each section so that the owner still agrees?" Surprisingly, these two questions have the same answer value. The owner's best profit equals the businessman's lowest acceptable rent. This mirror relationship is called duality, and every linear program has a twin problem, its dual.

What it is: Given an LP called the primal, the dual is another LP built from the same numbers, but turned sideways. If the primal maximises, the dual minimises. Each primal constraint becomes a dual variable, and each primal variable becomes a dual constraint. The right-hand sides of the primal become the objective coefficients of the dual, and the objective coefficients of the primal become the right-hand sides of the dual. The constraint matrix is transposed: rows become columns.

Why it matters: Duality is not just a mathematical curiosity. First, the dual's optimal variables are the shadow prices of the primal's resources: they tell a manager how much one more unit of each resource is worth. Second, the dual gives a certificate: if you find a primal plan and a dual price vector with the same objective value, both are proven optimal without any further search. Third, sometimes the dual is easier to solve, and the dual simplex method (lesson 08) uses this. Fourth, duality is the foundation of sensitivity analysis and of many algorithms in Advanced Algorithms (deep-cse-7-1).

Building the dual of the garments LP: Primal: maximise Z = 3x + 5y subject to x <= 4 (Line A), 2y <= 12 (Line B), 3x + 2y <= 18 (finishing), x, y >= 0. Give each constraint a dual variable: u1 for Line A, u2 for Line B, u3 for finishing. The dual is: minimise W = 4u1 + 12u2 + 18u3, subject to u1 + 3u3 >= 3 (from the x column: 1, 0, 3 and profit 3) and 2u2 + 2u3 >= 5 (from the y column: 0, 2, 2 and profit 5), with u1, u2, u3 >= 0.

Reading the dual as a story: u1, u2, u3 are rent prices per hour for Line A, Line B and finishing. A shirt batch uses 1 hour of Line A and 3 hours of finishing, so renting out those hours earns u1 + 3u3. The owner will only agree to rent instead of producing if that is at least the 3 thousand taka profit she would get from the batch: u1 + 3u3 >= 3. Similarly for jackets: 2u2 + 2u3 >= 5. The renter wants to pay as little total rent as possible for all 4 + 12 + 18 hours: minimise 4u1 + 12u2 + 18u3. That is exactly the dual.

Solving the dual: The optimal dual solution is u1 = 0, u2 = 3/2, u3 = 1, with W = 4(0) + 12(1.5) + 18(1) = 18 + 18 = 36. Check the constraints: u1 + 3u3 = 0 + 3 = 3 >= 3, and 2u2 + 2u3 = 3 + 2 = 5 >= 5, both satisfied exactly. And W = 36 equals the primal optimum Z = 36. Recall the final Z-row in lesson 05 had 0, 3/2 and 1 under s1, s2, s3: the dual solution was sitting in the primal's final tableau all along.

The conversion rules: For a maximisation primal with <= constraints and non-negative variables, the dual is a minimisation with >= constraints and non-negative variables; this pair is called the symmetric or canonical form. For other shapes, use this table. If a max primal has a >= constraint, its dual variable is <= 0. If it has an = constraint, its dual variable is free (any sign). If a primal variable is free, the matching dual constraint is an equation. If a primal variable is <= 0, the matching dual constraint flips direction. A safe exam strategy is to first rewrite the primal in canonical form (multiply >= rows by -1, split = into two inequalities) and then take the dual mechanically.

The dual of the dual is the primal: If you take the dual of the dual, you get back the original primal. So which one is called primal is just a matter of where you start. This also means every theorem works in both directions.

Weak duality: For a max primal and its min dual, the value of any feasible primal solution is at most the value of any feasible dual solution: Z <= W. Example: the primal plan (4, 3) is feasible with Z = 27. The dual point u = (3, 5/2, 0) is feasible, because 3 + 0 = 3 >= 3 and 5 + 0 = 5 >= 5, and has W = 12 + 30 = 42. Indeed 27 <= 42. Why? Multiply each primal constraint by its non-negative dual price and add; the dual constraints guarantee the left side is at least the primal objective. This gives a useful practical tool: any dual feasible solution gives an upper bound on how good the primal can possibly be.

Strong duality: If the primal has an optimal solution, so does the dual, and their optimal values are equal: Z* = W*. For the garments LP, both are 36. This is a deep theorem, and simplex proves it constructively: the final tableau's Z-row under the slacks is a dual feasible solution with the same value. Strong duality is what turns a pair of matching numbers into a certificate of optimality.

All possible outcomes: For a primal-dual pair, only certain combinations can happen. Both have optimal solutions with equal values. Or the primal is unbounded and the dual is infeasible (no upper bound can exist, so no feasible dual). Or the dual is unbounded and the primal infeasible. Or both are infeasible, which is rare but possible. It is impossible for both to be feasible while one is unbounded, because weak duality would then give a finite bound.

Complementary slackness: At optimality, for each constraint, either the constraint is tight or its dual price is zero (or both). And for each variable, either the variable is zero or its dual constraint is tight. In symbols: slack_i x u_i = 0 and x_j x (dual surplus_j) = 0. In the garments LP, Line A has slack 2 > 0, so u1 must be 0: an unused resource is worth nothing at the margin. Line B and finishing are tight, so their prices can be positive. x = 2 > 0 and y = 6 > 0, so both dual constraints must be tight, which we checked: 3 = 3 and 5 = 5.

Using complementary slackness to find the dual: Suppose someone tells you the primal optimum is (2, 6). You can find the dual without solving it. Line A has slack, so u1 = 0. x > 0, so u1 + 3u3 = 3, giving u3 = 1. y > 0, so 2u2 + 2u3 = 5, giving u2 = 3/2. Then check that W = 36 = Z. You have both solved the dual and proved (2, 6) optimal in a few lines. Exams love this.

Economic meaning, shadow prices: The optimal dual variable u_i is the rate at which the optimal objective changes when the right-hand side b_i increases by one unit, as long as the change is small enough that the same basis stays optimal. So one extra finishing hour raises the best profit by 1 thousand taka; one extra Line B hour by 1.5 thousand taka; one extra Line A hour by 0. If a contractor offers extra finishing hours at 800 taka an hour, accept; at 1,200 taka an hour, refuse. Lesson 08 shows how far b can change before these prices stop being valid.

Reduced costs and the dual: The Z-row entry under a decision variable in the final tableau is its reduced cost, which equals the dual constraint's surplus: the value of the resources a unit uses (priced at shadow prices) minus its profit. If a product's resources are worth more at shadow prices than the profit it brings, it should not be made. For x and y in the garments LP, the reduced costs are 0 because they are made and their dual constraints are tight.

The feed problem and its dual: Primal: minimise C = 40x + 30y subject to 2x + y >= 10 (protein) and x + 3y >= 15 (energy), x, y >= 0. Dual: maximise 10p + 15q subject to 2p + q <= 40 (feed X) and p + 3q <= 30 (feed Y), p, q >= 0. Story: a company sells pure protein and energy supplements and sets prices p and q per unit. Its prices must not make feed X or feed Y a cheaper way to get the same nutrients, otherwise the farmer would just buy feed. It wants to earn as much as possible from the 10 protein and 15 energy units. The optimum is p = 18, q = 4, earning 180 + 60 = 240, exactly the minimum feed cost. These are the shadow prices Big-M showed us in lesson 06.

Real-life example 1, a Chattogram port decision: The port authority models how to assign berths, cranes and yard space to ships to maximise containers handled per day. The dual prices tell them that one more crane-hour is worth, say, 40 extra containers, while one more square metre of yard is worth almost nothing because the yard is not a bottleneck. When the government considers buying new cranes versus expanding the yard, the dual prices point to cranes, before anyone spends money on a separate study.

Real-life example 2, electricity prices: In many electricity markets, the grid operator solves a large LP to dispatch power plants at minimum cost to meet demand at each location. The dual variable of the demand constraint at a location is the cost of serving one more megawatt there, called the locational marginal price. Customers in a congested area pay more because the dual price there is higher. Here duality is not a classroom idea; it literally sets the price of power.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to transpose: the dual constraint for x uses the x column, not a row. Getting the direction or sign wrong for >= or = constraints in a max primal. Writing the primal's objective coefficients as the dual's objective instead of its right-hand sides. Thinking a shadow price applies to any change in b, no matter how large. Saying a non-binding constraint can have a positive shadow price; complementary slackness forbids it.

What exams ask: Write the dual of a given LP, including mixed constraint types and free variables. State and prove weak duality. Verify optimality of a given pair using equal objective values. Use complementary slackness to find the dual solution from a primal one. Read shadow prices from a final tableau and interpret them in words. Explain the economic interpretation of the dual.

Recap: Every LP has a dual built by transposing: constraints become variables, variables become constraints, b and c swap roles, and max becomes min. Weak duality says any primal value is at most any dual value (for max primal); strong duality says the optimal values are equal. Complementary slackness links them: slack constraints have zero prices, and positive variables have tight dual constraints. The optimal dual variables are shadow prices, here 0, 1.5 and 1 thousand taka per hour. Next, lesson 08 asks how much the data can change before the plan and these prices change.
key_points: The dual swaps roles: primal constraints become dual variables, primal variables become dual constraints, b and c swap, max becomes min.
Garments dual: minimise 4u1 + 12u2 + 18u3 with u1 + 3u3 >= 3, 2u2 + 2u3 >= 5, u >= 0; optimum u = (0, 3/2, 1), W = 36.
Weak duality: any feasible primal Z <= any feasible dual W (e.g. 27 <= 42).
Strong duality: if one has an optimum, both do and Z* = W*.
Complementary slackness: slack constraint means zero price; positive variable means tight dual constraint.
Optimal dual variables are shadow prices: the gain from one more unit of each resource.
Primal unbounded implies dual infeasible, and vice versa; both infeasible is possible.
Feed dual: maximise 10p + 15q with 2p + q <= 40, p + 3q <= 30; optimum p = 18, q = 4, value 240.
lessons.tip: Write the primal's coefficients as a small grid with the objective on top and b on the right. The dual is that grid read sideways. Draw it, rotate your head, and you will never forget the transpose.
lessons.task: Write the dual of: maximise Z = 10p + 15m subject to p + 2m <= 100, p + m <= 70, p, m >= 0 (the tea stall). Use complementary slackness with the known optimum p = 40, m = 30 to find the dual prices, and check that the dual value equals 850. Explain in one sentence what each price means for the stall owner.

quiz.q: What is the dual objective of the garments LP (primal max 3x + 5y, x <= 4, 2y <= 12, 3x + 2y <= 18)?
quiz.explain: The primal right-hand sides 4, 12, 18 become the dual objective, and max becomes min.

quiz.q: A primal (max) feasible plan has Z = 27 and a dual feasible solution has W = 42. What does weak duality tell you?
options: The primal optimum is at most 42
quiz.explain: Any dual feasible value is an upper bound on every primal feasible value, including the optimum.

quiz.q: At the optimum, Line A has 2 unused hours. What must its dual price u1 be?
quiz.explain: By complementary slackness, a constraint with positive slack has a zero shadow price.

quiz.q: If the primal is unbounded, what can you say about the dual?
quiz.explain: A feasible dual would give a finite upper bound, contradicting unboundedness, so the dual must be infeasible.

quiz.q: What is the economic meaning of an optimal dual variable?
options: The marginal value of one more unit of a resource
quiz.explain: Optimal dual variables are shadow prices: how much the best objective improves per extra unit of that resource, within a range.

lessons.title: Sensitivity Analysis and the Dual Simplex Method
lessons.content:
Suppose you plan a picnic for Friday and decide to go to a park in Gazipur because it is the best choice. Then you hear the bus fare went up by 10 taka. Do you change the plan? Probably not; 10 taka is too small to matter. But if the fare doubled, maybe you would choose a closer park. Every plan has some room before small changes flip it. Sensitivity analysis is the OR tool that measures that room exactly: how much can each number in an LP change before the best plan changes, and what happens to the profit while it changes.

Why we need it: The numbers in an LP are almost never exact. Profits depend on market prices that move every week; machine hours depend on breakdowns; demand is a forecast. If a tiny change in one number completely changes the best plan, the manager should be nervous and gather better data. If the plan stays the same over a wide range, she can act with confidence. Sensitivity analysis also answers practical what-if questions without solving the LP again from scratch: should we buy more finishing hours, launch a new product, or accept a new rule?

Our final tableau: For the garments LP (maximise 3x + 5y with x <= 4, 2y <= 12, 3x + 2y <= 18), the final tableau has basis s1, y, x. Row s1: s1 + (1/3)s2 - (1/3)s3 = 2. Row y: y + (1/2)s2 = 6. Row x: x - (1/3)s2 + (1/3)s3 = 2. Z-row: Z + (3/2)s2 + 1 s3 = 36. The numbers under s1, s2, s3 in the constraint rows form B^-1, the inverse of the optimal basis matrix. Everything in this lesson is read from this one tableau.

Ranging an objective coefficient, graphically: The optimum (2, 6) is where Line B (y = 6, flat) meets finishing (3x + 2y = 18, slope -3/2). The objective line 3x + 5y has slope -3/5. As long as this slope stays between the slopes of those two lines, between 0 and -3/2, the corner (2, 6) stays optimal. With the shirt profit c1 and jacket profit 5, the slope is -c1/5, so we need 0 <= c1/5 <= 3/2, which gives 0 <= c1 <= 7.5. Shirt profit can fall to 0 or rise to 7.5 thousand taka per batch and the plan stays 2 shirts, 6 jackets.

Ranging an objective coefficient, with the tableau: x is basic in the x row. If c1 changes by d, the Z-row entries of the non-basic variables change by d times their entries in the x row, which are -1/3 for s2 and 1/3 for s3. So the new Z-row entries are 3/2 - d/3 and 1 + d/3. Optimality needs both >= 0: d <= 4.5 and d >= -3. So c1 = 3 + d is between 0 and 7.5, the same answer as the picture. For the jacket profit c2, using the y row (1/2 under s2, 0 under s3): 3/2 + d/2 >= 0 gives d >= -3, and no upper limit. So c2 >= 2: jackets can become as profitable as you like, and the plan stays.

Inside the range, what changes: Within the range, the plan (2, 6) stays, but the total profit changes. If shirt profit becomes 4 instead of 3, Z = 4(2) + 5(6) = 38. The shadow prices also change, because they depend on c. Outside the range, a different corner becomes optimal, and you must pivot to find it.

Non-basic variables and reduced cost: For a decision variable that is not produced (non-basic), the range is simpler: its profit can fall as much as you like, and it can rise until its reduced cost reaches zero. The reduced cost is how much the profit must improve before making it becomes worthwhile. This is why solver reports show a reduced cost for every variable that is zero in the plan.

Ranging a right-hand side: Now change a resource, like finishing hours b3 = 18 + d. The basic variables are x_B = B^-1 b, so each changes by d times the s3 column of B^-1: s1 = 2 - d/3, y = 6, x = 2 + d/3. For the basis to stay feasible all must stay >= 0: d <= 6 and d >= -6. So finishing hours between 12 and 24 keep the same basis, and within that range each extra hour adds exactly the shadow price of 1 thousand taka. For Line B, b2 = 12 + d: s1 = 2 + d/3, y = 6 + d/2, x = 2 - d/3, giving -6 <= d <= 6, so b2 between 6 and 18. For Line A, b1 = 4 + d: s1 = 2 + d, so b1 >= 2.

A worked what-if: The factory can rent 2 more finishing hours for 1,500 taka total. Is it worth it? b3 goes from 18 to 20, inside the range 12 to 24, so the shadow price 1 applies: profit rises by 2 x 1 = 2 thousand taka, to 38 thousand. The new plan: x = 2 + 2/3 = 8/3 batches, y = 6. Check: 3(8/3) + 2(6) = 8 + 12 = 20 and Z = 8 + 30 = 38. A 2,000 taka gain for 1,500 taka cost: rent them. If they offered 10 more hours, b3 = 28 is outside the range, so the shadow price no longer holds and the gain will be less than 10 thousand; re-solve.

Adding a new product, pricing out: The factory considers polo shirts: each batch uses 0 hours of Line A, 1 hour of Line B and 2 hours of finishing, and earns 4 thousand taka. Price its resources at the shadow prices: 0(0) + 1(1.5) + 2(1) = 3.5. The reduced cost is 3.5 - 4 = -0.5, negative in a max problem, so polos are worth making: each batch earns 0.5 more than the value of the resources it takes away. If the polo profit were only 3, the resources would be worth more than it earns, and you would skip it without re-solving. When it is worth it, add the column to the final tableau and continue simplex. Doing that here, the new optimum is y = 3 jackets, 6 polo batches and no shirts, with Z = 39.

Adding a new constraint: The packing section says it can only pack 7 batches a day: x + y <= 7. First check the current plan: 2 + 6 = 8 > 7, so it is violated. If the new constraint had been satisfied, nothing would change. Since it is violated, add it to the final tableau. Write s4 = 7 - x - y and substitute x and y from their rows: s4 = -1 + (1/6)s2 + (1/3)s3. The tableau is still optimal in the Z-row (no negative entries) but now infeasible (s4 = -1). That is exactly the situation the dual simplex method is designed for.

The dual simplex method: Ordinary simplex keeps feasibility and works toward optimality. Dual simplex does the opposite: it keeps optimality (no negative Z-row entries in a max problem) and works toward feasibility. Steps: 1. Choose the leaving variable: a basic variable with a negative value, usually the most negative. 2. In its row, look at the negative entries. For each, compute the ratio of the Z-row entry to the absolute value of that entry. 3. The smallest ratio picks the entering variable. 4. Pivot as usual. 5. Repeat until all basic variables are non-negative.

Dual simplex worked: The s4 row is s4 - (1/6)s2 - (1/3)s3 = -1. s4 leaves. Negative entries: -1/6 under s2 and -1/3 under s3. Ratios: (3/2) / (1/6) = 9 and 1 / (1/3) = 3. The smallest is 3, so s3 enters. Pivot: s3 = 3 + 3s4 - (1/2)s2 at s4 = s2 = 0 gives s3 = 3. Then x = 2 - (1/3)(3) = 1, y = 6, and Z = 36 - 1 x 3 = 33. Check: x + y = 7, finishing 3 + 12 = 15 <= 18, and Z = 3(1) + 5(6) = 33. The new rule costs 3 thousand taka a day, and the plan shifts to 1 shirt batch and 6 jacket batches.

Where dual simplex shines: It is used whenever you add constraints to an already solved LP: branch and bound for integer programs (lesson 12) adds a constraint at every node, and dual simplex re-optimises in a few pivots instead of starting over. It is also natural for minimisation problems with all >= constraints and positive costs, because the all-surplus start is optimal but infeasible, which avoids artificial variables entirely.

Changing several numbers at once, the 100% rule: The ranges above assume only one number changes. If several change together, a handy sufficient test is the 100% rule: for each change, compute what fraction it uses of its allowed increase or decrease, and add the fractions. If the total is at most 100%, the same basis stays optimal. If it is above 100%, the basis might or might not change; you have to check. For example, raising c1 by 1.5 (one third of its 4.5 allowance) and c2 by 1 (no limit, so 0%) totals about 33%, so (2, 6) remains optimal.

Reading a solver's sensitivity report: Excel Solver, PuLP and similar tools print a sensitivity report. For each variable: final value, reduced cost, objective coefficient, allowable increase and allowable decrease. For each constraint: final value, shadow price, right-hand side, allowable increase and allowable decrease. Every number in that report is exactly what we computed by hand in this lesson. For our LP, the finishing row would show shadow price 1, allowable increase 6 and allowable decrease 6.

Real-life example 1, a jute mill and the price of raw jute: A jute mill in Khulna runs an LP each month to decide how much yarn, sacking and carpet backing to produce. Raw jute prices swing with the harvest. The sensitivity report shows that the plan stays the same as long as sacking profit stays between 18 and 31 taka per kg. When a buyer offers a price that pushes it to 33, the manager knows before re-running anything that the mix will shift, and asks the planning team to re-solve.

Real-life example 2, a hospital adds a rule: A hospital's nurse-scheduling LP was solved and published. Then a new labour rule arrives: no nurse may work more than five night shifts per month. Rather than rebuild the whole schedule, the planner adds the constraint and runs dual simplex from the old optimal tableau. Only a few pivots are needed, and the report shows the rule costs the hospital the equivalent of 2 extra nurse-shifts a month, a number the management can discuss with the union.

Common mistakes: Applying a shadow price outside its range. Forgetting that changing an objective coefficient of a basic variable changes Z even when the plan does not change. Using ordinary simplex rules in dual simplex (in dual simplex you choose the leaving variable first). Choosing the entering variable in dual simplex from positive entries instead of negative ones. Assuming several simultaneous changes are safe just because each is within its own range; use the 100% rule.

What exams ask: Find the range of an objective coefficient for a basic and a non-basic variable. Find the range of a right-hand side and the new optimal value for a given change. Decide whether a new product is worth making by pricing out. Add a new constraint and re-optimise with dual simplex. Explain what an allowable increase and decrease mean on a solver report.

Recap: Sensitivity analysis measures how far the data can move before the optimal basis changes. Objective coefficient ranges keep the plan; for the garments LP, shirt profit 0 to 7.5 and jacket profit at least 2. Right-hand side ranges keep the shadow prices valid; finishing hours 12 to 24 with price 1. New products are tested by pricing out; new constraints are handled with the dual simplex method, which keeps optimality and restores feasibility. Our packing rule x + y <= 7 dropped profit from 36 to 33. Next, lesson 09 moves to a very common special LP: the transportation problem.
key_points: Sensitivity analysis asks how much each number can change before the optimal basis changes.
Garments LP: shirt profit range 0 to 7.5, jacket profit at least 2, keep the plan (2, 6).
RHS ranges: finishing 12 to 24, Line B 6 to 18, Line A at least 2; shadow prices are valid only inside these.
2 extra finishing hours raise profit by 2 thousand taka to 38, plan (8/3, 6).
Pricing out a new product: compare its profit with its resources valued at shadow prices (polo: 3.5 vs 4, so make it).
Dual simplex keeps optimality and restores feasibility: leaving variable first (negative value), then entering by minimum ratio over negative row entries.
Adding x + y <= 7 with dual simplex gives x = 1, y = 6, Z = 33.
The 100% rule: if the fractions of allowed changes add to at most 100%, the basis stays optimal.
lessons.tip: When you compute a range, always confirm it with one test value inside and one outside. Plugging in takes a minute and catches sign mistakes that cost full marks.
lessons.task: For the tea stall LP (maximise 10p + 15m, p + 2m <= 100, p + m <= 70), use the final tableau from lesson 05 to find the range of the milk-tea price that keeps p = 40, m = 30 optimal, and the range of sugar spoons over which the sugar shadow price of 5 taka holds. Then decide: is buying 10 extra spoons of sugar for 30 taka worth it?

quiz.q: For the garments LP, over what range of shirt profit c1 does the plan (2, 6) stay optimal?
quiz.explain: The Z-row conditions 3/2 - d/3 >= 0 and 1 + d/3 >= 0 give -3 <= d <= 4.5, so c1 is between 0 and 7.5.

quiz.q: Finishing hours rise from 18 to 20 (range 12 to 24, shadow price 1). What is the new optimal profit?
quiz.explain: The change is inside the range, so Z rises by 2 x 1 = 2, from 36 to 38.

quiz.q: A new product uses resources worth 3.5 at shadow prices and earns 3. What should you do?
options: Make it, because it earns money
Re-solve the whole LP from scratch
Raise its price to 3.5 and make it immediately
Do not make it; its resources are worth more elsewhere
quiz.explain: Its reduced cost is 3.5 - 3 = 0.5 > 0 in a max problem, so producing it would lower total profit.

quiz.q: In the dual simplex method, what is chosen first?
options: The leaving variable, a basic variable with negative value
The entering variable with the most negative Z-row entry
The pivot element with the largest value
quiz.explain: Dual simplex keeps optimality and fixes infeasibility, so it first picks a negative basic variable to leave.

quiz.q: After adding x + y <= 7 to the garments LP, what is the new optimum?
quiz.explain: Dual simplex brings s3 in, giving x = 1, y = 6, Z = 3 + 30 = 33; (0, 7) breaks Line B.

lessons.title: The Transportation Problem
lessons.content:
Every morning, trucks leave factories all over Bangladesh carrying cement, rice, soft drinks and garments to shops and depots. Each factory can only make so much, each depot needs a certain amount, and every road has its own cost per tonne. Sending everything from the nearest factory sounds smart but often fails: the nearest factory runs out, and the leftover demand ends up served from far away at a high price. The transportation problem asks: how much should each source send to each destination so that all demand is met, no source ships more than it has, and the total cost is as small as possible?

What it is: The transportation problem is a special linear program with m sources (factories, warehouses) and n destinations (shops, depots, cities). Source i has supply s_i, destination j has demand d_j, and sending one unit from i to j costs c_ij. The decision variables x_ij are the amounts shipped from i to j. It is an LP, so simplex could solve it, but its special shape allows a much faster and easier method that you can do by hand on a grid of numbers.

Why it deserves its own method: A problem with 3 sources and 4 destinations has 12 variables and 7 constraints. A real distribution network with 20 plants and 300 dealers has 6,000 variables. The ordinary simplex tableau would be huge and mostly zeros. The transportation method works directly on the m x n cost table, and every step is addition and subtraction. It also always gives whole-number answers when supplies and demands are whole numbers, which matters when you ship trucks or cartons.

The formulation: Minimise total cost Z = sum over all i and j of c_ij x_ij. Supply constraints: for each source i, the sum over j of x_ij = s_i (or <= s_i). Demand constraints: for each destination j, the sum over i of x_ij = d_j (or >= d_j). And all x_ij >= 0. Each variable appears in exactly one supply row and one demand row with coefficient 1. That special structure is why the method is so simple.

Our running example: A cement company has three plants, P1, P2 and P3, producing 50, 60 and 50 tonnes a day. Four dealers, D1 to D4, need 30, 40, 50 and 40 tonnes. Transport costs in hundred taka per tonne are: from P1 to D1 to D4: 8, 12, 6, 5. From P2: 13, 9, 3, 7. From P3: 10, 2, 11, 4. Total supply is 50 + 60 + 50 = 160 and total demand is 30 + 40 + 50 + 40 = 160, so the problem is balanced. We will find a starting plan with three methods and compare their costs.

Balanced and unbalanced problems: The standard method needs total supply to equal total demand. If supply is bigger, say 170 against 160, add a dummy destination with demand 10 and zero cost in every cell. Whatever goes to the dummy is simply left at the plant. If demand is bigger, add a dummy source with the missing supply and zero cost (or a penalty cost per unit of unmet demand, if the story gives one). Shipments from the dummy source are demand that will not be met. Always balance the problem first.

How many cells are used: A basic feasible solution of a balanced transportation problem has exactly m + n - 1 positive (basic) cells, not m + n. Why minus one? Because if all supply rows and all but one demand column are satisfied, the last column is automatically satisfied: one constraint is redundant. For our 3 x 4 problem, a basic solution uses 3 + 4 - 1 = 6 cells. If a method gives fewer, the solution is degenerate, and lesson 10 shows how to fix it with a tiny epsilon.

Method 1, northwest corner rule: Start at the top-left (northwest) cell and ship as much as possible: the smaller of the row's remaining supply and the column's remaining demand. Then move right if the column is satisfied, or down if the row is exhausted, and repeat. It ignores costs completely, so it is fast but usually expensive.

Northwest corner worked: Cell P1-D1: min(50, 30) = 30; D1 is done, P1 has 20 left; move right. P1-D2: min(20, 40) = 20; P1 is done, D2 needs 20 more; move down. P2-D2: min(60, 20) = 20; D2 done, P2 has 40 left; move right. P2-D3: min(40, 50) = 40; P2 done, D3 needs 10; move down. P3-D3: 10; D3 done, P3 has 40 left. P3-D4: 40. Six cells, good. Cost: 30 x 8 + 20 x 12 + 20 x 9 + 40 x 3 + 10 x 11 + 40 x 4 = 240 + 240 + 180 + 120 + 110 + 160 = 1,050 hundred taka, which is 105,000 taka a day.

Method 2, least cost method: Look at the whole table, find the cheapest cell, ship as much as possible there, cross out the satisfied row or column, and repeat with the cheapest remaining cell. It uses cost information, so it usually beats the northwest corner rule.

Least cost worked: The cheapest cell is P3-D2 at 2: ship min(50, 40) = 40; D2 is done, P3 has 10 left. Next cheapest is P2-D3 at 3: ship 50; D3 done, P2 has 10 left. Next P3-D4 at 4: ship 10; P3 done, D4 needs 30. Next P1-D4 at 5: ship 30; D4 done, P1 has 20 left. Cells P1-D3 at 6 and P2-D4 at 7 are in finished columns, so skip them. P1-D1 at 8: ship 20; P1 done, D1 needs 10. Finally P2-D1 at 13: ship 10. Cost: 40 x 2 + 50 x 3 + 10 x 4 + 30 x 5 + 20 x 8 + 10 x 13 = 80 + 150 + 40 + 150 + 160 + 130 = 710, or 71,000 taka. Much better than 105,000.

Why least cost is not perfect: Look at the last step. Because we greedily filled cheap cells first, P2 was forced to send 10 tonnes to D1 at the very expensive cost of 13. Being greedy early can trap you into an expensive move later. The next method looks ahead to avoid this.

Method 3, Vogel's approximation method (VAM): For every row and column, compute a penalty: the difference between its two smallest costs. The penalty says how much extra you will pay if you cannot use that row's or column's cheapest cell. Pick the row or column with the largest penalty, and ship as much as possible into its cheapest cell. Cross out what is satisfied, recompute the penalties for what remains, and repeat. VAM takes more work but very often gives an optimal or nearly optimal starting plan.

VAM worked, rounds 1 to 3: Row penalties: P1 has costs 8, 12, 6, 5, two smallest 5 and 6, penalty 1. P2: 3 and 7, penalty 4. P3: 2 and 4, penalty 2. Column penalties: D1: 8 and 10, penalty 2. D2: 2 and 9, penalty 7. D3: 3 and 6, penalty 3. D4: 4 and 5, penalty 1. The largest is 7 for D2, whose cheapest cell is P3-D2: ship 40. D2 is done. Round 2: P3's remaining costs are 10, 11, 4, so its penalty becomes 10 - 4 = 6, now the largest; its cheapest cell is P3-D4 at 4: ship 10 (all P3 has left). Round 3: remaining rows P1 and P2; column D1's penalty is 13 - 8 = 5, the largest; ship 30 into P1-D1.

VAM worked, rounds 4 to 6: Now P1 has 20 left and P2 has 60, with D3 needing 50 and D4 needing 30. Penalties: P1: 6 and 5, penalty 1; P2: 3 and 7, penalty 4; D3: 6 and 3, penalty 3; D4: 5 and 7, penalty 2. The largest is 4 for P2, cheapest cell P2-D3 at 3: ship 50. D3 done. Only D4 is left with 30 needed: P2 sends its last 10 and P1 sends 20. Final VAM plan: P1-D1 30, P1-D4 20, P2-D3 50, P2-D4 10, P3-D2 40, P3-D4 10. Cost: 240 + 100 + 150 + 70 + 80 + 40 = 680, or 68,000 taka. Six cells, non-degenerate.

Comparing the three: Northwest corner 105,000 taka, least cost 71,000 taka, VAM 68,000 taka a day. Over a year of about 300 working days, the difference between the northwest corner plan and VAM is 37,000 x 300, about 1.1 crore taka. In lesson 10 you will prove with the MODI method that 68,000 is actually the minimum for this problem, so here VAM found the optimum straight away. That does not always happen, but VAM is usually very close.

Real-life example 1, rice from northern districts: During Aman harvest, the government's food department buys rice from procurement centres in Dinajpur, Naogaon and Bogura and moves it to food warehouses in Dhaka, Chattogram, Sylhet and Khulna. Supplies at each centre and needs at each warehouse are known, and costs per tonne depend on distance and road or rail. Written as a transportation problem, the planners can see which routes to use and how much each centre should send. Even a few taka saved per tonne becomes a large sum over hundreds of thousands of tonnes.

Real-life example 2, a soft drinks distributor: A beverage company has bottling plants in Gazipur and Chattogram and 40 regional depots. In summer, demand exceeds supply, so the planner adds a dummy plant whose shipments represent shortages, with a penalty cost per crate equal to the lost profit. The solution shows which depots will be short and by how much, so marketing can avoid running promotions in areas that cannot be supplied.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to balance the problem with a dummy row or column before starting. Using the dummy's zero cost in least cost or VAM early and ending with silly allocations; some teachers prefer to give dummy cells the lowest priority. Computing VAM penalties as largest minus smallest instead of second smallest minus smallest. Not recomputing penalties after each allocation. Getting fewer than m + n - 1 cells and not noticing degeneracy. Mixing up rows (supply) and columns (demand).

What exams ask: Formulate a transportation problem as an LP. Balance an unbalanced problem. Find an initial basic feasible solution by northwest corner, least cost and VAM, with total costs, and comment on which is best. State why there are m + n - 1 basic cells. Often the same question continues with MODI to test optimality, which is lesson 10.

Recap: The transportation problem ships goods from m sources to n destinations at minimum cost, with supply and demand constraints. Balance it first using a dummy. A basic solution has m + n - 1 cells. Northwest corner ignores cost (105,000 taka here), least cost is greedy (71,000), and VAM uses penalties to look ahead (68,000). Next lesson, we test whether a plan is optimal and improve it if not.
key_points: Transportation problem: minimise sum c_ij x_ij with each source's shipments equal to supply and each destination's receipts equal to demand.
Balance first: add a dummy destination (extra supply) or dummy source (extra demand) with zero or penalty cost.
A basic feasible solution has m + n - 1 occupied cells; fewer means degeneracy.
Northwest corner ignores costs: 1,050 hundred taka for the cement example.
Least cost fills cheapest cells greedily: 710, but got trapped into a cost-13 cell at the end.
VAM uses penalties (second smallest minus smallest cost) to look ahead: 680, which turns out optimal.
Integer supplies and demands always give integer optimal shipments.
The gap between plans adds up: 37,000 taka a day is about 1.1 crore taka a year.
lessons.tip: Draw the cost table large, with supply on the right and demand at the bottom, and write each allocation in a circle inside its cell. Cross out finished rows and columns with a light pencil line so you can still read the costs later for MODI.
lessons.task: A rice mill owner has three godowns with 20, 30 and 25 tonnes and must supply four wholesalers needing 15, 25, 20 and 15 tonnes. Costs per tonne (hundred taka) are: godown 1: 3, 1, 7, 4; godown 2: 2, 6, 5, 9; godown 3: 8, 3, 3, 2. Check whether it is balanced and add a dummy if needed. Then find starting plans with northwest corner, least cost and VAM, and compare their costs.

quiz.q: How many occupied cells does a non-degenerate basic solution of a 3-source, 4-destination balanced problem have?
quiz.explain: A basic solution has m + n - 1 = 3 + 4 - 1 = 6 occupied cells.

quiz.q: Total supply is 170 tonnes and total demand is 160. What do you do?
options: Add a dummy source with 10 tonnes
Add a dummy destination needing 10 tonnes with zero cost
quiz.explain: Extra supply goes to a dummy destination; what is sent there simply stays at the plants.

quiz.q: In VAM, how is the penalty of a row computed?
options: Second smallest cost minus smallest cost
quiz.explain: The penalty is the extra cost of having to use the second-best cell instead of the best one.

quiz.q: Which initial method ignores costs entirely?
quiz.explain: Northwest corner just fills cells from the top-left, so it is quick but usually expensive.

quiz.q: For the cement example, what were the costs of the northwest corner, least cost and VAM plans (hundred taka)?
quiz.explain: Northwest corner 1,050, least cost 710 and VAM 680, which is also optimal.

lessons.title: Optimising Transportation: MODI and Stepping Stone
lessons.content:
You now have a shipping plan from lesson 09. But is it the cheapest possible? Imagine a cricket captain who has set the field. Before every over he asks, for each empty position, "if I moved one fielder here, would we save runs?" If the answer is no for every position, the field is as good as it gets. If one position would save runs, he moves a fielder there, and asks again. The MODI method does exactly this for a transportation plan: it checks every unused route, finds one that would lower the cost, shifts goods to it along a closed loop, and repeats until no unused route helps.

What we are testing: A transportation plan is basic feasible with m + n - 1 occupied cells. Each empty cell is a non-basic variable. If we start shipping one unit along an empty route, other shipments must adjust to keep all supplies and demands balanced. The net change in total cost from that one unit is the cell's opportunity cost (also called reduced cost or improvement index). If every empty cell has an opportunity cost >= 0, no change can lower the cost and the plan is optimal. If some cell has a negative opportunity cost, using it saves money.

Our starting plan: Take the least cost plan for the cement problem from lesson 09: P1-D1 20, P1-D4 30, P2-D1 10, P2-D3 50, P3-D2 40, P3-D4 10, with cost 710 hundred taka. Costs from P1 to D1 to D4 are 8, 12, 6, 5; from P2 are 13, 9, 3, 7; from P3 are 10, 2, 11, 4. Six occupied cells, which equals m + n - 1 = 6, so it is non-degenerate. Let's test it.

The MODI idea: MODI (modified distribution) gives each row i a number u_i and each column j a number v_j, chosen so that for every occupied cell, c_ij = u_i + v_j. You can think of u_i as a price for loading at plant i and v_j as a price for delivery at dealer j, set so that the used routes are exactly "fairly priced". Then for each empty cell, the opportunity cost is d_ij = c_ij - u_i - v_j: what the route really costs minus what the fair prices say it should cost. These u and v are exactly the dual variables of the transportation LP, so MODI is duality from lesson 07 in action.

Step 1, compute the potentials: There are m + n = 7 unknowns but only 6 equations, so set one of them freely; the usual choice is u1 = 0. Then: P1-D1 (cost 8) gives v1 = 8. P1-D4 (cost 5) gives v4 = 5. P2-D1 (cost 13) gives u2 = 13 - 8 = 5. P2-D3 (cost 3) gives v3 = 3 - 5 = -2. P3-D4 (cost 4) gives u3 = 4 - 5 = -1. P3-D2 (cost 2) gives v2 = 2 - (-1) = 3. Negative potentials are fine; they are just numbers.

Step 2, opportunity costs of empty cells: P1-D2: 12 - 0 - 3 = 9. P1-D3: 6 - 0 - (-2) = 8. P2-D2: 9 - 5 - 3 = 1. P2-D4: 7 - 5 - 5 = -3. P3-D1: 10 - (-1) - 8 = 3. P3-D3: 11 - (-1) - (-2) = 14. One is negative: P2-D4 at -3. Each tonne shipped on route P2-D4 would save 3 hundred taka. So the least cost plan is not optimal, and P2-D4 should enter.

Step 3, find the closed loop: Starting at the entering cell, draw a closed path that turns only at occupied cells, moving alternately along rows and columns. From P2-D4, go along row P2 to the occupied P2-D1, up column D1 to the occupied P1-D1, along row P1 to the occupied P1-D4, and down column D4 back to P2-D4. The loop is P2-D4, P2-D1, P1-D1, P1-D4. Mark the corners alternately plus and minus, starting with plus at the entering cell: P2-D4 plus, P2-D1 minus, P1-D1 plus, P1-D4 minus. Every row and column on the loop has one plus and one minus, so supplies and demands stay balanced.

Step 4, shift theta units: The amount we can move, theta, is the smallest allocation in a minus cell, because those decrease and cannot go negative. Minus cells are P2-D1 with 10 and P1-D4 with 30, so theta = 10. Add 10 to plus cells and subtract 10 from minus cells: P2-D4 becomes 10, P2-D1 becomes 0 and leaves the basis, P1-D1 becomes 30, P1-D4 becomes 20. New cost = 710 + theta x (opportunity cost) = 710 + 10 x (-3) = 680. Check by direct sum: 30 x 8 + 20 x 5 + 50 x 3 + 10 x 7 + 40 x 2 + 10 x 4 = 240 + 100 + 150 + 70 + 80 + 40 = 680.

Step 5, test again: New potentials with u1 = 0: v1 = 8, v4 = 5, u2 = 7 - 5 = 2 (from P2-D4), v3 = 3 - 2 = 1, u3 = 4 - 5 = -1, v2 = 2 + 1 = 3. Opportunity costs: P1-D2: 12 - 0 - 3 = 9. P1-D3: 6 - 0 - 1 = 5. P2-D1: 13 - 2 - 8 = 3. P2-D2: 9 - 2 - 3 = 4. P3-D1: 10 + 1 - 8 = 3. P3-D3: 11 + 1 - 1 = 11. All positive, so the plan is optimal: 68,000 taka a day. And since none is zero, it is the unique optimum. This is the same plan VAM found in lesson 09.

What if you start from the northwest corner: Starting from the northwest corner plan (cost 1,050), MODI needs three improvements: first route P3-D2 enters with opportunity cost -15 and the cost drops to 900, then P1-D4 enters and it drops to 720, then P2-D4 enters and it reaches 680. Same optimum, more work. A good starting method saves iterations; MODI guarantees you end at the optimum either way.

The stepping-stone method: An older method computes each empty cell's opportunity cost directly from its own loop instead of using potentials. For P2-D4 in the least cost plan, the loop P2-D4 plus, P2-D1 minus, P1-D1 plus, P1-D4 minus gives +7 - 13 + 8 - 5 = -3, the same as MODI. Stepping stone is easy to understand but needs one loop per empty cell, which is slow for big tables. MODI needs only one set of potentials and then one subtraction per cell, so it is the method of choice. Both use a loop to make the actual shift.

Degeneracy: If a plan has fewer than m + n - 1 occupied cells, you cannot compute all the potentials. This happens when a single allocation exhausts a row and a column at the same time. Example: supplies 30 and 20, demands 30, 10, 10. The northwest corner puts 30 in cell (1, 1), which finishes row 1 and column 1 together; then 10 and 10 go in (2, 2) and (2, 3). That is 3 cells, but m + n - 1 = 4. Fix: put a tiny amount epsilon (think of it as 0.0001, effectively zero) in one empty cell that does not form a closed loop with the occupied cells, for example (1, 2). Treat it as occupied when computing potentials, and drop it at the end. Degeneracy can also appear during MODI when two minus cells tie for theta; then one leaves and the other stays with zero, marked epsilon.

Alternative optima in transportation: If the final opportunity costs are all >= 0 but some empty cell has exactly 0, you can bring it in without changing the cost, giving another optimal plan. Managers like knowing this: if two plans cost the same, they can pick the one that uses fewer trucks or favours a reliable transporter.

Maximisation problems: Sometimes the table gives profit per unit instead of cost, and we want maximum total profit. Two common fixes: multiply every profit by -1 and minimise, or subtract every profit from the largest profit in the table to get an "opportunity loss" table and minimise that. Both give the same optimal plan. Then compute the total profit from the original profit table.

Prohibited routes: Sometimes a route cannot be used, for example a bridge is closed or a dealer refuses one transporter. Give that cell a cost of M, a very large number, just like the Big-M method in lesson 06. The method will avoid it unless the problem is impossible without it. If the final plan still uses an M cell, the problem has no feasible solution without that route.

Transshipment, briefly: In real networks, goods often pass through middle points, like a central warehouse or a river port, before reaching dealers. In a transshipment problem every node can both send and receive. It can be turned into an ordinary transportation problem by letting the middle nodes appear both as sources and as destinations, with a buffer amount equal to the total supply added to each. Lesson 14 shows a cleaner way: the minimum cost flow model, which covers transportation, transshipment and assignment as special cases.

Real-life example 1, garments export through two ports: A garments group ships finished cartons from four factories to Chattogram port and to Dhaka airport cargo. Port capacity per week is limited, and each factory-to-port route has a cost. After the planner finds a VAM plan, MODI shows that one route has an opportunity cost of -1,200 taka per container: sending more from the Ashulia factory to the airport and less to Chattogram saves money, because of the cheaper short road. Shifting 15 containers along the loop saves 18,000 taka a week.

Real-life example 2, relief goods after a flood: During a flood in the northeast, relief agencies move food packs from district stores to union distribution points. Some roads are under water, so those routes get cost M. The planner uses VAM and MODI to find the cheapest feasible plan that reaches all points. When MODI finds the final plan still needs an M route for one union, it signals that the union cannot be reached by road at all, so a boat must be arranged. The method not only optimises; it also detects impossibility.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that potentials need exactly m + n - 1 occupied cells. Calculating opportunity cost as u + v - c instead of c - u - v (or using the reverse sign convention inconsistently). Building a loop that turns at an empty cell. Taking theta from a plus cell instead of the smallest minus cell. Forgetting to remove the cell that becomes zero (or removing two when only one should leave). Stopping when an opportunity cost is still negative.

What exams ask: Starting from a given initial plan (often VAM), test optimality by MODI, find the entering cell, draw the loop, compute theta, update the plan and cost, and repeat until optimal. Handle a degenerate starting plan with epsilon. Convert a maximisation table. Explain why m + n - 1 cells are needed and how MODI potentials relate to the dual.

Recap: MODI sets u_i + v_j = c_ij on occupied cells (u1 = 0 to start), then computes d_ij = c_ij - u_i - v_j for every empty cell. If all are >= 0, the plan is optimal; otherwise the most negative cell enters, a plus-minus loop through occupied cells is drawn, and theta (the smallest minus allocation) is shifted. For the cement problem, the least cost plan improved from 710 to 680 in one step, the optimum. Use epsilon for degeneracy, M for prohibited routes, and negate or subtract from the maximum for profit tables. Next, lesson 11 solves an even more special case: the assignment problem.
key_points: MODI: choose u_i and v_j so that u_i + v_j = c_ij on every occupied cell, starting with u1 = 0.
Opportunity cost of an empty cell: d_ij = c_ij - u_i - v_j; all >= 0 means optimal.
Least cost plan: P2-D4 had d = 7 - 5 - 5 = -3, so it entered.
The new potentials give all positive opportunity costs, so 680 is the unique optimum.
MODI potentials are the dual variables of the transportation LP; stepping stone computes the same indices with one loop per cell.
Degenerate plans need epsilon in an independent empty cell; prohibited routes get cost M.
For maximisation, negate profits or subtract them from the largest profit, then minimise.
lessons.tip: After computing the potentials, check them on every occupied cell: u_i + v_j must equal the cost exactly. A single wrong potential makes every opportunity cost after it wrong, and this check takes seconds.
lessons.task: Take your VAM plan for the rice-mill task in lesson 09 (godowns 20, 30, 25; wholesalers 15, 25, 20, 15). Test it with MODI, writing u, v and every opportunity cost. If any is negative, draw the loop, shift theta, and repeat until optimal. Then verify the optimal cost by stepping stone for one empty cell.

quiz.q: In MODI, what condition defines the potentials u_i and v_j?
options: u_i + v_j = c_ij for every empty cell
u_i + v_j = c_ij for every occupied cell
quiz.explain: Potentials make every occupied (basic) route exactly fairly priced; empty cells are then compared with them.

quiz.q: With u2 = 5 and v4 = 5, what is the opportunity cost of empty cell P2-D4 whose cost is 7?
quiz.explain: d = c - u - v = 7 - 5 - 5 = -3, so using this route saves 3 per unit.

quiz.q: The minus cells on a loop hold 10 and 30 units. What is theta?
quiz.explain: Theta is the smallest allocation in a minus cell, so that no allocation becomes negative.

quiz.q: A 2 x 3 problem has only 3 occupied cells in its starting plan. What should you do?
options: Place epsilon in an independent empty cell to get m + n - 1 = 4
quiz.explain: Fewer than m + n - 1 cells means degeneracy; epsilon in a non-loop cell restores the count so potentials can be computed.

quiz.q: How do you handle a route that cannot be used?
options: Give it a cost of zero
Give it a very large cost M
quiz.explain: A huge cost M makes the method avoid that cell, just like the Big-M method in LP.

lessons.title: The Assignment Problem and the Hungarian Method
lessons.content:
A school is choosing four students to run four races on sports day: 100 metres, 200 metres, long jump and relay. Each student is good at different things, and each can only enter one event. The teacher wants to match students to events so the total time (or total score) is the best possible. Pairing people with jobs one to one shows up everywhere: riders to delivery zones, doctors to shifts, machines to orders, teachers to classes. It is called the assignment problem, and it has its own beautiful method, invented in 1955 by Harold Kuhn, who named it the Hungarian method in honour of the Hungarian mathematicians Denes Konig and Jeno Egervary whose earlier work it built on.

What it is: There are n workers and n jobs. Assigning worker i to job j costs c_ij (time, money or distance). Each worker gets exactly one job and each job gets exactly one worker. Find the assignment with the smallest total cost. As an LP: variables x_ij = 1 if worker i does job j, else 0. Minimise the sum of c_ij x_ij, subject to each row summing to 1 and each column summing to 1.

A special transportation problem: Look closely: that is exactly a transportation problem where every supply and every demand is 1. So you could use VAM and MODI. But every basic solution would have 2n - 1 basic cells while only n of them are 1 and the rest are 0, so it would be badly degenerate and MODI would crawl. The Hungarian method uses the special structure directly and is much faster by hand.

Why not try everything: With 4 workers, there are 4! = 24 possible assignments, easy to list. With 10 workers, 10! = 3,628,800. With 20, about 2.4 x 10^18. The Hungarian method needs a number of steps that grows roughly like n cubed, so 20 workers is trivial for it.

The key idea: If you subtract the same number from every cost in a row, the best assignment does not change, because every possible assignment uses exactly one cell from that row, so every total drops by the same amount. The same holds for columns. So we can subtract freely until many costs become zero, and then try to find an assignment using only zero cells. If we find one, it costs zero in the reduced table, which cannot be beaten since no reduced cost is negative, so it is optimal in the original table too.

Our example: Four delivery riders, A, B, C and D, must each take one zone: Mirpur, Dhanmondi, Gulshan and Uttara. Expected delivery times in minutes are: A: 19, 11, 23, 40. B: 12, 16, 20, 26. C: 29, 21, 39, 14. D: 20, 18, 39, 32. The company wants the smallest total time.

Step 1, row reduction: Subtract each row's smallest number from every number in that row. Row minimums are 11, 12, 14 and 18. New rows: A: 8, 0, 12, 29. B: 0, 4, 8, 14. C: 15, 7, 25, 0. D: 2, 0, 21, 14. Every row now has at least one zero.

Step 2, column reduction: Now subtract each column's smallest number from that column. Column minimums are 0, 0, 8 and 0 (only the Gulshan column has no zero yet). New table: A: 8, 0, 4, 29. B: 0, 4, 0, 14. C: 15, 7, 17, 0. D: 2, 0, 13, 14. Total subtracted so far: 11 + 12 + 14 + 18 + 8 = 63. This is a lower bound: no assignment can take less than 63 minutes.

Step 3, cover all zeros with the minimum number of lines: Draw the smallest number of horizontal and vertical lines that cover every zero. If that number equals n, an optimal assignment exists among the zeros. Here the zeros are at A-Dhanmondi, B-Mirpur, B-Gulshan, C-Uttara and D-Dhanmondi. Three lines are enough: one through row B, one through row C, and one down the Dhanmondi column. Three is less than 4, so we cannot yet assign.

How to find the minimum lines reliably: A practical rule: first assign zeros in rows that have only one zero, crossing out other zeros in the same column; then do the same for columns; repeat. Then mark rows with no assignment, mark columns having zeros in marked rows, mark rows having assignments in marked columns, and repeat until nothing new is marked. Draw lines through unmarked rows and marked columns. This gives the minimum number of lines, a fact guaranteed by Konig's theorem: the minimum number of lines equals the maximum number of independent zeros.

Step 4, adjust the table: Find the smallest number not covered by any line. Uncovered cells are in rows A and D and columns Mirpur, Gulshan and Uttara: 8, 4, 29, 2, 13, 14. The smallest is 2. Subtract 2 from every uncovered number, add 2 to every number at the crossing of two lines, and leave the other covered numbers unchanged. The crossings are B-Dhanmondi (4 becomes 6) and C-Dhanmondi (7 becomes 9). New table: A: 6, 0, 2, 27. B: 0, 6, 0, 14. C: 15, 9, 17, 0. D: 0, 0, 11, 12.

Why the adjustment is fair: Subtracting 2 from uncovered cells and adding 2 at crossings is the same as subtracting 2 from every uncovered row and adding 2 to every covered column. Those are legal row and column operations, so the best assignment is unchanged, but a new zero appears (here at D-Mirpur), and no number becomes negative because we subtracted the smallest uncovered value.

Step 5, cover again and assign: Now at least four lines are needed to cover all zeros, so an optimal assignment exists. Assign: row C has a single zero, at Uttara, so C goes to Uttara. Row A has a single zero, at Dhanmondi, so A goes to Dhanmondi; cross out D-Dhanmondi. Now row D's only remaining zero is Mirpur, so D goes to Mirpur; cross out B-Mirpur. B takes its remaining zero, Gulshan. Final assignment: A to Dhanmondi (11 minutes), B to Gulshan (20), C to Uttara (14), D to Mirpur (20). Total 11 + 20 + 14 + 20 = 65 minutes.

Checking the answer: The lower bound grew from 63 to 65 after the adjustment (2 subtracted from the 2 uncovered rows, 2 added back to 1 covered column: 63 + 2 x 2 - 2 x 1 = 65), and our assignment hits it exactly. Listing all 24 assignments confirms 65 is the unique minimum; the next best is 67. Notice the greedy idea, "give each rider the zone where they are fastest", fails here: A and D are both fastest in Dhanmondi, so one of them must give it up, and the method decides which one costs less to move.

Unbalanced problems: If there are more jobs than workers, say 3 riders and 4 zones, add a dummy rider with cost 0 for every zone. The zone assigned to the dummy is simply left unserved (or served later). If there are more workers than jobs, add a dummy job. Just like the transportation problem, always make the table square first.

Maximisation: If the table shows profits or scores and you want the largest total, convert it: subtract every number from the largest number in the table, then minimise. For example, if sales scores are 60, 75, 90 and the maximum is 90, they become 30, 15, 0. The best assignment for the new table is the best for the original. Then add up the original scores of the chosen cells.

Forbidden assignments: If a worker cannot do a job (a rider has no bike licence for the highway zone, a doctor is not trained for a ward), put a very large cost M in that cell. The method will avoid it. If the final assignment still uses an M, no valid assignment exists.

Assignment versus the travelling salesman: A delivery van visiting 4 shops once each and returning home looks like an assignment of "next shop" to each shop. But solving it as an assignment can give two separate small loops (shop 1 to 2 to 1, and shop 3 to 4 to 3) instead of one tour. Ruling out such subtours turns it into the travelling salesman problem, which is NP-hard (lesson 12 and lesson 24). So the assignment problem is easy, but its cousin the TSP is famously hard.

Why it always finishes and gives whole numbers: Each adjustment either raises the lower bound or creates new independent zeros, and the bound can never pass the true optimum, so the method must stop after a finite number of rounds. Also, even if you solved the assignment LP with simplex and allowed fractions like x = 0.5, the best corner would still be all 0s and 1s, because the constraint matrix has a special property called total unimodularity (lesson 14). So nobody ever gets half a job.

Real-life example 1, a ride sharing dispatch: Every few seconds, a ride sharing app in Dhaka has several waiting riders and several free drivers. It builds a table of pickup times and solves an assignment problem (often with more drivers than riders, so dummy riders are added). Matching globally, rather than giving each rider the nearest driver one by one, reduces total waiting time, because a driver who is nearest to two riders is given to the one who has no other good option.

Real-life example 2, exam invigilation: A university must assign 12 teachers to 12 exam halls for a morning session. Some teachers cannot climb stairs (forbidden for upper floors: cost M), and the cost of a pairing is the teacher's travel time from their department to the hall. A small Hungarian method run, or a spreadsheet solver, produces a fair assignment in seconds, and it can be re-run when a teacher calls in sick.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting column reduction after row reduction. Drawing more lines than necessary, or lines that miss a zero. Adding the smallest uncovered value to all covered cells instead of only the crossings. Not making the table square. Forgetting to convert a maximisation table. Exams ask you to solve a 4 x 4 or 5 x 5 assignment by the Hungarian method showing each step, handle unbalanced, maximisation or forbidden cells, and explain why the assignment problem is a special transportation problem and why it is degenerate.

Recap: The assignment problem matches n workers to n jobs one to one at minimum total cost. The Hungarian method: reduce rows, reduce columns, cover zeros with the fewest lines, and if fewer than n lines, subtract the smallest uncovered number from uncovered cells and add it at crossings; repeat until n lines are needed, then assign using zeros. For the riders, the optimum was A to Dhanmondi, B to Gulshan, C to Uttara and D to Mirpur, 65 minutes. Square the table with dummies, convert maximisation, and use M for forbidden pairs. Next, lesson 12 deals with variables that must be whole numbers in general.
key_points: Assignment: n workers to n jobs, one each, minimise total cost; it is a transportation problem with all supplies and demands 1.
Subtracting a constant from a row or column does not change the optimal assignment.
Hungarian steps: row reduction, column reduction, cover zeros with the fewest lines, adjust, assign.
If fewer than n lines cover the zeros, subtract the smallest uncovered value from uncovered cells and add it at line crossings.
Rider example: reductions total 63, adjustment by 2 gives 65; optimum A-Dhanmondi, B-Gulshan, C-Uttara, D-Mirpur = 65 minutes.
Unbalanced: add dummy row or column of zeros; maximisation: subtract every entry from the largest; forbidden: cost M.
Konig's theorem: the minimum number of covering lines equals the maximum number of independent zeros.
The TSP looks like assignment but forbids subtours, which makes it NP-hard.
lessons.tip: Write each new table fully rather than editing the old one, and next to it write the running total of everything you subtracted. That total is a lower bound, and your final assignment must cost exactly that much; if not, you made an arithmetic slip.
lessons.task: Five teachers must each take one of five subjects for a coaching centre. Make a 5 x 5 table of preparation hours (pick realistic numbers between 2 and 12). Solve it with the Hungarian method, showing every table and the lines drawn. Then change one teacher-subject pair to forbidden (cost M) and solve again to see what changes.

quiz.q: Why can we subtract the smallest number in a row from every entry of that row?
options: Every assignment uses exactly one cell of that row, so all totals drop equally
It makes the problem a maximisation
quiz.explain: Since each assignment takes one cell per row, the ranking of assignments does not change.

quiz.q: After reductions, the zeros can be covered by 3 lines in a 4 x 4 table. What next?
options: Adjust: subtract the smallest uncovered value from uncovered cells and add it at crossings
Start over with column reduction only
quiz.explain: Fewer lines than n means no complete zero assignment yet, so you adjust the table to create a new zero.

quiz.q: In the rider example, what was the smallest uncovered value used in the adjustment?
quiz.explain: Uncovered values were 8, 4, 29, 2, 13 and 14, so the minimum was 2.

quiz.q: You have 3 riders and 4 zones. What do you do?
options: Add a dummy rider with zero cost for every zone
quiz.explain: A dummy row makes the table square; the zone it gets is left unserved.

quiz.q: How do you convert a maximisation assignment table?
options: Divide every entry by the largest
Subtract every entry from the largest entry, then minimise
Add the largest entry to every cell
quiz.explain: Subtracting from the maximum turns large profits into small regrets, so minimising regret maximises profit.

lessons.title: Integer Programming
lessons.content:
You can buy 2.5 kg of rice, but you cannot buy 2.5 buses. You can run a machine for 3.7 hours, but you cannot open 3.7 bank branches. And some decisions are simply yes or no: build the bridge or not, hire this person or not. Linear programming assumes every variable can be a fraction (the divisibility assumption from lesson 02). When that assumption breaks, we need integer programming: linear programs in which some or all variables must be whole numbers. It sounds like a small change, but it turns an easy problem into one of the hardest in computer science.

What it is: An integer program (IP) is an LP with extra conditions that some variables must be integers. If all variables are integers, it is a pure integer program. If only some are, it is a mixed integer program (MIP or MILP). If the integer variables can only be 0 or 1, it is a binary or 0-1 integer program. Most real OR models in industry today are MIPs: continuous amounts (tonnes, hours) mixed with yes/no decisions (open a depot, start a machine).

Why not just round the LP answer: Rounding feels natural but can fail badly. Example: maximise Z = 21x + 11y subject to 7x + 4y <= 13, x, y >= 0 and integer. The LP optimum is x = 13/7, about 1.857, y = 0, with Z = 39. Round x up to 2: 7(2) = 14 > 13, infeasible. Round down to (1, 0): Z = 21. But the true integer optimum is (0, 3): 4(3) = 12 <= 13, Z = 33. It is nowhere near the rounded LP point. Rounding can give infeasible answers, or feasible answers far from optimal.

The LP relaxation: If you drop the integer conditions from an IP, you get its LP relaxation. Its feasible region contains every integer point, so for a maximisation, the relaxation's optimum is an upper bound on the IP's optimum. In the example, the relaxation gives 39 and the IP gives 33, so 33 <= 39. If the relaxation's optimum happens to be integer, it is also the IP optimum and you are done. This bound is the engine of the main solving method, branch and bound.

Modelling with binary variables, the knapsack: A rice-mill owner has 10 lakh taka and four possible upgrades: a dryer (cost 4 lakh, yearly gain 1.5 lakh), a husker (3 lakh, gain 1.2 lakh), solar panels (5 lakh, gain 1.6 lakh) and a truck (6 lakh, gain 2.0 lakh). Let x1 to x4 be 1 if the upgrade is bought and 0 if not. Maximise 1.5x1 + 1.2x2 + 1.6x3 + 2.0x4 subject to 4x1 + 3x2 + 5x3 + 6x4 <= 10, each x binary. This is the 0-1 knapsack problem, like packing the most valuable things into a bag with a weight limit.

Solving the knapsack and why greedy fails: The greedy idea is to buy in order of gain per lakh: husker 0.40, dryer 0.375, truck 0.333, solar 0.32. Buy husker (3) and dryer (4), total 7; the truck (6) and solar (5) no longer fit. Gain 2.7 lakh. But checking all 16 combinations shows the best is dryer plus truck: cost exactly 10, gain 3.5 lakh. The greedy choice wasted 3 lakh of budget. The LP relaxation would take husker, dryer and half a truck for a bound of 3.7, which tells us no plan can beat 3.7.

More binary tricks, fixed charge: A factory pays a setup cost of 50,000 taka if it runs a product line at all, plus a cost per unit. Let x be the units made and y a binary "line is running" variable. Cost = 50,000y + (unit cost)x, with the link x <= M y, where M is the most you could ever make. If y = 0, x must be 0. If y = 1, x can be anything up to M. The model will only pay the setup when it actually produces.

Either-or and if-then: Either-or: a machine can be used for job A (constraint 3x + 2y <= 18) or job B (x + 4y <= 16), but at least one must hold. Add a binary z: 3x + 2y <= 18 + M z and x + 4y <= 16 + M(1 - z). If z = 0 the first must hold; if z = 1 the second must. If-then: "if we open a depot in Sylhet (y1 = 1), we must also hire a manager there (y2 = 1)" is simply y1 <= y2. "At most 2 of these 5 projects" is y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 <= 2. "Exactly one supplier" is a sum equal to 1. With such tricks, binary variables can express almost any logical rule.

Branch and bound, the idea: Solve the LP relaxation. If its answer is integer, done. If not, pick a variable with a fractional value, say x = 3.75, and split the problem into two branches: one with x <= 3 and one with x >= 4. No integer solution is lost, because no integer lies between 3 and 4. Solve the LP in each branch and repeat. The trick that makes it practical is bounding: keep the best integer solution found so far (the incumbent), and stop exploring any branch whose LP bound is no better than the incumbent, because nothing below it can win. This is called pruning.

Branch and bound worked, the root: Maximise Z = 5x + 4y subject to x + y <= 5, 10x + 6y <= 45, x, y >= 0 and integer. The LP relaxation's optimum is where the two lines meet: from x + y = 5 and 10x + 6y = 45 we get 4x = 15, so x = 3.75 and y = 1.25, with Z = 18.75 + 5 = 23.75. Not integer. Since Z must be an integer combination of integers, we already know the IP optimum is at most 23.

Branch and bound worked, branching on x: Branch 1, add x <= 3: the best LP point is x = 3, y = 2 (from x + y = 5; check 30 + 12 = 42 <= 45), Z = 15 + 8 = 23. It is integer, so it becomes the incumbent, Z = 23. Branch 2, add x >= 4: now 10x + 6y <= 45 limits y; the LP optimum is x = 4, y = 5/6, Z = 20 + 3.33 = 23.33. Its bound 23.33 is above 23, so we cannot prune yet.

Branch and bound worked, finishing: In branch 2, branch on y. Branch 2a, y <= 0: then x <= 4.5 from 10x <= 45, so the LP gives x = 4.5, y = 0, Z = 22.5, which is below the incumbent 23: prune. Branch 2b, y >= 1: 10x + 6 <= 45 means x <= 3.9, which contradicts x >= 4: infeasible, prune. No branches remain. The optimum is x = 3, y = 2, Z = 23. Notice that rounding the root LP point (3.75, 1.25) to (4, 1) would break 10x + 6y <= 45 (46 > 45).

Choices inside branch and bound: Which fractional variable to branch on, and which open branch to explore next, affect speed a lot. Depth-first search finds feasible integer solutions quickly (giving a good incumbent for pruning); best-bound search explores the branch with the best LP bound and proves optimality sooner. Each branch adds one constraint to a solved LP, so the dual simplex method from lesson 08 re-optimises in a few pivots. Real solvers combine all of this with clever heuristics.

Cutting planes: Another way to reach integer answers is to add constraints, called cuts, that remove fractional LP solutions without removing any integer point. Ralph Gomory showed in 1958 how to derive such a cut from a row of the final simplex tableau: take the fractional parts of the row's numbers to build a new inequality that the current fractional point violates. In our example, a cut like 2x + y <= 8 (true for every feasible integer point, since (3, 2) gives 8 and (4, 0) gives 8, and violated by (3.75, 1.25), which gives 8.75) slices off the fractional corner. Modern solvers use branch and cut: branch and bound plus cuts at each node.

How hard is integer programming: General integer programming is NP-hard: no known algorithm solves every instance in polynomial time, and the travelling salesman and knapsack problems are special cases. That is why a solver may report a gap, for example "best found 3.5, best bound 3.7, gap 5.7%": it has a good answer and a proof that nothing can be more than 5.7% better, but has not closed the gap yet. Some special IPs are easy: transportation and assignment problems always have integer LP optima (lesson 14 explains why), so no branching is needed.

Real-life example 1, where to open depots: An FMCG company wants to serve 64 districts and is considering 8 possible depot locations. Opening a depot has a fixed yearly cost; shipping costs depend on which depot serves which district. Binary variables decide which depots open; continuous variables decide shipments, linked by fixed-charge constraints. This facility location MIP might say "open Bogura, Cumilla and Jashore only", and the solver's gap tells the manager how sure the answer is.

Real-life example 2, a university class timetable: A university must assign courses to rooms and time slots so that no teacher or student batch has two classes at once, rooms are big enough, and labs get lab rooms. Each possible (course, room, slot) gets a binary variable, with constraints like "each course is scheduled exactly once" and "each room holds at most one course per slot". Thousands of binaries, solved by a MIP solver or by heuristics (lesson 24) when it gets too large.

Common mistakes: Rounding the LP solution and calling it optimal. Forgetting that the LP relaxation gives an upper bound (max) or lower bound (min), not the answer. Choosing M too small in big-M constraints (it must be at least as large as the variable can ever be), or far too large (it weakens the relaxation and slows the solver). Pruning a branch whose bound is better than the incumbent. Branching with x <= 3 and x >= 3, which leaves x = 3 in both and can loop.

What exams ask: Show by example why rounding fails. Formulate problems with binary variables: knapsack, capital budgeting, fixed charge, either-or, if-then, at most k of n. Solve a two-variable IP by branch and bound, drawing the tree with the LP solution and bound at each node and saying why each node is pruned (integer, worse bound, or infeasible). Explain the idea of a Gomory cut. State that general IP is NP-hard.

Recap: Integer programs require some variables to be whole numbers or 0/1. Rounding the LP answer can be infeasible or far from optimal: in our example the LP gave 39 but the integer optimum was 33 at a totally different point. Binary variables model yes/no choices and logic: knapsack, fixed charge, either-or, if-then. Branch and bound splits on fractional variables, uses LP bounds to prune, and found (3, 2) with Z = 23 in our worked tree. Cutting planes tighten the relaxation, and solvers combine both. General IP is NP-hard, so solvers report gaps. Next, lesson 13 turns to networks: shortest paths and spanning trees.
key_points: Integer programs require some (mixed) or all (pure) variables to be integers; binary variables are 0 or 1.
Rounding fails: max 21x + 11y, 7x + 4y <= 13 has LP optimum Z = 39 at x = 1.857, but integer optimum (0, 3) with Z = 33.
The LP relaxation gives an upper bound for a max IP (lower bound for min).
Knapsack example: greedy by ratio gains 2.7 lakh; the optimum (dryer + truck) gains 3.5 lakh.
Binary modelling: fixed charge x <= M y, either-or with M z, if-then y1 <= y2, at most k of n.
Branch and bound: branch x <= floor and x >= ceil, prune when integer, infeasible or bound not better than incumbent.
Worked B&B: root (3.75, 1.25) Z = 23.75; optimum (3, 2) Z = 23.
Gomory cuts remove fractional points without losing integer ones; general IP is NP-hard, so solvers report an optimality gap.
lessons.tip: When you draw a branch and bound tree, write three things in every node: the added constraint, the LP solution with its Z, and the reason it was closed (integer, bound, or infeasible). Examiners mark exactly those three things.
lessons.task: Solve by branch and bound: maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to 2x + 2y <= 9, 3x + y <= 11, x, y >= 0 and integer. Solve each LP by the graphical method, draw the full tree, and check your answer by listing all integer points in the region.

quiz.q: For max 21x + 11y with 7x + 4y <= 13 and integers, why is rounding the LP answer (1.857, 0) a bad idea?
options: Rounding up is infeasible and rounding down gives 21, far below the integer optimum 33
quiz.explain: (2, 0) breaks the constraint and (1, 0) gives only 21, while (0, 3) gives 33.

quiz.q: For a maximisation IP, what does the LP relaxation's optimal value give?
quiz.explain: The relaxation's region contains every integer point, so its best value is at least the IP's best.

quiz.q: Which constraint forces x = 0 unless a setup binary y equals 1?
quiz.explain: With y = 0, x <= 0 forces x = 0; with y = 1, x can go up to M.

quiz.q: In branch and bound, when is a node pruned?
options: When its LP solution is fractional
When its LP is infeasible, integer, or its bound is not better than the incumbent
When it is the first node
quiz.explain: Those three cases mean nothing better can be found below that node.

quiz.q: In the worked example (max 5x + 4y, x + y <= 5, 10x + 6y <= 45), what is the integer optimum?
quiz.explain: (4, 1) and (5, 0) break 10x + 6y <= 45; branch and bound proves (3, 2) with Z = 23 is best.

lessons.title: Network Models I: Shortest Path and Minimum Spanning Tree
lessons.content:
Open a map app in Dhaka and ask for the fastest way from Mirpur to Gulshan. In a second it suggests a route. Behind that answer is one of the oldest and most useful OR models: the shortest path problem on a network. Now imagine a telecom company that wants to connect six areas with fibre cable using as little cable as possible, so that every area can reach every other. That is a different network problem: the minimum spanning tree. This lesson covers both. You have met the algorithms in Algorithms (deep-cse-3-1) and Graph Theory (deep-cse-3-9); here we focus on modelling real decisions with them and seeing how they fit into OR.

What a network is: A network (or graph) has nodes (also called vertices), like road junctions, cities or computers, and arcs (or edges), like roads, cables or flights, that join pairs of nodes. Each arc can carry a number: a distance, a time, a cost, or a capacity. Arcs can be directed (one-way, like a one-way street) or undirected (two-way). Many OR problems become simple and fast once you see them as networks, because network structure is much more special than a general LP.

Our example network: Six areas: Mirpur, Agargaon, Farmgate, Mohakhali, Tejgaon and Gulshan. Two-way roads with travel times in minutes: Mirpur-Agargaon 10, Mirpur-Mohakhali 25, Agargaon-Farmgate 8, Agargaon-Mohakhali 12, Farmgate-Tejgaon 6, Mohakhali-Tejgaon 7, Mohakhali-Gulshan 9 and Tejgaon-Gulshan 14. Draw it on paper with circles for areas and lines labelled with minutes; it will make the steps much easier to follow.

The shortest path problem: Given a start node (source) and an end node (sink), find the path whose total arc length is smallest. Length can mean minutes, kilometres, taka or even risk. If all lengths are non-negative, Dijkstra's algorithm (Edsger Dijkstra, published 1959) solves it efficiently. The idea is to grow a set of nodes whose shortest distance is known for sure, one node at a time, always adding the closest one.

Dijkstra, the rules: Give the source a label of 0 and every other node infinity. Repeat: pick the node with the smallest temporary label and make it permanent (its distance is now final).
