Then, for each neighbour that is not yet permanent, check whether going through the new permanent node is shorter: if label(new) + arc length < label(neighbour), update the neighbour's label and remember the new node as its predecessor. Stop when the sink becomes permanent.

Dijkstra worked, part 1: Start: Mirpur 0, all others infinity. Make Mirpur permanent. Update its neighbours: Agargaon 0 + 10 = 10, Mohakhali 0 + 25 = 25. The smallest temporary label is Agargaon 10: make it permanent. From Agargaon: Farmgate 10 + 8 = 18 (new), Mohakhali 10 + 12 = 22, which beats 25, so Mohakhali becomes 22 with predecessor Agargaon. Notice how the direct road to Mohakhali lost: 25 minutes direct is slower than 10 + 12 = 22 through Agargaon.

Dijkstra worked, part 2: Smallest temporary label: Farmgate 18, make it permanent. From Farmgate: Tejgaon 18 + 6 = 24. Next smallest: Mohakhali 22, permanent. From Mohakhali: Tejgaon 22 + 7 = 29, not better than 24, no change; Gulshan 22 + 9 = 31. Next: Tejgaon 24, permanent. From Tejgaon: Gulshan 24 + 14 = 38, not better than 31. Next: Gulshan 31, permanent. Done. Follow predecessors back from Gulshan: Gulshan from Mohakhali, Mohakhali from Agargaon, Agargaon from Mirpur. The shortest route is Mirpur, Agargaon, Mohakhali, Gulshan, 31 minutes.

Why Dijkstra is correct: When a node has the smallest temporary label, any other path to it would have to leave the permanent set through some other temporary node, which already has a label at least as large, and then add non-negative arcs. So no other path can be shorter. That argument breaks if an arc has negative length, which is why Dijkstra needs non-negative lengths. With negative lengths (for example, a route that earns a refund), use the Bellman-Ford algorithm, which relaxes every arc n - 1 times and can also detect negative cycles.

Shortest path as a linear program: Let x_ij = 1 if the path uses arc i to j. Minimise the sum of length_ij times x_ij, subject to flow conservation: the source sends out one unit (outflow minus inflow = 1), the sink takes in one unit (inflow minus outflow = 1), and every other node passes on whatever it receives (inflow = outflow). With x_ij >= 0, the LP's optimal solution is automatically 0 or 1 (lesson 14 explains why), and its dual variables are exactly the shortest distances to each node. So shortest path is an LP, but one with a much faster special algorithm.

All pairs and other variants: If you need the shortest distance between every pair of nodes, for example to build a distance table for a delivery company, the Floyd-Warshall algorithm does it in about n cubed steps using dynamic programming (lesson 17). Other useful variants: the longest path in a project network (that is the critical path, lesson 15), the most reliable path (multiply reliabilities, or add their logarithms), and the k shortest paths (backup routes).

The minimum spanning tree problem: Now forget source and sink. A spanning tree is a set of arcs that connects all nodes with no cycles; with n nodes it has exactly n - 1 arcs. The minimum spanning tree (MST) is the spanning tree with the smallest total length. Use it when you need everything connected at least cost, and any connection path is acceptable: laying cables, pipes, electric lines or rural roads.

Kruskal's algorithm: Sort all arcs from shortest to longest. Go through them in order and take an arc if it does not create a cycle with the arcs already taken; otherwise skip it. Stop when you have n - 1 arcs. Treat our numbers as the cost in lakh taka of laying fibre along each road. Sorted: Farmgate-Tejgaon 6, Mohakhali-Tejgaon 7, Agargaon-Farmgate 8, Mohakhali-Gulshan 9, Mirpur-Agargaon 10, Agargaon-Mohakhali 12, Tejgaon-Gulshan 14, Mirpur-Mohakhali 25.

Kruskal worked: Take 6 (Farmgate-Tejgaon). Take 7 (Mohakhali-Tejgaon). Take 8 (Agargaon-Farmgate). Take 9 (Mohakhali-Gulshan). Take 10 (Mirpur-Agargaon). That is 5 arcs for 6 nodes, so we are done; the remaining arcs would all make cycles anyway (Agargaon-Mohakhali 12 would close the loop Agargaon, Farmgate, Tejgaon, Mohakhali). Total cost: 6 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 10 = 40 lakh taka, compared with 91 lakh to lay cable on every road. Every area is connected.

Prim's algorithm and why greedy works here: Prim's algorithm grows one tree from any starting node, each time adding the cheapest arc that joins a tree node to a non-tree node. It gives the same total, 40. Both are greedy, and greedy is safe for MST because of the cut property: for any split of the nodes into two groups, the cheapest arc crossing between them belongs to some minimum spanning tree. Contrast this with the knapsack in lesson 12, where greedy failed.

Shortest path tree versus minimum spanning tree: They are different. In our network, the MST connects Mirpur to Gulshan through Agargaon, Farmgate, Tejgaon and Mohakhali, a path of 10 + 8 + 6 + 7 + 9 = 40 minutes, while the shortest path is 31 minutes. The MST minimises the total length of the whole network; the shortest path minimises the length of one trip. Choosing the wrong model is a classic mistake: a cable company wants an MST, a commuter wants a shortest path.

How fast these algorithms are: With a simple list, Dijkstra scans all nodes to find the smallest label each round, about n squared steps in total, fine for a few thousand nodes. With a priority queue (a heap, from Data Structures, deep-cse-2-2) it runs in about (n + m) log n steps for m arcs, which is how map apps handle millions of junctions. Kruskal's cost is mostly the sorting of arcs, about m log m, plus a union-find structure to detect cycles quickly. Both are polynomial and fast, unlike the integer programs of lesson 12.

Choosing what the arc length means: The model is only as good as the number on each arc. Kilometres give the shortest route, minutes give the fastest, and taka give the cheapest; these can be three different routes. For a delivery company, a good arc length might be fuel cost plus the rider's time cost plus toll. When two goals matter, such as time and safety at night, a common trick is a weighted sum, for example minutes plus 5 times a risk score, and then running the same shortest path algorithm on that combined length.

Real-life example 1, ambulance routing: An emergency service in Chattogram keeps a network of roads with travel times that change by time of day. When a call comes in, it runs a shortest path from each available ambulance's location to the patient and sends the one with the smallest time. During rush hour the arc times on main roads increase, so the shortest path may switch to side roads. The same model, re-run with updated arc lengths, gives a fresh answer every time.

Real-life example 2, rural electrification: A power company plans to connect 12 villages in a char area to a substation. Line cost depends on distance and on crossing water, which is more expensive. Building lines between every pair is absurd; any set of lines that connects all villages will do. The MST gives the cheapest such set. Engineers then add one or two extra lines for reliability, so that a single fault does not cut off half the villages, which is a trade-off between cost and robustness the MST alone does not consider.

Common mistakes: Running Dijkstra with negative arc lengths. Making a node permanent before it has the smallest temporary label. Forgetting to record predecessors, so you know the distance but not the route. In Kruskal, taking an arc that forms a cycle, or stopping before n - 1 arcs. Confusing MST with shortest path, as shown above. Assuming the MST is unique: if several arcs have equal lengths, different MSTs with the same total can exist.

What exams ask: Find the shortest path from a source to all nodes by Dijkstra, showing the labels at each step and the final route. Formulate shortest path as an LP. Find an MST by Kruskal and by Prim and give its total length. Explain the difference between the two problems, and when Dijkstra fails. Sometimes a road network is given with one-way streets, so be careful with arc direction.

Recap: Networks have nodes and arcs with lengths, costs or capacities. Dijkstra finds shortest paths with non-negative lengths by making the smallest temporary label permanent each step: Mirpur to Gulshan is 31 minutes via Agargaon and Mohakhali. Shortest path is also an LP with flow conservation. The MST connects all nodes with minimum total length: Kruskal took arcs 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 for a total of 40. The two problems answer different questions. Next, lesson 14 puts capacities on arcs and asks how much can flow through a network.
key_points: A network has nodes and arcs; arcs carry lengths, costs, times or capacities and may be directed.
Dijkstra: make the smallest temporary label permanent, update neighbours, repeat; needs non-negative lengths.
Example: Mirpur to Gulshan shortest path is Mirpur, Agargaon, Mohakhali, Gulshan = 31 minutes (the direct 25-minute road is not used).
Negative lengths need Bellman-Ford; all-pairs distances use Floyd-Warshall.
Shortest path as LP: minimise sum of lengths times x_ij with flow conservation; duals are the distances.
MST: n - 1 arcs connecting all nodes at minimum total length; Kruskal takes cheapest arcs that do not form cycles.
Example MST uses arcs 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 for a total of 40 (versus 91 for all roads).
Shortest path minimises one trip; MST minimises the whole network's length; choose the model that fits the question.
lessons.tip: During Dijkstra, keep a small table with columns node, label, predecessor and permanent yes/no, and update it row by row. It prevents the most common slip: forgetting which nodes are already final.
lessons.task: Draw the road network between your home, school, a bazar, a mosque or temple, a park and a friend's house, with your estimate of walking minutes on each path. Run Dijkstra from home to every place and write the shortest routes. Then treat the minutes as costs and find the minimum spanning tree with Kruskal. Compare the two answers.

quiz.q: In the example, what is the shortest time from Mirpur to Gulshan?
quiz.explain: Mirpur, Agargaon, Mohakhali, Gulshan takes 10 + 12 + 9 = 31 minutes.

quiz.q: Why does Dijkstra update Mohakhali from 25 to 22?
options: The route through Agargaon, 10 + 12 = 22, is shorter than the direct 25
Dijkstra always picks the second road
quiz.explain: A label is replaced whenever a newly permanent node gives a shorter way in.

quiz.q: When should you NOT use Dijkstra's algorithm?
options: When there are more than 5 nodes
When you need the route, not just the distance
When some arc lengths are negative
quiz.explain: Dijkstra's correctness depends on non-negative arc lengths; use Bellman-Ford otherwise.

quiz.q: How many arcs does a spanning tree on 6 nodes have?
quiz.explain: A spanning tree on n nodes always has exactly n - 1 arcs.

quiz.q: A company wants to connect all six areas with fibre at minimum total cost. Which model fits?
quiz.explain: Connecting all nodes with minimum total arc length is exactly the MST problem.

lessons.title: Network Models II: Maximum Flow and Minimum Cost Flow
lessons.content:
During a cyclone warning, thousands of people must move from a coastal union to a cyclone shelter in the upazila town. There are several roads, and each road can carry only so many buses per hour before it jams. The officer in charge asks: what is the largest number of people per hour we can move, and which roads are the bottleneck? This is the maximum flow problem. Water in pipes, gas in pipelines, data in computer networks, cars on roads and goods in supply chains all follow the same model: stuff flows from a source to a sink through arcs that each have a capacity.

What it is: A flow network is a directed graph with a source s, a sink t, and a capacity u_ij on each arc i to j. A flow assigns an amount x_ij to each arc so that two rules hold. Capacity: 0 <= x_ij <= u_ij. Conservation: at every node other than s and t, flow in equals flow out, nothing is created or lost. The value of the flow is the net amount leaving s (which equals the amount entering t). The maximum flow problem asks for the flow with the largest value.

Our example: Source S is the coastal union, sink T is the shelter town, and A and B are two junction villages. Road capacities in buses per hour: S to A 10, S to B 6, A to B 6, A to T 8, B to T 8. Draw it: S on the left, T on the right, A above, B below, with an arc from A down to B.

The obvious greedy idea and why it fails: Find any path from S to T with spare capacity, push as much as possible, and repeat until no path is left. Try it: path S, A, B, T can carry min(10, 6, 8) = 6. Then S, A, T can carry min(10 - 6, 8) = 4; S to A is now full. Then S, B, T can carry min(6, 8 - 6) = 2; B to T is now full. Total 12. No simple forward path with spare capacity remains: S to A is full and B to T is full. But is 12 the maximum? Look at S to B: 4 more buses could leave S that way, and A to T still has 4 spare. The problem is the first path sent 6 buses through A to B to T, using up B to T capacity that S to B needed. We need a way to undo part of an earlier choice.

The residual network: For a current flow, build the residual network. For each arc i to j with flow x_ij and capacity u_ij, it has a forward residual arc with capacity u_ij - x_ij (room to send more) and a backward residual arc j to i with capacity x_ij (room to cancel flow already sent). Sending flow along a backward arc means undoing some of the earlier flow on that arc. An augmenting path is any path from s to t in the residual network.

The augmenting path that fixes it: After the three paths, the residual network has: S to B with 6 - 2 = 4 left, the backward arc B to A with capacity 6 (because A to B carries 6), and A to T with 8 - 4 = 4 left. So S, B, A, T is an augmenting path with bottleneck min(4, 6, 4) = 4. Push 4: S to B goes to 6, A to B drops from 6 to 2 (we cancelled 4), and A to T goes to 8. In plain words: 4 of the buses that were going A to B to T now go A to T directly, and that frees space on B to T for 4 more buses from S to B. Total flow 16.

The Ford-Fulkerson method: Lester Ford and Delbert Fulkerson published this in 1956. Start with zero flow. Repeat: find an augmenting path in the residual network, push the bottleneck amount along it, and update the residual network. Stop when no augmenting path exists. With integer capacities, each augmentation adds at least 1, so it must stop, and the final flow is integer on every arc. If you always choose the shortest augmenting path (fewest arcs), found by breadth-first search, the method is called Edmonds-Karp and runs in polynomial time, about n x m squared steps.

Cuts: An s-t cut splits the nodes into two groups, one containing s and the other containing t. Its capacity is the total capacity of arcs going from the s side to the t side (arcs going the other way are not counted). Every unit of flow must cross every cut from the s side to the t side, so the value of any flow is at most the capacity of any cut. In our example, the cut with {S} on one side has capacity 10 + 6 = 16. The cut with {S, A, B} on one side has capacity 8 + 8 = 16. The cut {S, A} versus {B, T} has capacity 6 + 6 + 8 = 20.

The max-flow min-cut theorem: The maximum flow value equals the minimum cut capacity. When Ford-Fulkerson stops, the nodes reachable from s in the residual network form one side of a minimum cut, and every arc leaving that side is full. In our final flow, nothing can leave S in the residual network (both S arcs are full), so the reachable set is {S}, and its cut has capacity 16, equal to the flow. That proves 16 buses per hour is the true maximum. This theorem is a special case of LP duality from lesson 07: the min cut problem is the dual of the max flow LP.

Reading the answer for the officer: Maximum 16 buses per hour. Final flows: S to A 10, S to B 6, A to B 2, A to T 8, B to T 8. Bottlenecks: the minimum cuts show that the roads out of the union (S to A and S to B) are both full, and so are the roads into town (A to T and B to T). Widening only A to B would achieve nothing. To move more people, you must increase capacity on both arcs of some minimum cut, for example on both roads out of the union and on the roads into town. The cut tells you exactly where money should go.

Max flow as an LP: Maximise v subject to: for node s, outflow minus inflow = v; for t, inflow minus outflow = v; for every other node, inflow = outflow; and 0 <= x_ij <= u_ij. So max flow is an LP with special structure, and specialised algorithms (augmenting paths, push-relabel) solve it much faster than general simplex.

Minimum cost flow: Now give every arc a cost per unit c_ij as well as a capacity, give each node a supply (positive) or demand (negative), and ask for the cheapest flow that meets all demands within capacities. That is the minimum cost flow problem, the most general of the basic network models. Many earlier models are special cases. Transportation: sources with supply, destinations with demand, arcs between them with costs (lesson 09). Assignment: supplies and demands all 1 (lesson 11). Shortest path: one unit of supply at s and one unit of demand at t, costs are lengths (lesson 13). Max flow: add an arc from t back to s with cost -1 and minimise. Transshipment: middle nodes with zero supply.

Why integer answers come free, total unimodularity: In all these network LPs, every variable appears in exactly two conservation constraints, once with +1 (leaving a node) and once with -1 (entering a node). Such a matrix is totally unimodular: every square sub-matrix has determinant 0, 1 or -1. By Cramer's rule from Linear Algebra (deep-cse-2-5), every basic solution is then integer whenever supplies, demands and capacities are integers. That is why transportation, assignment, shortest path and max flow never need branch and bound, even though they are integer problems in disguise.

Other applications of max flow and min cut: Bipartite matching: to match job seekers to jobs they are qualified for, make a source arc to each person (capacity 1), arcs from people to suitable jobs (capacity 1), and arcs from jobs to the sink (capacity 1); the maximum flow is the largest number of matches. Network reliability: the minimum cut tells you the fewest links whose failure disconnects two cities. Image segmentation in computer vision uses min cuts to separate an object from the background. Project selection problems can also be written as min cuts.

Real-life example 1, a gas pipeline network: Natural gas flows from fields in the northeast through a network of pipelines with different diameters to power plants and city distribution points. Engineers model it as a flow network to find the maximum gas that can reach Dhaka in a day. The minimum cut shows which pipeline segments limit supply; when the country plans a new pipeline, the cut tells planners which corridor would raise the maximum flow the most, rather than adding capacity where it is not the bottleneck.

Real-life example 2, internet traffic: An internet service provider connects Dhaka to two international gateways through fibre links of different bandwidths. Max flow tells the provider how much traffic can be carried from Dhaka to the gateways at peak hours. The min cut tells it the cheapest set of links to upgrade, and also which few links, if cut by roadwork, would most reduce capacity, so they can add backup routes there.

Common mistakes: Forgetting backward residual arcs, which leads to the stuck greedy answer (12 instead of 16 here). Counting arcs going from the t side back to the s side in a cut's capacity. Thinking the minimum cut is unique; here two different cuts both have capacity 16. Forgetting conservation at middle nodes when writing the LP. Confusing max flow (largest amount) with shortest path (cheapest single route) or min cost flow (cheapest way to send a given amount).

What exams ask: Find the maximum flow by Ford-Fulkerson, listing each augmenting path, its bottleneck, and the residual capacities, including at least one backward arc. Identify a minimum cut and verify max flow equals min cut. Formulate max flow as an LP. Show how transportation or assignment is a special case of min cost flow. Explain why network LPs have integer solutions.

Recap: In a flow network, flows respect capacities and conservation. Ford-Fulkerson repeatedly pushes flow along augmenting paths in the residual network, where backward arcs let it undo earlier choices; in the evacuation example, greedy got stuck at 12 but the backward arc B to A raised it to 16. Every flow is at most every cut's capacity, and the maximum flow equals the minimum cut (here 16 for the cut around S and for the cut around T). Min cost flow unifies transportation, assignment, shortest path and max flow, and total unimodularity guarantees integer answers. Next, lesson 15 uses networks to plan projects with CPM.
key_points: Flow network: source, sink, arc capacities; flows obey capacity limits and conservation at middle nodes.
Residual network: forward residual u - x and backward residual x; backward arcs let you undo earlier flow.
Example: greedy paths got stuck at 12; the augmenting path S, B, A, T using the backward arc B to A raised the flow to 16.
Ford-Fulkerson: augment along residual paths until none exist; with integer capacities the flow is integer; BFS paths give Edmonds-Karp.
Cut capacity counts only arcs from the s side to the t side; every flow is at most every cut.
Max-flow min-cut theorem: maximum flow = minimum cut capacity (16 = 10 + 6 = 8 + 8 here); it is a case of LP duality.
Min cost flow covers transportation, assignment, shortest path, transshipment and max flow as special cases.
Network constraint matrices are totally unimodular, so integer data give integer optimal solutions.
lessons.tip: After each augmentation, redraw the network with two numbers on every arc: flow and capacity, like 6/8. When you search for the next path, read forward room as capacity minus flow and backward room as flow. Most errors come from skipping this redraw.
lessons.task: Draw a network for water from an overhead tank (S) to a hostel's ground floor taps (T) through three junction pipes, with capacities in litres per minute that you choose (at least 6 arcs). Find the maximum flow by Ford-Fulkerson, writing each augmenting path and bottleneck. Then find a minimum cut and check that its capacity equals your flow.

quiz.q: In the residual network, what is the capacity of the backward arc for an arc carrying flow 6 with capacity 8?
quiz.explain: The backward residual capacity equals the current flow, 6, which is how much could be cancelled.

quiz.q: In the evacuation example, why did plain greedy stop at 12?
options: The first path used B to T capacity that S to B needed, and greedy cannot undo it
There was no path from S to T at the start
quiz.explain: Only the backward arc B to A lets 4 units be rerouted A to T, raising the flow to 16.

quiz.q: Which arcs count toward the capacity of an s-t cut?
options: Arcs from the t side to the s side
Arcs from the s side to the t side
quiz.explain: Only forward-crossing arcs limit the flow; arcs going back are not counted.

quiz.q: What does the max-flow min-cut theorem state?
options: Max flow is twice the min cut
Max flow equals the minimum capacity over all s-t cuts
Every cut has the same capacity
Min cut is always the arcs out of s
quiz.explain: The largest flow value equals the smallest cut capacity, and Ford-Fulkerson finds both.

quiz.q: Why do transportation and assignment LPs always have integer optimal solutions with integer data?
options: Because their constraint matrices are totally unimodular
quiz.explain: Totally unimodular matrices make every basic solution integer when the right-hand sides are integers.

lessons.title: Project Scheduling with CPM
lessons.content:
Think about a wedding in your family. The venue must be booked before the decorators come, invitation cards must be printed before they are delivered, the cook must know the guest count before buying meat. Some jobs can happen at the same time; others must wait. If the card printing is late, does the wedding move? It depends: some delays matter and some do not. The critical path method (CPM) answers exactly this for any project: how long will the whole thing take, which jobs can never be late without delaying everything, and how much slack the other jobs have.

What it is: CPM is a network method for scheduling a project made of activities with known durations and precedence relations (which activity must finish before which can start). It was developed in the late 1950s by engineers at the DuPont company together with Remington Rand to plan plant maintenance and construction. Its sibling PERT, which handles uncertain durations, came from the US Navy's Polaris missile programme at about the same time; that is lesson 16. Software Project Management (deep-cse-6-11) uses these ideas in practice; here we learn the method precisely.

The pieces: An activity is a job that takes time and resources, like "design the UI". Its duration is how long it takes. A precedence relation says activity X cannot start until activity Y finishes; Y is an immediate predecessor of X. A milestone or event is a moment in time, like "app launched", taking zero time. The project is finished when all activities are finished.

Our project, an app launch: A small startup in Dhaka is launching a food-ordering app. Activities and durations in days: A, requirements, 4 days, no predecessor. B, UI design, 5 days, after A. C, backend API, 9 days, after A. D, frontend build, 7 days, after B. E, integration, 4 days, after C and D. F, testing, 5 days, after E and H. G, marketing material, 6 days, after B. H, API documentation, 2 days, after C. The launch happens when F and G are both done.

Drawing the network, activity on node: In the activity-on-node (AON) style, each activity is a box and arrows show precedence. Draw a Start node, arrow to A. From A, arrows to B and C. From B, arrows to D and G. From C, arrows to E and H. From D, an arrow to E. From E and H, arrows to F. From F and G, arrows to Finish. The older activity-on-arrow (AOA) style puts activities on arrows and sometimes needs fake zero-duration "dummy" activities to show precedence correctly; AON avoids dummies, so most software uses it.

Forward pass, earliest times: For each activity, the earliest start ES is the largest earliest finish EF among its predecessors (0 if none), and EF = ES + duration. Go from left to right. A: ES 0, EF 4. B: ES 4, EF 9. C: ES 4, EF 13. D: ES 9 (after B), EF 16. G: ES 9, EF 15. H: ES 13 (after C), EF 15. E: ES = max(EF of C, EF of D) = max(13, 16) = 16, EF 20. F: ES = max(EF of E, EF of H) = max(20, 15) = 20, EF 25. The project's earliest completion is the largest EF among final activities: max(25, 15) = 25 days.

Why the maximum: An activity with two predecessors must wait for the slower one. E needs both the backend (ready on day 13) and the frontend (ready on day 16), so E cannot start before day 16. Taking the minimum here is the most common forward-pass mistake.

Backward pass, latest times: Now go right to left. The latest finish LF of a final activity is the project duration, 25. For any other activity, LF is the smallest latest start LS among its successors, and LS = LF - duration. F: LF 25, LS 20. G: LF 25, LS 19. E: LF = LS of F = 20, LS 16. H: LF = LS of F = 20, LS 18. D: LF = LS of E = 16, LS 9. C: LF = min(LS of E, LS of H) = min(16, 18) = 16, LS 7. B: LF = min(LS of D, LS of G) = min(9, 19) = 9, LS 4. A: LF = min(LS of B, LS of C) = min(4, 7) = 4, LS 0. A's LS is 0, which is a good consistency check.

Total float: Total float (or total slack) TF = LS - ES = LF - EF: how long an activity can be delayed without delaying the whole project. A: 0. B: 0. C: 7 - 4 = 3. D: 0. E: 0. F: 0. G: 19 - 9 = 10. H: 18 - 13 = 5. So the marketing material can slip up to 10 days, the API documentation 5 days and the backend 3 days, and the launch is still on day 25.

The critical path: Activities with zero total float are critical: A, B, D, E and F. They form a path from start to finish, A to B to D to E to F, with length 4 + 5 + 7 + 4 + 5 = 25 days. This is the critical path: the longest path through the network, and the project cannot finish faster than it. Compare other paths: A, C, E, F is 4 + 9 + 4 + 5 = 22 days; A, C, H, F is 4 + 9 + 2 + 5 = 20; A, B, G is 4 + 5 + 6 = 15. The longest is 25, which is why it is critical. A network can have more than one critical path.

Free float: Free float FF is how long an activity can be delayed without delaying the earliest start of any successor: FF = (smallest ES among successors) - EF. C: successors E (ES 16) and H (ES 13), so FF = 13 - 13 = 0, even though its total float is 3. H: FF = 20 - 15 = 5. G: FF = 25 - 15 = 10. Free float is never larger than total float. The difference matters: if the backend team (C) is late by even 1 day, the documentation writer (H) must also start later, though the launch is still safe up to 3 days. Total float is shared along a chain; free float belongs to one activity alone.

What delays do: Suppose the backend C takes 11 days instead of 9 (2 days late). Its total float is 3, so the launch stays on day 25, but H now starts on day 15 instead of 13. If C takes 13 days (4 days late), it uses all 3 days of float and the launch moves to day 26: path A, C, E, F becomes 4 + 13 + 4 + 5 = 26, and C becomes critical. On the other hand, any 1-day delay to A, B, D, E or F immediately pushes the launch to day 26. That is why managers watch critical activities most closely.

Gantt chart: A Gantt chart (named after Henry Gantt, early 1900s) draws each activity as a horizontal bar on a time axis from its ES to its EF, often with the float shown as a lighter extension up to LF. For our project, A spans days 0 to 4, B 4 to 9, C 4 to 13 with float to 16, D 9 to 16, G 9 to 15 with float to 25, H 13 to 15 with float to 20, E 16 to 20, F 20 to 25. Gantt charts are easy for everyone to read; the CPM network underneath is what makes the bars correct.

CPM as a longest path and as an LP: The project duration is the length of the longest path in the network, which can be found with the same kind of label-setting as shortest path, but taking the maximum. It can also be written as an LP: let t_j be the start time of activity j; minimise the finish time T subject to t_j >= t_i + d_i for every precedence i before j, and T >= t_j + d_j for every final activity. The forward pass is simply solving this LP by hand.

Resources and limitations: Basic CPM assumes unlimited resources and fixed durations. If B and C both need the same single developer, they cannot run in parallel, and the schedule must be stretched; this is resource levelling or resource-constrained scheduling, which is much harder (often NP-hard) and handled by heuristics in tools. Durations are also rarely certain, which PERT addresses next lesson. And CPM says nothing about cost, which crashing (also lesson 16) adds.

Real-life example 1, building a school in a char: An NGO plans a primary school building in a river char. Activities include land filling, waiting for the land to settle, foundation, walls, roof, toilets, a tube well, furniture and teacher hiring. Some, like the tube well and teacher hiring, are not on the critical path and have weeks of float, while land settling is critical and cannot be rushed. CPM tells the NGO to start teacher hiring late (saving salary) and to start land filling before the monsoon, because a delay there moves the whole opening date.

Real-life example 2, a software release: A bank's mobile app team plans a release with 40 activities. The project management tool computes the critical path every day as tasks are updated. One morning, a security review that had 6 days of float slips by 8 days and becomes critical; the tool turns it red and the manager moves a senior engineer to it. Without CPM, the team would likely have noticed only when the release date was already missed.

Common mistakes: Using the minimum instead of the maximum of predecessors' EF in the forward pass, or the maximum instead of the minimum of successors' LS in the backward pass. Forgetting that the project ends when all final activities end. Thinking float can be added up across a chain; total float is shared. Confusing free float with total float. Calling any long activity critical; criticality is about float, not duration. Forgetting that a critical activity's delay always delays the project, day for day.

What exams ask: Draw an AON (or AOA with dummies) network from a precedence table. Do the forward and backward passes, make a table of ES, EF, LS, LF, total float and free float, identify the critical path and project duration, and list all paths with their lengths. Explain what happens if an activity is delayed by a given number of days. Draw a Gantt chart.

Recap: CPM models a project as a network of activities with durations and precedences. The forward pass gives earliest times using the maximum of predecessors; the backward pass gives latest times using the minimum of successors. Total float = LS - ES; free float = earliest successor start - EF. Zero-float activities form the critical path, the longest path, which sets the project duration: for the app launch, A, B, D, E, F with 25 days, while C has 3 days of total float but 0 free float, G 10 and H 5. Next, lesson 16 adds uncertainty with PERT and cost with crashing.
key_points: CPM schedules activities with known durations and precedences on a network (activity on node avoids dummies).
Forward pass: ES = max EF of predecessors, EF = ES + duration; project duration = largest final EF.
Backward pass: LF = min LS of successors, LS = LF - duration; the first activity's LS should be 0.
Total float = LS - ES; free float = (smallest successor ES) - EF; free float <= total float.
App launch: critical path A, B, D, E, F = 25 days; other paths 22, 20 and 15 days.
Floats: C total 3 but free 0, H 5, G 10; a 4-day delay to C pushes the launch to day 26.
Delaying any critical activity delays the project day for day.
Basic CPM assumes unlimited resources and certain durations; PERT and crashing extend it.
lessons.tip: Write ES and EF on the top of each node box and LS and LF on the bottom, doing the whole forward pass first and then the whole backward pass. Floats then fall out by subtracting top from bottom, and critical activities are the boxes where top equals bottom.
lessons.task: Plan a class picnic as a project with at least 7 activities (collect money, book bus, buy food, cook, get permission, plan games, travel) with your own durations and precedences. Draw the AON network, do forward and backward passes, find the critical path, total and free float, and decide which activity you could start late without risk.

quiz.q: In the forward pass, how is the earliest start of an activity with several predecessors found?
options: The smallest EF of its predecessors
The largest EF of its predecessors
quiz.explain: It must wait for every predecessor, so it starts at the latest of their earliest finishes.

quiz.q: What is the critical path and duration of the app-launch project?
options: A, C, E, F with 22 days
A, B, D, E, F with 25 days
A, C, H, F with 20 days
quiz.explain: It is the longest path, 4 + 5 + 7 + 4 + 5 = 25, and all its activities have zero float.

quiz.q: Activity G has ES 9 and LS 19. What is its total float?
quiz.explain: Total float = LS - ES = 19 - 9 = 10 days.

quiz.q: Backend C has total float 3 and free float 0. What happens if C is 1 day late?
options: The project is delayed by 1 day
C becomes the only critical activity
Successor H must start 1 day later, but the project end is unchanged
quiz.explain: Zero free float means a successor's earliest start moves, but total float 3 protects the finish date.

quiz.q: Which statement about critical activities is true?
options: They are always the longest activities
Delaying any of them delays the project by the same amount
They have the largest free float
There is always exactly one critical path
quiz.explain: Critical activities have zero float, so every day of delay moves the finish date.

lessons.title: PERT and Project Crashing
lessons.content:
Ask a builder how long it will take to finish your roof, and a wise one will say, "about 8 days, maybe 5 if the weather is perfect, but up to 17 if it rains and the cement is late." Real activity times are uncertain. CPM in lesson 15 pretended every duration was known exactly. PERT keeps the same network but treats durations as random, so it can answer questions like "what is the chance we finish before Pohela Boishakh?" And crashing adds money to the picture: if we pay for overtime or extra workers, how much faster can we finish, and is it worth it?

What PERT is: PERT stands for Program Evaluation and Review Technique. It was developed in 1958 for the US Navy's Polaris submarine missile programme, where many activities had never been done before, so nobody could give exact durations. PERT asks for three estimates per activity and uses them to compute an expected duration and a variance. Then it applies the critical path idea and basic probability to estimate the chance of meeting a deadline.

The three estimates: For each activity, ask the people who will do it for three numbers. The optimistic time a: how long it takes if everything goes right. The most likely time m: the usual case. The pessimistic time b: how long it takes if many things go wrong, but not a total disaster. Example: an activity with a = 5, m = 8, b = 17 days. Notice it is lopsided: things can go much more wrong than right, which is common in real projects.

Expected time and variance: PERT assumes each activity time follows a beta distribution, which can be lopsided, and approximates its mean and variance with simple formulas. Expected time te = (a + 4m + b) / 6. Variance = ((b - a) / 6) squared. The standard deviation is (b - a) / 6. For a = 5, m = 8, b = 17: te = (5 + 32 + 17) / 6 = 54 / 6 = 9 days, and variance = (12 / 6) squared = 4, so the standard deviation is 2 days. The expected time 9 is larger than the most likely 8 because of the long pessimistic tail.

Our PERT project: A small factory is installing a new production line. Activities with (a, m, b) in weeks: A, site preparation, (2, 4, 6), no predecessor. B, order machines, (3, 5, 13), after A. C, train workers, (4, 7, 10), after A. D, install machines, (1, 3, 5), after B. E, electrical work, (5, 8, 17), after C. F, trial run, (2, 3, 4), after D and E. Expected times: A 4, B 6, C 7, D 3, E 9, F 3. Variances: A 0.444, B 2.778, C 1, D 0.444, E 4, F 0.111.

Finding the critical path with expected times: Run CPM with the expected times. Path A, B, D, F: 4 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 16 weeks. Path A, C, E, F: 4 + 7 + 9 + 3 = 23 weeks. The longer one, A, C, E, F, is critical, and the expected project duration is 23 weeks.

Project variance: PERT assumes activity times are independent, so the variance of the project duration is the sum of the variances of the activities on the critical path: 0.444 + 1 + 4 + 0.111 = 5.556. The standard deviation is the square root, about 2.357 weeks. By the central limit theorem from Probability & Statistics (deep-cse-2-6), the sum of several independent activity times is approximately normally distributed, so the project duration is roughly normal with mean 23 and standard deviation 2.357.

Probability of meeting a deadline: The owner wants to start production within 25 weeks. Compute z = (deadline - mean) / standard deviation = (25 - 23) / 2.357 = 0.849. From the standard normal table, P(Z <= 0.849) is about 0.80. So there is roughly an 80% chance of finishing in 25 weeks. For a deadline of 20 weeks, z = (20 - 23) / 2.357 = -1.273, and the probability is only about 10%. For the mean itself, 23 weeks, the chance is 50%: a plan built only on expected times is a coin toss.

Working backwards from a target probability: The bank funding the project wants 95% confidence. The z value for 95% is 1.645, so the deadline should be 23 + 1.645 x 2.357, about 26.9 weeks. The owner should promise about 27 weeks, not 23. This is one of the most useful outputs of PERT: a schedule buffer based on actual uncertainty instead of a guess.

PERT's limitations: First, it looks only at the critical path. A near-critical path with high variance can also cause delays; here path A, B, D, F has mean 16 and variance about 3.78, so it is safe, but in other projects a second path with mean 22 and large variance could easily become the longest. This is called merge-event bias, and PERT tends to be optimistic because of it. Second, activities are often not independent: bad weather delays several at once. Third, the three estimates are themselves guesses. Monte Carlo simulation (Simulation & Modeling, deep-cse-6-5) handles all of these by sampling random durations thousands of times.

Crashing, the idea: Sometimes we must finish sooner than the normal schedule, for example to meet an export shipment. Most activities can be shortened by spending more: overtime, extra workers, faster machines, express delivery. Crashing means shortening activity durations at extra cost. For each activity we know a normal time and normal cost, and a crash time (the shortest possible) and crash cost. The cost slope = (crash cost - normal cost) / (normal time - crash time) is the extra cost per day saved, assumed constant.

Direct and indirect costs: Crashing raises direct costs (labour, materials for the activities). But finishing sooner lowers indirect costs: site rent, supervisor salaries, overhead, late penalties, which grow with every day the project runs. The best duration minimises total cost = direct + indirect. That is the time-cost trade-off.

Crashing worked, the data: A 4-activity project: P (4 days normal, 3 crash, slope 3,000 taka per day) comes first; then Q (7 normal, 5 crash, slope 2,000) and R (5 normal, 4 crash, slope 1,000) run in parallel after P; then S (3 normal, 2 crash, slope 6,000) after both Q and R. Normal direct cost totals 40,000 taka. Indirect cost is 5,000 taka per day. Paths: P, Q, S is 4 + 7 + 3 = 14 days (critical); P, R, S is 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 days. Normal total cost: 40,000 + 14 x 5,000 = 110,000 taka.

Crashing worked, step by step: Rule: crash the cheapest activity on the critical path(s), one step at a time, as long as its slope is below the indirect cost per day saved. Step 1: the critical path is P, Q, S; the cheapest is Q at 2,000. Crash Q by 2 days (to its limit of 5), but watch the other path: after 2 days both paths are 12 days. Direct cost rises by 4,000 to 44,000; indirect falls to 60,000; total 104,000. Step 2: now both paths are critical, so we must shorten both together. Options: P (on both paths) at 3,000, S (on both) at 6,000, or Q plus R together, but Q is already at its limit. Crash P by 1 day for 3,000: duration 11, direct 47,000, indirect 55,000, total 102,000.

Crashing worked, when to stop: Step 3: P is now at its limit. The only way to shorten both paths further is S at 6,000 per day. That costs more than the 5,000 per day of indirect cost it saves: duration 10 would give direct 53,000 plus indirect 50,000 = 103,000, higher than 102,000. So the optimal duration is 11 days with total cost 102,000 taka. If the buyer pays a bonus for finishing in 10 days, say more than 1,000 taka, it would then be worth crashing S as well. Notice we never crashed R even though it is the cheapest activity, because R was never critical; crashing non-critical activities wastes money.

Crashing as an LP: For bigger projects, crashing is written as an LP: variables are start times and the number of days each activity is crashed, y_j, with 0 <= y_j <= (normal - crash). Minimise the sum of slope_j times y_j plus the indirect cost times the project duration, subject to precedence constraints using shortened durations (d_j - y_j). Project management software solves exactly this.

Real-life example 1, a road and bridge project: A district road project with a contractual completion date has a penalty of 50,000 taka per day of delay. Mid-way, the planner uses PERT to estimate only a 60% chance of finishing on time. Using the crashing analysis, the contractor finds that adding a second shift to the bridge pier work (on the critical path) costs 30,000 taka per day saved, less than the penalty, while speeding up the roadside drains (not critical) would waste money. The decision is clear and defensible.

Real-life example 2, an export order: A garments factory receives an order that must reach the buyer's ship in 21 days, but the normal schedule says 24. The production planner lists activities (fabric arrival, cutting, sewing, washing, finishing, packing, inspection, trucking to Chattogram), estimates crash times and costs (overtime for sewing, air freight for accessories), and crashes the cheapest critical activities first. The plan meets 21 days for an extra 3.2 lakh taka, much less than the cost of missing the ship and paying air freight for the whole order.

Common mistakes: Using the simple average (a + m + b) / 3 instead of (a + 4m + b) / 6. Adding standard deviations instead of variances along the path. Using variances of all activities rather than just critical ones. Forgetting that a new path can become critical while crashing. Crashing a non-critical activity. Continuing to crash after the slope exceeds the indirect cost saved. Reading the normal table wrongly for negative z values.

What exams ask: Compute te and variance for each activity from (a, m, b), find the critical path and expected duration, compute the project standard deviation, and find the probability of finishing by a given date or the date for a given probability. Crash a small network step by step with a cost table, showing the total cost at each duration and the optimal duration. Discuss PERT's assumptions and limitations.

Recap: PERT uses three estimates per activity: te = (a + 4m + b) / 6 and variance ((b - a) / 6) squared. The project mean is the critical path length and its variance is the sum of critical variances; with a normal approximation you get probabilities: 23 weeks expected, about 80% chance for 25 weeks, about 27 weeks for 95%. Crashing shortens critical activities at their cost slopes, cheapest first, until slopes exceed the indirect cost per day; in our example the best is 11 days at 102,000 taka. Next, lesson 17 introduces dynamic programming, a method for problems that unfold in stages.
key_points: PERT uses optimistic a, most likely m and pessimistic b times for each activity.
Expected time te = (a + 4m + b) / 6; variance = ((b - a) / 6) squared; e.g. (5, 8, 17) gives 9 and 4.
Project mean = sum of critical te; project variance = sum of critical variances (not standard deviations).
Example: critical A, C, E, F has mean 23 weeks, variance 5.556, sd 2.357; P(finish <= 25) is about 80%, P(<= 20) about 10%.
For 95% confidence promise mean + 1.645 sd, about 27 weeks here.
Crashing: cost slope = (crash cost - normal cost) / (normal time - crash time); crash the cheapest critical activity first.
Stop crashing when the slope exceeds the indirect cost saved per day; example optimum 11 days at 102,000 taka.
PERT ignores near-critical paths and dependence; Monte Carlo simulation (deep-cse-6-5) is the modern fix.
lessons.tip: When crashing, keep a running table with columns: duration, activity crashed, cost added, direct total, indirect total, grand total, and the length of every path. Updating every path length each step is how you catch a new critical path before it catches you.
lessons.task: Pick a real project you know, like preparing for a family event or a school science fair. List 6 activities with your own a, m and b estimates and precedences. Compute te and variance for each, find the critical path, and calculate the probability of finishing within a deadline you choose. Then decide where extra help (crashing) would buy the most time.

quiz.q: An activity has a = 5, m = 8, b = 17. What is its PERT expected time?
How is the variance of the project duration computed in PERT?
options: Sum of variances of activities on the critical path
Sum of standard deviations on the critical path
quiz.explain: Independent activity times add in variance, so you sum critical-path variances and then take the square root.

quiz.q: Mean 23 weeks, sd 2.357. What is the approximate probability of finishing within 25 weeks?
Normal 7 days at 15,000 taka, crash 5 days at 19,000 taka. What is the cost slope?
quiz.explain: Slope = (19,000 - 15,000) / (7 - 5) = 2,000 taka per day saved.

quiz.q: In the crashing example, why was S (slope 6,000) not crashed?
options: Its slope exceeded the 5,000 per day indirect cost saved
Crashing is not allowed on the last activity
quiz.explain: Crashing S would add 6,000 but save only 5,000 of indirect cost, raising total cost from 102,000 to 103,000.

lessons.title: Dynamic Programming in Operations Research
lessons.content:
Imagine you are travelling from Dhaka to Cox's Bazar by bus, changing at towns along the way. At each town you choose the next leg. If you always grab the cheapest next ticket, you might end up in a town from which every onward ticket is expensive. A smarter traveller thinks backwards: "from each town near the end, what is the cheapest way to finish? Knowing that, what is the cheapest way from each town one step earlier?" and so on back to Dhaka. That backwards thinking is dynamic programming (DP), a method for decisions made in stages, where each choice changes what is possible next.

What it is: Dynamic programming solves a big problem by breaking it into stages, solving small sub-problems first, storing their answers, and building up. The name was chosen in the 1950s by Richard Bellman, who developed the theory; the word programming again means planning, as in linear programming. Unlike the simplex method, DP is not one algorithm; it is a way of thinking that must be adapted to each problem. You met DP for algorithms like longest common subsequence in Algorithms (deep-cse-3-1); here we use it for OR decisions.

The vocabulary: Stages: the steps at which decisions are made (legs of the trip, months, clinics). States: the information you need at a stage to decide the rest (which town you are in, how much budget is left). Decisions: the choices available at a stage in a given state. Return or cost: what each decision earns or costs. Transition: how a decision moves you from a state at one stage to a state at the next. The value function f_n(s) is the best total you can get from stage n onwards if you are in state s.

Bellman's principle of optimality: An optimal policy has the property that, whatever the initial state and first decision, the remaining decisions must form an optimal policy for the state that results. In plain words: if the best route from Dhaka to Cox's Bazar passes through Noakhali, then the part from Noakhali onwards must be the best route from Noakhali. Otherwise you could swap in the better tail and improve the whole route. This is what lets us solve the tail first and reuse it.

The recursive equation: For a minimisation, f_n(s) = minimum over decisions x of [cost of x in state s + f_(n+1)(next state)]. At the last stage, f is just the final cost (often 0 at the destination). You compute f backwards, stage by stage, and record the best decision for each state. Then you read the answer forwards from the starting state, following the recorded decisions.

The stagecoach problem, data: Travel from Dhaka to Cox's Bazar in four legs. Stage 1 choices from Dhaka: Cumilla (cost 4) or Chandpur (5). From Cumilla: Feni 3 or Noakhali 5. From Chandpur: Feni 4 or Noakhali 2. From Feni: Chattogram 3 or Bandarban 6. From Noakhali: Chattogram 5 or Bandarban 3. From Chattogram to Cox's Bazar 4; from Bandarban to Cox's Bazar 3. Costs are in hundred taka and include fare, food and waiting. The routes are a teaching example, not real bus routes.

Stagecoach, solving backwards: Last stage: f(Chattogram) = 4, f(Bandarban) = 3. One stage earlier: from Feni, going to Chattogram costs 3 + 4 = 7 and to Bandarban 6 + 3 = 9, so f(Feni) = 7, go to Chattogram. From Noakhali: Chattogram 5 + 4 = 9, Bandarban 3 + 3 = 6, so f(Noakhali) = 6, go to Bandarban. Next: from Cumilla: Feni 3 + 7 = 10, Noakhali 5 + 6 = 11, so f(Cumilla) = 10. From Chandpur: Feni 4 + 7 = 11, Noakhali 2 + 6 = 8, so f(Chandpur) = 8. Finally from Dhaka: Cumilla 4 + 10 = 14, Chandpur 5 + 8 = 13, so f(Dhaka) = 13, go to Chandpur.

Reading the answer and beating greed: Follow the decisions forwards: Dhaka to Chandpur to Noakhali to Bandarban to Cox's Bazar, total 5 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 13 hundred taka. The greedy traveller takes the cheapest next leg each time: Dhaka to Cumilla (4), Cumilla to Feni (3), Feni to Chattogram (3), Chattogram to Cox's Bazar (4), total 14. Greedy started with the cheaper ticket but landed in a worse position. DP evaluated each position by its whole future, not just the next step.

How much work DP saves: There are 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 complete routes here, so brute force is easy. But with 10 stages and 10 towns per stage, there are 10^9 routes, while DP only computes about 10 stages x 10 states x 10 choices = 1,000 additions and comparisons. DP reuses the answer for each town instead of recomputing it for every route that passes through. That is the core trick: overlapping sub-problems solved once and stored.

Resource allocation, data: A district health office has 4 doctors to send to 3 upazila clinics. Patients treated per day depend on how many doctors each clinic gets. Clinic 1: 0, 30, 50, 62, 70 for 0 to 4 doctors. Clinic 2: 0, 26, 45, 58, 66. Clinic 3: 0, 22, 36, 46, 52. Notice diminishing returns: the second doctor adds less than the first. Maximise total patients treated. Stages: clinics. State: doctors still available. Decision: how many to send to this clinic.

Resource allocation, solving: Stage 3 (clinic 3 alone): f3(s) = clinic 3's value with s doctors: 0, 22, 36, 46, 52. Stage 2 (clinics 2 and 3 with s doctors): f2(s) = max over x of [clinic 2 with x + f3(s - x)]. f2(1) = max(0 + 22, 26 + 0) = 26. f2(2) = max(36, 26 + 22, 45) = 48, with x = 1. f2(3) = max(46, 26 + 36, 45 + 22, 58) = 67, with x = 2. f2(4) = max(52, 26 + 46, 45 + 36, 58 + 22, 66) = 81, with x = 2. Stage 1 with all 4: options 0 + 81, 30 + 67, 50 + 48, 62 + 26, 70 + 0 = 81, 97, 98, 88, 70. Best is 98 with 2 doctors at clinic 1.

Resource allocation, the plan: Clinic 1 gets 2 doctors, leaving 2. From f2(2), clinic 2 gets 1, leaving 1 for clinic 3. Total patients: 50 + 26 + 22 = 98 per day. Compare the tempting plan of 2 doctors each to clinics 1 and 2: 50 + 45 = 95, or putting all 4 in the biggest clinic: 70. DP checks every combination implicitly with very little work.

Backward or forward recursion: We solved from the destination backwards, which is natural when the start is fixed and you want a plan from it. You can also go forwards, defining g(s) as the best cost from the start to state s; for the stagecoach, g(Chandpur) = 5, g(Noakhali) = min(4 + 5, 5 + 2) = 7, and so on, reaching 13 at Cox's Bazar. Both give the same optimum. Backward recursion has one extra benefit: it gives the best plan from every state, so if the bus breaks down in Feni, you already know the best way on from Feni (7).

The knapsack as DP: The 0-1 knapsack from lesson 12 also has a DP. Stages are items, the state is remaining budget b, and f_i(b) = max(f_(i+1)(b), value_i + f_(i+1)(b - cost_i)) when the item fits. For the rice mill with budget 10 lakh, the table has 4 items x 11 budget values, and it finds dryer plus truck with gain 3.5 lakh. The work grows with the number of items times the budget, which is fast when the budget is a small whole number but slow when it is huge, so knapsack is called pseudo-polynomial.

Other DP models in OR: Production planning over months, where the state is inventory at the start of the month and the decision is how much to produce (balancing setup, production and holding costs). Equipment replacement: each year decide to keep an old machine (rising repair cost) or replace it (purchase cost), with state = machine age. Shortest paths in general (Floyd-Warshall from lesson 13 is DP). Inventory with random demand, where the value function becomes an expected value, leading to Markov decision processes.

Stochastic DP and the link to reinforcement learning: When the next state is random, for example demand next month, the recursion uses expected values: f_n(s) = best over x of [immediate cost + expected f_(n+1)(next state)]. This is a Markov decision process, solved by value iteration or policy iteration. Reinforcement Learning (deep-cse-8-4) builds on exactly these Bellman equations, learning the value function from experience when the probabilities are unknown.

The curse of dimensionality: DP's weakness is the number of states. If the state is one number (doctors left), it is small. But if the state must record the stock of 20 products, each from 0 to 100, there are 101^20 states, far too many to store. Bellman himself named this the curse of dimensionality. In practice, analysts reduce the state, approximate the value function, or switch to integer programming or heuristics.

Real-life example 1, a reservoir's water release: A hydroelectric dam must decide each month how much water to release to generate electricity, while keeping enough for the dry season and leaving space for monsoon floods. Stages are months, the state is the water level, and inflows are random. Stochastic DP gives a release rule for each month and level, balancing power now against power and safety later.

Real-life example 2, replacing a delivery fleet's motorbikes: A courier company asks each year whether to keep each motorbike or replace it. Repair costs and breakdowns rise with age; resale value falls. With state = age (0 to 6 years) and stages = years in the planning horizon, a small DP table shows that replacing at 4 years minimises total cost over 10 years. The answer is easy to explain to management because each table entry has a meaning: the best future cost from that age.

Common mistakes: Choosing a state that does not contain enough information (then the principle of optimality fails). Solving forwards greedily instead of backwards with value functions. Forgetting to record the best decision at each state, so you have the optimal value but cannot rebuild the plan. Mixing up stage numbering. Using DP on a problem with a huge state space without simplification.

What exams ask: State Bellman's principle of optimality. Define stages, states, decisions and the recursive equation for a given problem. Solve a stagecoach (shortest route) problem with backward recursion, showing a table per stage. Solve a resource allocation or knapsack problem by DP. Explain the curse of dimensionality and compare DP with greedy and brute force.

Recap: Dynamic programming splits a decision into stages, defines the state, and solves backwards using f_n(s) = best over decisions of [immediate return + f_(n+1)(next state)], based on Bellman's principle of optimality. The stagecoach answer was Dhaka, Chandpur, Noakhali, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar for 13, beating greedy's 14; the doctor allocation was 2, 1, 1 for 98 patients. DP reuses sub-problem answers, extends to random settings as Markov decision processes, but suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Next, lesson 18 starts inventory theory: how much to order and when.
key_points: DP splits a problem into stages with states and decisions, and solves backwards with stored sub-answers.
Bellman's principle: the remaining decisions of an optimal policy are optimal for the resulting state.
Recursion: f_n(s) = best over x of [return of x in s + f_(n+1)(next state)].
Stagecoach: optimal route Dhaka, Chandpur, Noakhali, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar = 13; greedy gets 14.
Doctor allocation: f1 options 81, 97, 98, 88, 70; optimum 2, 1, 1 doctors for 98 patients a day.
DP turns 10^9 routes into about 1,000 operations by solving each state once.
Knapsack DP is pseudo-polynomial; stochastic DP is a Markov decision process, the base of reinforcement learning.
The curse of dimensionality: state spaces explode when the state has many components.
lessons.tip: Before writing any equation, say the state in words: 'what do I need to know at this stage to decide the rest optimally?' If the answer is short, DP will work well. If it is long, look for a smaller state or another method.
lessons.task: You have 5 hours to study for 3 exams. Make a table of expected marks gained for 0 to 5 hours on each subject (use diminishing returns). Solve by dynamic programming with stages = subjects and state = hours left, showing each stage table. Compare your answer with the greedy plan of always putting the next hour where it gains the most.

quiz.q: What does Bellman's principle of optimality say?
options: Always pick the cheapest next decision
The remaining decisions of an optimal policy must be optimal for the state they start from
Every DP has exactly two stages
The first decision is always the most important
quiz.explain: If the tail of an optimal plan were not optimal, swapping in a better tail would improve the whole plan.

quiz.q: In the stagecoach example, what is f(Noakhali)?
quiz.explain: From Noakhali: Chattogram 5 + 4 = 9 or Bandarban 3 + 3 = 6; the minimum is 6.

quiz.q: What total cost does the greedy traveller get, compared with DP's 13?
quiz.explain: Greedy goes Dhaka, Cumilla, Feni, Chattogram, Cox's Bazar: 4 + 3 + 3 + 4 = 14.

quiz.q: In the doctor allocation, why does clinic 1 get 2 doctors?
options: Stage 1 options give 81, 97, 98, 88, 70 and 98 is the largest, at x = 2
quiz.explain: 50 + f2(2) = 50 + 48 = 98 beats every other choice for clinic 1.

quiz.q: What is the curse of dimensionality?
options: The number of states grows explosively when the state has many components
DP always needs exactly n cubed steps
quiz.explain: A state with many parts, like stock levels of 20 products, creates far too many states to store and compute.

lessons.title: Inventory Models I: The Economic Order Quantity
lessons.content:
Your mother buys rice. If she buys 2 kg every day, she spends a lot of time and rickshaw fare going to the bazar. If she buys a 50 kg sack once in a few months, the trips stop, but the money is stuck in rice, the sack takes space, and insects might get in. Somewhere in between there is a sensible amount to buy each time. Every shop, pharmacy, factory and hospital faces the same question for thousands of items. Inventory theory is the part of OR that answers it, and its most famous result, the economic order quantity, is over a hundred years old and still used every day.

What inventory is and why we hold it: Inventory is stock kept for future use: raw materials, parts, finished goods, medicines, cash at an agent shop. We hold it because supply and demand do not happen at the same moment: ordering takes time, buying in batches is cheaper per trip, demand is uncertain, and running out loses sales or stops production. But holding stock also costs money. Inventory models balance these costs.

The costs: Ordering (or setup) cost S: a fixed cost each time you place an order, regardless of size: paperwork, transport trip, delivery fee, or for a factory the cost of setting up a machine. Holding (or carrying) cost H: the cost of keeping one unit in stock for a year: the interest the money could have earned, storage space, insurance, spoilage. Often H is a percentage of the unit price, like 20% a year. Purchase cost: the price per unit, which matters only if it depends on order size (lesson 19). Shortage cost: lost profit or goodwill when you run out; the basic EOQ model does not allow shortages.

The basic EOQ assumptions: Demand is known and constant, D units per year. The lead time (time between ordering and receiving) is known and constant. The whole order arrives at once. No shortages are allowed. Ordering cost per order and holding cost per unit per year are constant, and the unit price does not depend on the order size. These are strong assumptions, but the model is surprisingly robust, as we will see.

The sawtooth picture: With order quantity Q, stock jumps up to Q when an order arrives, then falls steadily at rate D until it hits zero, exactly when the next order arrives. Plotted against time, it looks like the teeth of a saw. The average stock is Q / 2 (halfway between Q and 0). The number of orders per year is D / Q.

The total cost: Annual ordering cost = (D / Q) x S: more orders when Q is small. Annual holding cost = (Q / 2) x H: more stock held when Q is large. Total relevant cost TC(Q) = (D / Q) S + (Q / 2) H. As Q grows, the first term falls and the second rises. The best Q balances them.

Deriving the EOQ: Take the derivative of TC with respect to Q and set it to zero: -D S / Q squared + H / 2 = 0, so Q squared = 2 D S / H, and Q* = square root of (2 D S / H). At this point the ordering cost and holding cost are exactly equal. This formula is often called the Wilson formula; it was first published by Ford W. Harris in 1913. If you do not like calculus, you can also find it by noticing that the sum of a falling and a rising curve of these shapes is smallest where they cross.

Worked example, a pharmacy: A pharmacy in Mohammadpur sells 12,000 boxes of a common medicine a year, steadily. Each order costs 500 taka (delivery and paperwork). Holding one box for a year costs 12 taka. EOQ = square root of (2 x 12,000 x 500 / 12) = square root of 1,000,000 = 1,000 boxes. Number of orders per year = 12,000 / 1,000 = 12, about one a month. Annual ordering cost = 12 x 500 = 6,000 taka. Annual holding cost = (1,000 / 2) x 12 = 6,000 taka. Total = 12,000 taka, with the two parts equal as promised.

Cycle time: The time between orders is Q / D years. Here 1,000 / 12,000 = 1/12 of a year. If the pharmacy works 300 days a year, that is 300 / 12 = 25 working days between orders. Daily demand is 12,000 / 300 = 40 boxes.

Reorder point: Orders do not arrive instantly. If the supplier takes L days to deliver (the lead time), you must order when the remaining stock just covers demand during those days. Reorder point R = daily demand x lead time. With 40 boxes a day and a 5-day lead time, R = 200 boxes: whenever stock drops to 200 boxes, place an order for 1,000. The stock reaches zero exactly when the new boxes arrive. If the lead time is longer than a cycle, multiple orders are outstanding at once, but the rule R = d x L still works if you count stock on order.

How sensitive is the cost: Suppose the pharmacy orders 800 boxes instead of 1,000. Total cost = (12,000 / 800) x 500 + (800 / 2) x 12 = 7,500 + 4,800 = 12,300 taka, only 2.5% more. Ordering 1,200 gives 5,000 + 7,200 = 12,200 taka, 1.7% more. Ordering 1,500 gives 13,000, 8.3% more, and ordering 500 or 2,000 gives 15,000, 25% more. The cost curve is flat near the optimum. So rounding the EOQ to a convenient pack size, like full cartons, costs almost nothing, and moderate errors in D, S or H do little harm.

Why the square root matters: Because of the square root, if demand quadruples, the EOQ only doubles: with D = 48,000, EOQ = 2,000, not 4,000. If the ordering cost falls to a quarter (for example, online ordering with free delivery), the EOQ halves to 500 and the shop orders twice as often. This is the logic behind just-in-time manufacturing: cut setup costs dramatically, and small frequent batches become optimal, which reduces inventory.

Holding cost as a percentage: Often you are given the unit price C and an annual carrying rate i, so H = i x C. If the medicine costs 60 taka a box and the carrying rate is 20%, H = 0.20 x 60 = 12 taka, which is where our number came from. Do not forget to convert: if H is given per month, multiply by 12 to match annual demand. Mixing a monthly H with an annual D is a classic error.

A second worked example with unit conversion: A tea stall uses 35 kg of sugar a week. Each trip to the wholesale market costs 60 taka in rickshaw fare and time. Keeping sugar costs about 2 taka per kg per month (money tied up plus ants and moisture). Convert to years first: D = 35 x 52 = 1,820 kg a year and H = 2 x 12 = 24 taka per kg per year. EOQ = square root of (2 x 1,820 x 60 / 24) = square root of 9,100, about 95 kg. That is about 19 trips a year, one every 2.7 weeks. The owner can simply buy two 50 kg sacks per trip: Q = 100 costs 2,292 taka a year against about 2,289 at the exact EOQ, a difference of 3 taka.

Why holding cost is real even when nothing is paid: Many shop owners say "the stock is mine, holding it costs nothing". But the 1,00,000 taka sitting in boxes could have paid off a loan, earned bank interest or bought a faster-selling item. That lost earning is an opportunity cost, and it is usually the largest part of H. Add rent for shelf space, breakage, theft, expiry and insurance, and textbooks commonly assume 20% to 30% of the item's value per year.

Beyond the formula, practical limits: Real orders have limits: the supplier may sell only in cartons of 100, the warehouse may hold only 800 boxes, medicines expire. These become constraints, and because the cost curve is flat, the best feasible Q is usually just the nearest allowed value to the EOQ. If storage allows only 800, order 800 at a cost of 12,300 instead of 12,000; the shelf limit costs only 300 taka a year.

Real-life example 1, a bKash-style agent's cash: An agent shop must keep cash for customers who cash out. Each trip to the bank to withdraw cash costs time and transport, a fixed cost S per trip. Holding a large cash pile has an opportunity cost (the money could earn interest or e-money commission) and a risk cost, a holding cost H. With steady daily cash-out demand, the EOQ logic tells the agent roughly how much cash to bring each trip. This is the Baumol model of cash management, which is the EOQ in disguise.

Real-life example 2, a garments factory's buttons and zippers: A factory uses 2,40,000 buttons of one type a year. Each import order has a fixed cost of LC opening, clearing and transport. Holding buttons ties up working capital. The EOQ gives the economical batch size; the factory then rounds it to whole shipping cartons and checks it against the supplier's minimum order. Doing this across hundreds of accessories can free a large amount of working capital.

Common mistakes: Using monthly demand with annual holding cost. Forgetting the factor 2 in the formula. Using average stock = Q instead of Q / 2. Confusing reorder point (when to order) with order quantity (how much). Treating EOQ as exact when the inputs are rough; it is a guide, and the flat curve gives freedom. Applying EOQ when demand is very lumpy or seasonal, where other methods (lesson 19 or dynamic programming) fit better.

What exams ask: Derive the EOQ formula. Compute EOQ, number of orders, cycle time, annual ordering and holding costs and total cost for given data. Find the reorder point with a given lead time. Show the effect of ordering a different quantity and comment on sensitivity. Explain the assumptions and what happens when demand or ordering cost changes.

Recap: Inventory balances ordering cost S per order against holding cost H per unit per year. With constant demand D and no shortages, total cost is (D / Q) S + (Q / 2) H, minimised at EOQ = square root of (2 D S / H), where the two costs are equal. The pharmacy orders 1,000 boxes, 12 times a year, for 12,000 taka total, reordering at 200 boxes with a 5-day lead time. The cost curve is flat: 800 boxes costs only 2.5% more. Next, lesson 19 relaxes the assumptions: production at a finite rate, quantity discounts, uncertain demand and safety stock.
key_points: Inventory balances ordering cost S (per order) against holding cost H (per unit per year).
Basic EOQ assumes constant known demand, constant lead time, instant delivery and no shortages.
Total cost TC(Q) = (D / Q) S + (Q / 2) H; average stock is Q / 2.
EOQ = square root of (2 D S / H); at the optimum ordering cost equals holding cost.
Pharmacy: D = 12,000, S = 500, H = 12 gives EOQ 1,000, 12 orders a year, total cost 12,000 taka.
Reorder point = daily demand x lead time: 40 x 5 = 200 boxes.
The cost curve is flat: ordering 800 costs only 2.5% more; quadrupling demand only doubles EOQ.
H is often i x price (20% of 60 taka = 12); keep all units annual.
lessons.tip: Before plugging into the EOQ formula, write D, S and H with their units in a line, like D = 12,000 per year, S = 500 per order, H = 12 per unit per year. If any unit says month or week, fix it first. Most EOQ mistakes are unit mistakes, not formula mistakes.
lessons.task: Pick an item your family or a local shop buys regularly (rice, gas cylinders, mobile recharge cards). Estimate yearly demand, the cost of one buying trip, and a yearly holding cost per unit. Compute the EOQ, number of orders per year and total cost, then compare with what is actually done. Finally, compute how much more it costs to order half or double the EOQ.

quiz.q: What is the EOQ for D = 12,000 per year, S = 500 taka per order, H = 12 taka per unit per year?
quiz.explain: EOQ = square root of (2 x 12,000 x 500 / 12) = square root of 1,000,000 = 1,000.

quiz.q: At the EOQ, how do annual ordering and holding costs compare?
quiz.explain: Setting the derivative to zero gives (D/Q)S = (Q/2)H, so the two costs are equal (6,000 each here).

quiz.q: Daily demand is 40 boxes and lead time is 5 days. What is the reorder point?
quiz.explain: Reorder point = daily demand x lead time = 40 x 5 = 200 boxes.

quiz.q: If annual demand quadruples and everything else stays the same, the EOQ:
quiz.explain: EOQ grows with the square root of D, and the square root of 4 is 2.

quiz.q: The pharmacy orders 800 instead of the EOQ of 1,000. Roughly how much does total cost rise?
quiz.explain: Cost becomes 7,500 + 4,800 = 12,300 versus 12,000, about 2.5% more, because the curve is flat near the optimum.

lessons.title: Inventory Models II: Production, Discounts, Safety Stock and the Newsvendor
lessons.content:
The EOQ in lesson 18 lived in a perfect world: steady demand, instant delivery of the whole order, one fixed price, and no surprises. Real life breaks each of those. A factory makes its own goods slowly instead of receiving them all at once. A supplier offers a lower price if you buy more. Demand jumps around, so you can run out even with a good reorder point. And some goods, like newspapers, fresh fish or Eid clothes, lose their value if unsold by the end of the day or season. This lesson extends the EOQ to handle each of these, one at a time.

Production order quantity (EPQ), the idea: When a company produces an item itself, stock does not jump to Q at once. During a production run, units are made at rate P per year while being used at rate D (with P > D), so stock rises at the rate P - D. When the run ends, stock falls at rate D until the next run. The maximum stock is therefore less than Q: it is Q x (1 - D / P). Because less stock is held, the optimal batch is larger than the EOQ.

EPQ formula: Total cost = (D / Q) S + (Imax / 2) H, with Imax = Q (1 - D / P). Minimising gives Q* = square root of [2 D S / (H (1 - D / P))]. Here S is the setup cost of a production run. When P is huge compared with D, (1 - D / P) is close to 1 and the EPQ becomes the ordinary EOQ.

EPQ worked: A small pharmaceutical plant in Gazipur needs 12,000 cartons of a syrup a year and can produce at a rate of 48,000 cartons a year. Each production run costs 500 taka to set up, and holding a carton costs 16 taka a year. 1 - D / P = 1 - 12,000 / 48,000 = 0.75. Q* = square root of (2 x 12,000 x 500 / (16 x 0.75)) = square root of (12,000,000 / 12) = square root of 1,000,000 = 1,000 cartons. Maximum stock = 1,000 x 0.75 = 750 cartons. Each run lasts 1,000 / 48,000 of a year, about 6.25 working days out of 300. There are 12 runs a year. Setup cost 12 x 500 = 6,000 and holding cost (750 / 2) x 16 = 6,000, total 12,000 taka.

Planned shortages, briefly: Sometimes customers are willing to wait (backorders), like a furniture shop where buyers accept delivery next week. Allowing planned shortages, with a cost B per unit short per year, lets you hold less stock. The optimal order quantity becomes the EOQ multiplied by the square root of (H + B) / B. If B is very large (customers hate waiting), this factor approaches 1 and we are back to no shortages.

Quantity discounts, the problem: Suppliers often say "buy more, pay less per unit". Now the purchase cost D x price matters, because it changes with Q. The pharmacy from lesson 18 (D = 12,000, S = 500, holding rate 20% of price) is offered: 60 taka per box for orders below 1,500, 58 taka for 1,500 to 2,999, and 57 taka for 3,000 or more. Bigger orders cut the price but raise holding cost.

Quantity discounts, the method: For each price level: 1. Compute the EOQ with that price's H. 2. If the EOQ is below the level's minimum quantity, raise Q to that minimum (the cost curve is rising there, so the closest feasible point is best). 3. Compute total cost = ordering + holding + purchase. Choose the level with the lowest total.

Quantity discounts worked: Price 60: H = 12, EOQ = 1,000, feasible. Total = 6,000 + 6,000 + 12,000 x 60 = 7,32,000 taka. Price 58: H = 11.6, EOQ about 1,017, below 1,500, so use Q = 1,500. Total = (12,000 / 1,500) x 500 + (1,500 / 2) x 11.6 + 12,000 x 58 = 4,000 + 8,700 + 6,96,000 = 7,08,700 taka. Price 57: H = 11.4, EOQ about 1,026, so use Q = 3,000. Total = 2,000 + 17,100 + 6,84,000 = 7,03,100 taka. The cheapest is ordering 3,000 boxes at 57 taka, saving about 29,000 taka a year compared with the EOQ at 60. But check practical limits first: is there space for 3,000 boxes, and will they expire before being sold?

Uncertain demand and safety stock: In reality daily demand varies. If you reorder at exactly the average lead-time demand, you will run out about half the time. The fix is safety stock: extra stock kept to absorb higher-than-average demand during the lead time. Reorder point R = average demand during lead time + safety stock.

Safety stock worked: The pharmacy's daily demand is roughly normal with mean 40 and standard deviation 10 boxes, and lead time is 5 days. Demand during lead time has mean 5 x 40 = 200 and standard deviation 10 x square root of 5, about 22.36 (variances add over independent days, as in PERT). For a 95% cycle service level (no stockout in 95% of order cycles), z = 1.645, so safety stock = 1.645 x 22.36, about 37 boxes, and R = 200 + 37 = 237 boxes. For 99%, z = 2.326 and safety stock is about 52. Each extra percent of service gets more expensive.

Service level trade-off: Safety stock costs holding cost forever: 37 boxes x 12 taka = 444 taka a year here. Stockouts cost lost sales and lost customers. A pharmacy might choose 98% for life-saving medicines and 90% for cosmetics. This choice is a management decision about risk, and the model's job is to show its cost clearly.

Continuous and periodic review: In a continuous review (Q, R) system, stock is watched all the time and an order of fixed size Q is placed whenever stock hits R; barcode systems make this easy. In a periodic review system, stock is checked every T days (say every Monday), and you order enough to bring stock up to a target level. Periodic review is simpler to manage, especially when many items come from one supplier, but needs more safety stock because it must cover demand over T plus the lead time.

ABC analysis: A shop with 3,000 items cannot model each one carefully. ABC analysis sorts items by annual value (demand x price).
