Typically a small share of items, the A items (around 10 to 20%), account for most of the value (around 70 to 80%); B items are the middle; and C items, the majority by count, are a small share of value. Use careful models and tight control for A, simple rules for C. It is the Pareto principle applied to stock.

The newsvendor problem, the idea: Some goods have one selling period: newspapers, fresh fish, Eid fashion, cricket World Cup jerseys. You order once, before demand is known. Order too many and you lose money on leftovers; order too few and you lose profit on missed sales. Let Cu be the cost of understocking per unit (lost profit = price - cost) and Co the cost of overstocking per unit (cost - salvage value). The optimal order is the smallest Q such that the probability of demand <= Q is at least the critical ratio Cu / (Cu + Co).

Newsvendor worked: A newspaper hawker at Farmgate buys papers at 7 taka, sells at 10, and returns unsold ones for 1 taka. Cu = 10 - 7 = 3 and Co = 7 - 1 = 6. Critical ratio = 3 / (3 + 6) = 1/3, about 0.333. Daily demand: 40 papers with probability 0.10, 50 with 0.20, 60 with 0.30, 70 with 0.25, 80 with 0.15. Cumulative probabilities: 0.10, 0.30, 0.60, 0.85, 1.00. The smallest Q with cumulative probability at least 0.333 is 60. Expected profits confirm it: ordering 40, 50, 60, 70 or 80 gives 120, 141, 144, 120 and 73.5 taka a day; 60 is best.

Why the hawker orders below the most popular amount: Because leftovers hurt twice as much as shortages here (6 versus 3), the hawker should lean low. If the newspaper company took back unsold papers at the full 7 taka (Co = 0), the ratio would be 1 and he should order the maximum demand. This is why publishers and fashion brands sometimes offer buy-back deals: they push retailers to stock more.

Real-life example 1, Eid clothing at a Dhaka boutique: A boutique orders a special Eid collection months ahead from a factory. Unsold pieces after Eid sell at half price. Using last year's sales and the newsvendor critical ratio, the owner sets order quantities per design, stocking more of designs with high margins and higher salvage value, and fewer of risky trendy designs. The model turns a gut-feel bet into a calculated one.

Real-life example 2, a hospital's blood bank and medicines: A district hospital keeps insulin, saline and antibiotics. For each it uses a (Q, R) policy: EOQ-style batch sizes from the central medical store, reorder points with safety stock based on daily usage variability and the supply lead time, and a higher service level for critical items. Expiry adds a constraint: Q must be used before expiry, which caps the order size for slow-moving items.

Common mistakes: Using the EOQ formula when production is gradual (forgetting 1 - D / P). In quantity discounts, ignoring the purchase cost or forgetting to raise an infeasible EOQ to the price break. Using the lead-time demand standard deviation as sd times L instead of sd times the square root of L. Confusing cycle service level with fill rate. In the newsvendor, using Co / (Cu + Co) instead of Cu / (Cu + Co), or picking the most likely demand instead of the critical fractile.

What exams ask: Compute EPQ, maximum inventory, run length and total cost. Solve a quantity discount problem with two or three price breaks. Compute safety stock and reorder point for a given service level with normal demand. Solve a discrete newsvendor problem with the critical ratio and verify with expected profit. Explain ABC analysis and the difference between continuous and periodic review.

Recap: EPQ = square root of [2DS / (H(1 - D/P))] for gradual production: 1,000 cartons with maximum stock 750. For quantity discounts, compute the EOQ per price, push it up to the break if needed, and compare total costs including purchase: ordering 3,000 at 57 taka wins. Safety stock = z x sd of lead-time demand: about 37 boxes for 95%, so R = 237. ABC focuses effort on high-value items. The newsvendor orders up to the critical ratio Cu / (Cu + Co): the hawker buys 60 papers. Next, lesson 20 turns to queues: waiting lines at counters, servers and roads.
key_points: EPQ = square root of [2DS / (H(1 - D/P))]; maximum stock = Q(1 - D/P); example 1,000 cartons, max 750, total 12,000 taka.
Planned backorders multiply the EOQ by the square root of (H + B) / B.
Quantity discounts: compute EOQ per price, raise it to the break if below, compare total cost including purchase cost.
Pharmacy discounts: 60 taka gives 7,32,000, 58 taka at 1,500 gives 7,08,700, 57 taka at 3,000 gives 7,03,100 (best).
Safety stock = z x sd of lead-time demand; sd over L days = daily sd x square root of L; 95% gives about 37 boxes, R = 237.
Continuous review orders Q at R; periodic review orders up to a level every T days and needs more safety stock.
ABC analysis: few A items carry most value; control them tightly.
Newsvendor: order the smallest Q with P(demand <= Q) >= Cu / (Cu + Co); hawker's ratio 1/3 gives 60 papers.
lessons.tip: For every inventory problem, first ask which assumption of the basic EOQ is broken: gradual production, price breaks, random demand, or a single selling period. That one question tells you which of the four models in this lesson to use.
lessons.task: Ask a local shop how they order one fast-moving item: how often, how much, and whether bigger orders get a discount. Estimate D, S, H and the price breaks, and solve the quantity discount problem. Then think of one item they sell that loses value quickly (bread, flowers, fish) and set up the newsvendor critical ratio for it.

quiz.q: For D = 12,000, P = 48,000, S = 500 and H = 16, what is the EPQ?
quiz.explain: EPQ = square root of (2 x 12,000 x 500 / (16 x 0.75)) = square root of 1,000,000 = 1,000.

quiz.q: In the quantity discount example, the EOQ at 58 taka is about 1,017 but that price needs at least 1,500. What do you do?
quiz.explain: Below the break the cost is falling toward it, so the best feasible order at that price is the break quantity.

quiz.q: Daily demand has sd 10 and lead time is 5 days. What is the sd of lead-time demand?
quiz.explain: Variances add over independent days: sd = 10 x square root of 5, about 22.36.

quiz.q: For the hawker, Cu = 3 and Co = 6. What is the critical ratio?
quiz.explain: Critical ratio = Cu / (Cu + Co) = 3 / 9 = 1/3.

quiz.q: Which items get the tightest inventory control in ABC analysis?
options: C items, because they are the most numerous
A items, the few that make up most of the annual value
quiz.explain: A items carry most of the money, so careful models and close monitoring pay off most there.

lessons.title: Queuing Theory I: Little's Law and the M/M/1 Queue
lessons.content:
Think of the last time you stood in a line: at a bank, a bKash agent shop, a passport office, a ticket counter at Kamalapur, or even at the school canteen. Waiting feels like wasted time, and it is: for customers, for businesses that lose impatient customers, and for whole cities stuck in traffic. But adding more counters costs money, and counters standing idle waste money too. Queuing theory is the mathematics of waiting lines. It predicts how long the line will be and how long people will wait, before anyone builds anything, so managers can decide how many servers to provide.

What a queue is: A queuing system has customers who arrive, wait in a line if the server is busy, get served, and leave. The customer might be a person, a phone call, a data packet in a router, a truck at a port, a job sent to a printer or a request to a web server. The server might be a cashier, a doctor, a crane, a CPU. The theory began in 1909 with A. K. Erlang, a Danish engineer who wanted to know how many telephone lines a Copenhagen exchange needed.

Why queues form at all: If a counter can serve 25 people an hour and only 20 come, why does anyone wait? Because arrivals are random. Sometimes three people arrive within one minute and sometimes nobody comes for ten minutes. Service times are random too. During a burst, a line builds up; during a quiet spell, the server sits idle and that idle time can never be used later. Randomness is the reason a system with spare capacity on average still has lines.

The parts of a queue: The arrival process: how customers arrive, usually described by the arrival rate lambda (customers per hour). The service process: how long service takes, described by the service rate mu (customers per hour one server can handle when busy). The number of servers c. The queue discipline: usually first come, first served (FCFS), but also priority (emergency patients first) or last in, first out. The system capacity: is there a maximum line length? The calling population: is it effectively infinite, like a city, or small, like 5 machines that may break down?

Kendall notation: Queues are named in the form A/B/c, introduced by D. G. Kendall in 1953. A describes arrivals, B describes service times, and c is the number of servers. M stands for Markovian (memoryless): Poisson arrivals or exponential service times. D means deterministic (constant), and G means general (any distribution). So M/M/1 is Poisson arrivals, exponential service, one server. M/D/1 has constant service time, like an automatic car wash. M/M/3 is a bank with three counters. Extra letters can add capacity K and population size, as in M/M/1/K.

Poisson arrivals and exponential service: In a Poisson process with rate lambda, the number of arrivals in any period follows a Poisson distribution, and the time between arrivals is exponential with mean 1 / lambda. This fits well when many independent people each decide on their own when to come, which you studied in Probability & Statistics (deep-cse-2-6). The exponential distribution is memoryless: if a service has already taken 5 minutes, the expected remaining time is the same as for a fresh one. That property is what makes M/M models easy to solve.

Utilisation: The traffic intensity or utilisation is rho = lambda / mu for one server: the fraction of time the server is busy. If 20 customers arrive per hour and the server can do 25 per hour, rho = 0.8: busy 80% of the time and idle 20%. For a stable queue, rho must be less than 1. If lambda >= mu, more people arrive than can be served on average and the line grows without limit.

The four key measures: L = average number of customers in the system (waiting plus being served). Lq = average number waiting in the queue only. W = average time a customer spends in the system. Wq = average time waiting before service starts. Managers care about Wq (customer annoyance), Lq (space needed for the line) and rho (staff use).

Little's law: The most useful result in queuing: L = lambda x W. It holds for almost any stable queue, whatever the distributions, and also for the waiting line alone: Lq = lambda x Wq. It was proven in general by John Little in 1961. Intuition: if 20 people arrive per hour and each stays 0.2 hours, then on average 20 x 0.2 = 4 people are inside. It works for a shop, a hospital ward (patients per day times length of stay = beds occupied) or a university (students admitted per year times years of study = students enrolled).

M/M/1 formulas: For one server with Poisson arrivals and exponential service: L = rho / (1 - rho). Lq = rho squared / (1 - rho). W = 1 / (mu - lambda). Wq = rho / (mu - lambda). The probability the system is empty is P0 = 1 - rho, and the probability of exactly n customers is (1 - rho) x rho to the power n. The probability of at least k customers in the system is rho to the power k.

M/M/1 worked, a bKash agent shop: An agent shop in Mirpur serves cash-in and cash-out customers one at a time. On a weekday evening, customers arrive at about lambda = 20 per hour, and the agent takes on average 2.4 minutes per customer, so mu = 60 / 2.4 = 25 per hour. rho = 20 / 25 = 0.8. L = 0.8 / 0.2 = 4 customers in the shop on average. Lq = 0.64 / 0.2 = 3.2 waiting. W = 1 / (25 - 20) = 0.2 hours = 12 minutes in the shop. Wq = 0.8 / 5 = 0.16 hours = 9.6 minutes waiting. Check Little's law: L = 20 x 0.2 = 4, and Lq = 20 x 0.16 = 3.2. P0 = 0.2: the agent is idle 20% of the time, or 12 minutes each hour.

More from the same example: What is the chance a customer finds at least 4 people already in the shop? rho to the power 4 = 0.8^4, about 0.41. So about 41% of the time, an arriving customer sees a crowd of 4 or more and may walk away to another agent. The chance of finding the shop empty is 20%, and of finding exactly one person is 0.2 x 0.8 = 0.16.

The explosion near full utilisation: Now suppose it is the evening before Eid and arrivals rise. With mu = 25 fixed: lambda = 10 (rho 0.4) gives W = 4 minutes. lambda = 15 (rho 0.6) gives W = 6 minutes. lambda = 20 (rho 0.8) gives 12 minutes. lambda = 22 (rho 0.88) gives 20 minutes. lambda = 24 (rho 0.96) gives 60 minutes, with about 24 people in the system. A 20% rise in customers from 20 to 24 makes the wait five times longer. This sharp curve is the most important lesson of queuing: running a server close to 100% busy makes waits explode.

Why this matters for computers: The same curve appears in CPUs, disks, routers and web servers. A server at 50% CPU responds quickly; at 95% response times shoot up even though there is still 5% spare. This is why system designers target 60 to 70% utilisation for latency-sensitive services, and why autoscaling starts new machines long before a server reaches 100%. Operating Systems (deep-cse-4-1) scheduling and Computer Networks (deep-cse-4-3) router buffers both rely on this result.

Single line or separate lines: Suppose a shop has two agents. Should customers form one shared line or pick a line in front of each agent? With separate lines, one agent can sit idle while the other has three people waiting, and customers who pick a slow line feel cheated. A single shared line feeding both servers never lets a server idle while someone waits, and it is fairer because people are served in arrival order. That is why banks, airports and passport offices increasingly use one snake line or a token system. Lesson 21 puts numbers on this pooling effect.

How to improve a queue: Increase mu: train staff, simplify forms, use a faster machine. Add servers (lesson 21). Reduce variability: appointments or token systems smooth arrivals; standard procedures make service times more even. Shift demand: off-peak discounts. Change perception: show the expected wait, give a token number so people can sit, entertain them. Even if the real wait does not change, people are less unhappy when they know how long it will be.

Real-life example 1, a hospital outdoor ticket counter: A district hospital's outdoor ticket counter sees long lines from 8 to 10 am. Measurements show lambda = 90 patients per hour and one clerk serving 100 per hour, rho = 0.9, so W = 1 / (100 - 90) hours = 6 minutes on paper but much worse during bursts, and lines spill outside. A second counter or online tickets during the peak hours, plus a token display, cut both the actual and the perceived wait.

Real-life example 2, a web API: A small startup's API server processes 50 requests per second on average, and arrivals average 40 per second. As an M/M/1 approximation, rho = 0.8 and W = 1 / (50 - 40) = 0.1 seconds = 100 ms. Marketing plans a campaign that may raise traffic to 48 per second: W would become 1 / 2 = 0.5 seconds, five times slower. The team adds a second server before the campaign instead of after the complaints.

Common mistakes: Mixing units: lambda per hour with mu per minute. Using service time instead of service rate (2.4 minutes per customer means mu = 25 per hour, not 2.4). Forgetting that W includes service time while Wq does not. Applying M/M/1 formulas when rho >= 1 (no steady state exists). Thinking a server at 80% is underused; that 20% idle time is what keeps waits reasonable.

What exams ask: Explain the parts of a queuing system and Kendall notation. State and use Little's law. For given lambda and mu, compute rho, L, Lq, W, Wq, P0 and probabilities of n customers. Show what happens to waiting time as lambda approaches mu. Choose between options, like a faster single server or a slower one, by comparing W or total cost.

Recap: Queues form because arrivals and service are random. Kendall notation A/B/c names a model; M/M/1 has Poisson arrivals, exponential service and one server. Utilisation rho = lambda / mu must be below 1. Little's law L = lambda W holds for almost any stable system. In M/M/1, L = rho / (1 - rho) and W = 1 / (mu - lambda): the agent shop with 20 arrivals and rate 25 has 4 customers inside and a 12-minute visit, rising to 60 minutes when arrivals reach 24. Next, lesson 21 adds more servers, finite waiting rooms and the cost of waiting.
key_points: Queues form because arrivals and service times are random, even when average capacity is enough.
Kendall notation A/B/c: M = Markovian (Poisson/exponential), D = constant, G = general; M/M/1 has one server.
Utilisation rho = lambda / mu must be below 1; P0 = 1 - rho is the idle probability.
Little's law: L = lambda W and Lq = lambda Wq, valid for almost any stable queue.
M/M/1: L = rho/(1 - rho), Lq = rho squared/(1 - rho), W = 1/(mu - lambda), Wq = rho/(mu - lambda).
Agent shop: lambda 20, mu 25 gives rho 0.8, L 4, Lq 3.2, W 12 minutes, Wq 9.6 minutes.
Waits explode near rho = 1: lambda 24 gives W = 60 minutes, five times the wait at 20.
Improve queues by faster service, more servers, less variability, shifting demand and managing perception.
lessons.tip: Always convert service time into service rate first and put both rates in the same unit. Write lambda = ... per hour and mu = ... per hour on one line before using any formula, then check rho < 1. Most queuing mistakes are unit or rate-versus-time mix-ups.
lessons.task: Stand near a busy counter for 30 minutes (a shop, canteen, or ATM). Count arrivals and time several services. Estimate lambda and mu per hour, compute rho, L, Lq, W and Wq with the M/M/1 formulas, and compare W with the waiting times you observed. Then compute what would happen if arrivals rose by 20%.

quiz.q: In Kendall notation, what does M/M/1 mean?
options: Many arrivals, many servers, one queue
Poisson arrivals, exponential service times, one server
Constant arrivals, constant service, one server
Markov arrivals, multiple queues, one customer
quiz.explain: M stands for Markovian (memoryless): Poisson arrivals and exponential service; 1 is the number of servers.

quiz.q: A ward admits 12 patients a day and each stays 5 days on average. How many beds are occupied on average?
quiz.explain: Little's law: L = lambda x W = 12 x 5 = 60 beds.

quiz.q: For lambda = 20 per hour and mu = 25 per hour, what is W in an M/M/1 queue?
quiz.explain: W = 1 / (mu - lambda) = 1 / 5 hour = 12 minutes.

quiz.q: With mu = 25 fixed, arrivals rise from 20 to 24 per hour. What happens to W?
options: It rises from 12 to 60 minutes, five times longer
quiz.explain: W = 1/(25 - 24) hour = 60 minutes versus 1/5 hour = 12 minutes; waits explode near full utilisation.

quiz.q: An agent shop has rho = 0.8. What fraction of the time is the agent idle?
quiz.explain: P0 = 1 - rho = 0.2, so the agent is idle 20% of the time.

lessons.title: Queuing Theory II: Multiple Servers, Limited Space and Cost
lessons.content:
A bank branch in Motijheel opens at 10 am. Should it run three counters or four? A call centre must decide how many agents to roster for the evening shift. A small agent shop has room for only five people inside; anyone else turns away. A hospital wonders whether constant-time lab tests would shorten queues. Lesson 20 handled one server. This lesson extends queuing to several servers, finite waiting rooms and general service times, and then puts a price on waiting so we can choose the number of servers that costs least overall.

The M/M/c model: Customers arrive as a Poisson stream with rate lambda and join one shared line. There are c identical servers, each serving at rate mu with exponential service times. Whenever a server becomes free, the first person in line goes to it. Total capacity is c x mu, and the utilisation per server is rho = lambda / (c mu), which must be below 1. The offered load a = lambda / mu is the average number of busy servers.

Erlang C, the probability of waiting: Erlang worked out the probability that an arriving customer must wait because all c servers are busy. First, P0 = 1 / [sum for n from 0 to c - 1 of a^n / n! + a^c / (c! (1 - rho))]. Then P(wait) = a^c / (c! (1 - rho)) x P0. From it: Lq = P(wait) x rho / (1 - rho), Wq = Lq / lambda (Little's law), W = Wq + 1 / mu, and L = Lq + a. The formulas look heavy, but a calculator or a few lines of Python do them in seconds.

M/M/c worked, a bank with three counters: Customers arrive at lambda = 48 per hour. Each teller takes 3 minutes per customer on average, so mu = 20 per hour. With c = 3: a = 48 / 20 = 2.4 and rho = 2.4 / 3 = 0.8. Computing: P0 is about 0.056 and P(wait) is about 0.647, so about 65% of customers wait at least a little. Lq is about 2.59 people, Wq = 2.59 / 48 hours, about 3.24 minutes, W = 3.24 + 3 = about 6.24 minutes, and L = 2.59 + 2.4, about 4.99 customers in the branch.

Adding a fourth counter: With c = 4, rho = 2.4 / 4 = 0.6. Now P(wait) drops to about 0.29, Lq to about 0.43, and Wq to about 0.54 minutes, roughly 32 seconds. One extra teller cut the average wait by about 83%. Like the M/M/1 curve, the effect is strongest when servers are heavily loaded.

Pooling, one line versus separate lines: What if the same three tellers each had their own line, and customers split evenly, 16 per hour each? Each line is then an M/M/1 with lambda = 16 and mu = 20, rho = 0.8. Wq = 0.8 / (20 - 16) hours = 12 minutes and W = 15 minutes. The shared line gave Wq of about 3.24 minutes with the very same staff and the same utilisation. Pooling servers behind one line cuts waiting by almost three quarters here because no teller sits idle while someone waits in another line. This is the mathematics behind single snake lines, token systems, and shared server pools in cloud computing.

Economies of scale: Pooling also explains why big systems run more efficiently. A call centre with 100 agents at 90% utilisation can have short waits, while one agent at 90% would have long ones. Larger pools can run at higher utilisation for the same service level. That is why big hospitals, big data centres and big ride-hailing networks have an advantage in speed per unit of capacity.

Finite capacity, M/M/1/K: Sometimes the waiting space is limited to K customers in the system, including the one in service. When it is full, new arrivals are lost: they go elsewhere, or calls get a busy signal. With rho = lambda / mu (which may now even exceed 1): P0 = (1 - rho) / (1 - rho^(K + 1)) and Pn = P0 rho^n for n = 0 to K. The blocking probability is PK. The effective arrival rate is lambda (1 - PK), and Little's law must use this effective rate.

M/M/1/K worked: The agent shop from lesson 20 (lambda = 20, mu = 25, rho = 0.8) has room for only 5 people inside. P0 = 0.2 / (1 - 0.8^6), about 0.271, and P5 = 0.271 x 0.8^5, about 0.089. So about 8.9% of arriving customers find the shop full and leave: about 1.78 customers per hour lost. The effective arrival rate is about 18.22 per hour. L, the average number inside, is about 1.87, and W = L / effective rate, about 6.15 minutes. Waits are shorter than in the unlimited queue (12 minutes) only because some customers were turned away, which is lost business.

General service times, the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula: For one server with Poisson arrivals but any service distribution (M/G/1) with mean service time 1 / mu and standard deviation sigma: Lq = (lambda^2 sigma^2 + rho^2) / (2 (1 - rho)). For exponential service, sigma = 1 / mu and this gives the M/M/1 answer. For constant service (M/D/1), sigma = 0 and Lq is exactly half of the M/M/1 value.

P-K worked: For the agent shop, lambda = 20 per hour and mean service 2.4 minutes = 0.04 hours, so rho = 0.8. With exponential service (sigma = 0.04 hours), Lq = 3.2 and Wq = 9.6 minutes, as before. If the agent's service time were perfectly constant (sigma = 0), Lq = 0.64 / 0.4 = 1.6 and Wq = 4.8 minutes. With sigma = 0.02 hours, half the exponential spread, Lq = 2.0 and Wq = 6 minutes. Same average speed, less variability, much shorter queues. This is why standardised procedures and automation reduce waiting even without making service faster on average.

Priority, balking and reneging: Real customers do not always behave like the model. Some get priority: an emergency patient jumps the line, which shortens their wait but lengthens everyone else's. Some balk: they see a long line and leave without joining, like the full agent shop. Some renege: they join, wait a while, lose patience and leave. Each behaviour has its own formulas or is handled by simulation, but the main lessons stay the same: high utilisation and high variability make lines long, and pooling makes them shorter.

Measuring lambda and mu in practice: Count arrivals in many short periods (for example, every 15 minutes) and divide by the length to get lambda for each time of day; demand at 10 am is very different from 3 pm, so analyse each busy period separately. Time a few dozen services with a phone stopwatch to get the mean service time and its standard deviation. If the standard deviation is close to the mean, exponential service is a fair model; if much smaller, use the P-K formula.

Putting a cost on waiting: To choose the number of servers, compare service cost with waiting cost. Total cost per hour = c x (cost per server per hour) + (cost of waiting per customer per hour) x (number waiting or in system). The waiting cost might be lost productivity, lost goodwill, or, for a company's own staff or trucks, paid time spent waiting.

Cost model worked: The bank pays 300 taka per teller per hour, and management values a customer's time in the queue at 200 taka per hour (lost goodwill and business). With lambda = 48 and mu = 20: c = 3 gives 900 + 200 x 2.59, about 1,418 taka per hour. c = 4 gives 1,200 + 200 x 0.43, about 1,286 taka. c = 5 gives 1,500 + 200 x about 0.10, about 1,521 taka. The best choice is 4 tellers. A fifth teller costs 300 taka but saves only about 65 taka of waiting cost.

Workforce planning with queues: Call centres use Erlang C every day. For each half-hour, they forecast lambda, compute the minimum number of agents c so that, say, 80% of calls are answered within 20 seconds, then build shift rosters covering those numbers. Telecom companies size base stations and trunk lines with the Erlang B formula, the version for systems with no waiting room, where blocked calls are simply lost.

Networks of queues: Many systems are chains of queues: in a hospital, registration, then the doctor, then the lab, then the pharmacy. Jackson networks show that, under Poisson arrivals and exponential service, each station can be analysed as its own M/M/c queue using the total flow into it. The bottleneck is the station with the highest utilisation. For complex networks with priorities and breakdowns, analysts switch to simulation (Simulation & Modeling, deep-cse-6-5).

Real-life example 1, a passport office: A regional passport office had one long line at the biometric booths, with people waiting over two hours. Data showed lambda of about 100 applicants per hour and 6 booths each handling about 18 per hour, so rho was about 0.93. Using M/M/c, the office found that a seventh booth would bring rho to about 0.79 and cut average waiting dramatically, while online appointments smoothed arrivals. The combination costs far less than the hours lost by thousands of applicants.

Real-life example 2, cloud servers: A Bangladeshi e-commerce site runs on a pool of identical servers behind a load balancer, which is an M/M/c system. Before the 11.11 sale, engineers forecast peak lambda, set a target such as 99% of requests waiting less than 50 ms, and compute the number of servers needed with Erlang C. Pooling makes the shared cluster far more efficient than giving each product category its own server.

Common mistakes: Computing rho as lambda / mu instead of lambda / (c mu) for multiple servers. Forgetting that W = Wq + 1 / mu. In finite-capacity queues, using lambda instead of the effective rate in Little's law. Assuming separate lines are as good as one shared line. Choosing the number of servers by utilisation alone, without considering waiting cost or service targets.

What exams ask: Compute P0, P(wait), Lq, Wq, W and L for an M/M/2 or M/M/3 system. Compare a pooled system with separate M/M/1 lines. Compute blocking probability and effective arrival rate for M/M/1/K. Use the P-K formula to compare exponential and constant service. Find the number of servers that minimises total cost.

Recap: M/M/c uses Erlang C: the three-teller bank (lambda 48, mu 20) has rho 0.8, 65% of customers waiting and Wq about 3.24 minutes; a fourth teller cuts Wq to about half a minute. Pooling three separate lines into one cut Wq from 12 to about 3.24 minutes. M/M/1/K with room for 5 loses about 8.9% of customers. The P-K formula shows constant service halves the queue. A cost model chose 4 tellers at about 1,286 taka per hour. Next, lesson 22 moves to game theory: decisions when your opponent is also deciding.
key_points: M/M/c: shared line, c servers; per-server utilisation rho = lambda / (c mu) must be below 1.
Erlang C gives P(wait); then Lq = P(wait) rho / (1 - rho), Wq = Lq / lambda, W = Wq + 1 / mu.
Bank: lambda 48, mu 20, c = 3 gives P(wait) 0.65, Wq about 3.24 min; c = 4 gives Wq about 0.54 min.
Pooling: one shared line gives Wq 3.24 min versus 12 min for three separate M/M/1 lines with the same staff.
M/M/1/K: blocking probability PK; use the effective rate lambda (1 - PK) in Little's law; agent shop with K = 5 loses about 8.9%.
P-K formula: Lq = (lambda^2 sigma^2 + rho^2) / (2(1 - rho)); constant service halves Lq (3.2 to 1.6).
Cost model: minimise c x server cost + waiting cost x Lq; the bank's best is 4 tellers at about 1,286 taka per hour.
Erlang C sizes call centres; Erlang B sizes systems with no waiting room; complex networks need simulation.
lessons.tip: When comparing designs, keep a small table with columns c, rho, P(wait), Lq, Wq, W and total cost per hour. Five rows of that table usually make the decision obvious, and a few lines of Python with the Erlang C formula fill it in seconds.
lessons.task: Find a place with several servers (bank counters, toll booths, fuel pumps). Estimate lambda and mu by watching for 30 minutes. Compute Wq with the current number of servers and with one more, using Erlang C. Then check whether customers use one shared line or separate lines, and estimate how much waiting would change if they switched.

quiz.q: For lambda = 48, mu = 20 and c = 3, what is the per-server utilisation?
quiz.explain: rho = lambda / (c mu) = 48 / 60 = 0.8.

quiz.q: Three tellers each with their own line (16 per hour each, mu 20) give Wq = 12 minutes. One shared line gives about:
quiz.explain: Pooling uses idle tellers for anyone waiting; the M/M/3 calculation gives Wq about 3.24 minutes.

quiz.q: In an M/M/1/K queue, which arrival rate goes into Little's law?
quiz.explain: Blocked customers never enter, so only lambda (1 - PK) contributes to L = lambda W.

quiz.q: According to the P-K formula, how does constant service time change Lq compared with exponential service of the same mean?
quiz.explain: With sigma = 0, Lq = rho^2 / (2(1 - rho)), exactly half the M/M/1 value: 1.6 versus 3.2 here.

quiz.q: Tellers cost 300 taka per hour and waiting costs 200 taka per customer-hour in queue. Why is 5 tellers worse than 4?
options: The fifth costs 300 but saves only about 65 taka of waiting cost
Five tellers cannot share a line
Waiting cost rises with more tellers
quiz.explain: Total cost rises from about 1,286 to about 1,521 taka per hour because the extra wage exceeds the waiting cost saved.

lessons.title: Game Theory: Decisions Against a Thinking Opponent
lessons.content:
In every OR model so far, the world did not fight back. Demand, travel times and arrivals might be uncertain, but nature was not trying to beat you. Business is different. When one mobile operator cuts its data prices, the others respond. When a cricket captain sets a field, the batter adjusts. When you play rock-paper-scissors, your friend is trying to predict you. Game theory studies decisions where the outcome depends on the choices of two or more thinking players, each trying to do well for themselves.

What a game is: A game has players, strategies (the choices each player can make) and payoffs (what each player gets for every combination of choices). In this lesson we focus on the classic OR case: two-person zero-sum games, where one player's gain is exactly the other's loss, like two brands fighting over a fixed market share. The modern theory began with John von Neumann's minimax theorem in 1928 and his 1944 book with Oskar Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior.

The payoff matrix: Rows are player A's strategies, columns are player B's, and each cell is the payoff to A (and therefore the loss to B). A wants large numbers; B wants small numbers. Example: two cold drink brands in Dhaka, A and B, each plan a summer campaign. A can choose A1 (TV ads), A2 (social media) or A3 (shop discounts). B can choose B1, B2 or B3. The cell shows market share points A gains from B: A1 row: 4, 2, 5. A2 row: 6, 3, 4. A3 row: 1, 0, 7. These numbers are invented for teaching.

Maximin and minimax: A careful A assumes B will respond in the worst way for A. For each row, find the minimum: A1 gives 2, A2 gives 3, A3 gives 0. A picks the row with the largest minimum: A2, guaranteeing at least 3. That is A's maximin value. B thinks the same way: for each column, find the maximum (A's best response): B1 gives 6, B2 gives 3, B3 gives 7. B picks the smallest maximum: B2, guaranteeing A gets at most 3. That is B's minimax value.

Saddle points: When maximin equals minimax, as here (both 3), the game has a saddle point at (A2, B2) and the value of the game is 3. Neither player can gain by changing alone: if A switches from A2 to A1 or A3 while B stays at B2, A gets 2 or 0, less than 3; if B switches away from B2 while A stays at A2, A gets 6 or 4, worse for B. The cell 3 is the smallest in its row and the largest in its column, like the centre of a horse saddle. These are pure strategies: each player always plays one choice.

Games without a saddle point: Take the matrix with rows A1: 3, -1 and A2: -2, 4. Row minimums: -1 and -2, so maximin is -1. Column maximums: 3 and 4, so minimax is 3. They differ, so there is no saddle point. If A always plays A1, B will play B2 and A loses 1; if A always plays A2, B plays B1 and A loses 2. Any predictable choice can be exploited. The answer is to be unpredictable on purpose: a mixed strategy, choosing randomly with chosen probabilities.

Solving a 2x2 game with mixed strategies: Let A play A1 with probability p and A2 with 1 - p. A picks p so that B gets the same result whichever column B chooses; then B cannot exploit A. Against B1: 3p - 2(1 - p) = 5p - 2. Against B2: -p + 4(1 - p) = 4 - 5p. Set them equal: 5p - 2 = 4 - 5p, so p = 0.6. A plays A1 60% of the time and A2 40%. The value is 5 x 0.6 - 2 = 1. Similarly for B with probability q for B1: 3q - (1 - q) = -2q + 4(1 - q), giving 4q - 1 = 4 - 6q, so q = 0.5. The short formula for a 2x2 game with matrix a, b / c, d is value = (ad - bc) / (a + d - b - c) = (12 - 2) / (3 + 4 + 1 + 2) = 1.

Checking the mix: Suppose A plays 60:40 and B stubbornly always plays B1. A's average is 0.6 x 3 + 0.4 x (-2) = 1.8 - 0.8 = 1. If B always plays B2 instead: 0.6 x (-1) + 0.4 x 4 = -0.6 + 1.6 = 1. Any mix B tries also gives 1, because it is an average of two 1s. That is the whole idea: A's mix makes B indifferent, so B's choice no longer matters. In practice the random choice must be truly random, like a dice roll or a phone random number, not a pattern the opponent can learn.

What the mixed solution means: By mixing 60:40, A guarantees an average gain of 1 per play no matter what B does, even though every single pure strategy could lose. B, by mixing 50:50, guarantees A gets no more than 1 on average. Von Neumann's minimax theorem says every finite two-person zero-sum game has a value when mixed strategies are allowed. A penalty taker who always shoots left is easy to save; one who mixes is not. Studies of real football penalties have found players mixing close to what theory predicts.

Dominance, shrinking the game: A strategy is dominated if another strategy is always at least as good for that player, whatever the opponent does. Remove dominated strategies first. Example: rows A1: 3, -1, 4; A2: -2, 4, 5; A3: 2, -2, 3. Every entry of A3 is less than A1's (2 < 3, -2 < -1, 3 < 4), so A never plays A3: remove it. Now look at columns, where B prefers small numbers: B3's entries (4, 5) are larger than B1's (3, -2) in both rows, so B never plays B3: remove it. We are left with the 2x2 game above: value 1, A mixes 60:40, B mixes 50:50, and A3 and B3 are played with probability 0.

Graphical method for 2 x n games: When A has 2 strategies and B has many, plot A's expected payoff against p (probability of A1) for each of B's columns: each is a straight line. B will pick the column giving the lowest line at each p, so A looks at the lower envelope and chooses the p at its highest point. Example: A's rows are 1, 3, 6 and 5, 2, 1. Lines: B1 gives 5 - 4p, B2 gives 2 + p, B3 gives 1 + 5p. The highest point of the lower envelope is where B1 and B2 cross: 5 - 4p = 2 + p, p = 0.6, value 2.6. B3 gives 4 there, so B never uses it. Solving the 2x2 of B1 and B2 gives B's mix: 20% B1, 80% B2.

Games as linear programs: Any zero-sum game can be solved by LP. For A: maximise v subject to, for each column j, the sum over i of p_i x a_ij >= v, with the p_i adding to 1 and all p_i >= 0. B's problem is exactly the dual of A's problem, which is why maximin equals minimax: it is LP duality from lesson 7 in disguise. This lets computers solve games with hundreds of strategies, like security patrol scheduling.

Beyond zero-sum, the Nash equilibrium: Many real games are not zero-sum: both players can win or both can lose. Each player has their own payoff. A Nash equilibrium, defined by John Nash in 1950, is a set of strategies where no player can do better by changing only their own strategy. Every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium, possibly in mixed strategies. In zero-sum games, the Nash equilibrium is exactly the minimax solution.

The prisoner's dilemma, a price war: Two shops on the same road sell the same goods. If both keep prices high, each earns 10 thousand taka a day. If both cut prices, each earns 6. If one cuts and the other does not, the cutter earns 12 and the other 4. Whatever the other shop does, cutting is better for you (12 > 10 and 6 > 4), so cutting is a dominant strategy and the Nash equilibrium is both cutting, earning 6 each, even though both keeping high prices (10 each) is better for both. Individual logic leads to a worse shared outcome. Repeated play, trust, contracts and reputation can help escape the trap; that is one reason long-time neighbours often cooperate.

Limits of game theory: It assumes players are rational, know the payoffs, and know that the others are rational too. Real people make mistakes, have limited information, and care about fairness. Payoff numbers are often rough estimates. Still, the way of thinking is valuable: list your opponent's options, think about their best reply, avoid being predictable when that can be exploited, and look for dominated choices to discard.

Real-life example 1, telecom pricing: When mobile operators in a country plan data packs, each considers the others' likely responses. A deep discount might win share only until rivals match it, leaving everyone with lower revenue, a prisoner's dilemma. Analysts model these choices as games to estimate whether a move will trigger a price war, and regulators study the same structure when judging competition.

Real-life example 2, security patrols: Police or airport security cannot guard every place all the time. If patrols follow a fixed pattern, attackers learn it. Game theory, solved as an LP, computes randomised patrol schedules that make the best use of limited guards, giving more probability to high-value targets but never making any target completely predictable. Systems based on this idea have been used at real airports and ports.

Common mistakes: Taking row maximums instead of minimums for maximin. Forgetting that payoffs are to the row player, so the column player wants small numbers. Removing a strategy that is better in only some cells (it must be at least as good in every cell). Mixing up p and q when solving 2x2 games. Assuming a saddle point exists without checking maximin = minimax. Treating a non-zero-sum game as zero-sum.

What exams ask: Find a saddle point and the value of a game. Use dominance to reduce a matrix. Solve a 2x2 game for mixed strategies and value. Solve a 2 x n or m x 2 game graphically. Write a game as a linear program. Explain Nash equilibrium and the prisoner's dilemma with an example.

Recap: Game theory handles decisions against thinking opponents. In zero-sum games, A maximises its minimum and B minimises A's maximum; when they meet, the saddle point gives pure strategies, as in the drink campaign with value 3 at (A2, B2). Otherwise, mixed strategies make you unexploitable: the 3, -1 / -2, 4 game has A mixing 60:40, B 50:50, value 1. Dominance shrinks games, the graphical method solves 2 x n games, and LP duality proves minimax. Outside zero-sum, Nash equilibria can trap players in bad outcomes like price wars. Next, lesson 23 covers decisions against nature, under risk and uncertainty.
key_points: Game theory studies decisions where outcomes depend on other thinking players' choices.
Zero-sum payoff matrix: entries are A's gains; A wants large values, B wants small.
Maximin (best row minimum) and minimax (smallest column maximum); equal values mean a saddle point and pure strategies.
Drink example: maximin = minimax = 3 at (A2, B2).
No saddle point means mixed strategies; 2x2 value = (ad - bc) / (a + d - b - c); example 3, -1 / -2, 4 gives p = 0.6, q = 0.5, value 1.
Remove dominated strategies first; the graphical method solves 2 x n games (example value 2.6 at p = 0.6).
Every zero-sum game is an LP, and B's LP is the dual of A's.
Nash equilibrium: nobody gains by changing alone; the prisoner's dilemma shows it can be worse for everyone.
lessons.tip: Always check for a saddle point first: write row minimums down the side and column maximums along the bottom. If max of the first equals min of the second, you are done in one minute. Only if they differ, reduce by dominance and then mix.
lessons.task: Play rock-paper-scissors 30 times with a friend and record their choices. Write the 3x3 payoff matrix (win 1, draw 0, lose -1), check that it has no saddle point, and argue why the best mixed strategy is one third each. Then look at your friend's record: were they predictable, and how could you have exploited it?

quiz.q: Rows: 4, 2, 5 / 6, 3, 4 / 1, 0, 7. What is A's maximin value?
quiz.explain: Row minimums are 2, 3, 0; the largest is 3, from A2.

quiz.q: When does a game have a saddle point?
options: When A has more strategies than B
quiz.explain: If the best guaranteed outcome for A equals the best limit B can impose, both play pure strategies at that cell.

quiz.q: For the game 3, -1 / -2, 4, what is the value?
Why is row A3 (2, -2, 3) removed when A1 is (3, -1, 4)?
options: A1 is at least as good as A3 in every column
quiz.explain: Each A1 entry beats the matching A3 entry, so A3 is dominated and never played.

quiz.q: In the price war (both high 10 each, both low 6 each, cutter 12 and other 4), what is the Nash equilibrium?
quiz.explain: Cutting is better whatever the rival does (12 > 10, 6 > 4), so both cut and earn 6, though both high would give 10.

lessons.title: Decision Analysis: Choosing Under Risk and Uncertainty
lessons.content:
A businessman in Bogura wants to build a cold storage for potatoes. A large one earns a lot if the harvest and prices are good but loses heavily in a bad year. A small one is safe but earns little. He cannot know next year's market. Unlike game theory, nobody is plotting against him; the unknown is "nature": weather, prices, demand. Decision analysis gives structured ways to choose when the outcome depends on such uncertain states of nature, and to decide whether it is worth paying for more information first.

The parts of a decision problem: Alternatives: the actions you can choose (build large, medium, small, or nothing). States of nature: the possible futures you cannot control (high, medium or low demand). Payoffs: the result of each action in each state, often profit. These go in a payoff table with alternatives as rows and states as columns. Three settings exist: under certainty you know the state, which is ordinary optimisation; under risk you know the probabilities of the states; under uncertainty you do not even know the probabilities.

The payoff table: Profits in lakh taka over the storage's first years, invented for teaching. Large: 200 if demand is high, 50 if medium, -120 if low. Medium: 120, 80, -30. Small: 60, 40, 10. Do nothing: 0, 0, 0. Do nothing is dominated by Small, which is better in every state, so a sensible owner would never choose it; we keep it only to show regret.

Decisions under uncertainty, maximax: The optimist assumes the best will happen and picks the alternative with the largest best payoff. Best payoffs: Large 200, Medium 120, Small 60. Maximax chooses Large. It suits someone who can absorb a loss and wants the biggest upside, but it ignores the -120 risk completely.

Maximin: The pessimist assumes the worst and picks the alternative with the best worst case. Worst payoffs: Large -120, Medium -30, Small 10, None 0. Maximin chooses Small, guaranteeing at least 10. It suits a small business that cannot survive a big loss. It is the same idea as A's maximin in game theory, but here nature is not really an enemy, so it can be too cautious.

Laplace (equally likely): If you have no idea about probabilities, treat all states as equally likely and pick the best average. Averages: Large 130 / 3, about 43.3; Medium 170 / 3, about 56.7; Small 110 / 3, about 36.7. Laplace chooses Medium. The weakness is that the answer depends on how you list the states: splitting "low" into two states would change the weights.

Hurwicz (realism): A middle way between optimism and pessimism. Choose a coefficient of optimism alpha between 0 and 1, and score each alternative as alpha x best + (1 - alpha) x worst. With alpha = 0.6: Large 0.6 x 200 + 0.4 x (-120) = 120 - 48 = 72. Medium 72 - 12 = 60. Small 36 + 4 = 40. Hurwicz with 0.6 chooses Large. With alpha = 0 it becomes maximin and with alpha = 1 maximax. The choice of alpha is the decision maker's attitude, written as a number.

Minimax regret (Savage): Regret is how much you lose by not having chosen the best action for the state that happened. For each state, find the best payoff: 200 for high, 80 for medium, 10 for low. Regret = best in column minus your payoff. Large: 0, 30, 130, maximum 130. Medium: 80, 0, 40, maximum 80. Small: 140, 40, 0, maximum 140. None: 200, 80, 10, maximum 200. Choose the smallest maximum regret: Medium with 80. It suits managers who will be judged afterwards on "you should have known".

Five rules, three answers: Maximax picks Large, maximin picks Small, Laplace picks Medium, Hurwicz (0.6) picks Large, regret picks Medium. There is no single correct rule under true uncertainty; each encodes a different attitude to risk. The useful part is that the table makes the trade-offs visible and forces the decision maker to state their attitude openly.

Decisions under risk, expected monetary value: Now suppose market studies give probabilities: high demand 0.3, medium 0.5, low 0.2. The expected monetary value (EMV) is the probability-weighted average payoff. Large: 0.3 x 200 + 0.5 x 50 + 0.2 x (-120) = 60 + 25 - 24 = 61. Medium: 36 + 40 - 6 = 70. Small: 18 + 20 + 2 = 40. Choose Medium, with EMV 70 lakh. EMV is the right rule when the decision is repeated many times or the amounts are small compared with total wealth, because averages win in the long run.

Expected value of perfect information: What if a perfect forecaster could tell you the state before you build? You would build Large if high (200), Medium if medium (80) and Small if low (10). Before hearing the forecast, your expected payoff with perfect information is 0.3 x 200 + 0.5 x 80 + 0.2 x 10 = 60 + 40 + 2 = 102. Without it, the best EMV is 70. EVPI = 102 - 70 = 32 lakh. No study, survey or consultant can be worth more than 32 lakh to this decision. If someone offers a survey for 40 lakh, refuse immediately.

Expected opportunity loss: Another route to the same answer uses the regret table with the probabilities. Expected opportunity loss (EOL) for Large = 0.3 x 0 + 0.5 x 30 + 0.2 x 130 = 41. For Medium = 0.3 x 80 + 0.5 x 0 + 0.2 x 40 = 32. For Small = 0.3 x 140 + 0.5 x 40 + 0.2 x 0 = 62. The smallest EOL is Medium, the same choice as the largest EMV, and always will be. Even better, the minimum EOL, 32, equals the EVPI exactly. That makes sense: the expected regret of your best choice is exactly what perfect knowledge would save you.

Drawing the cold storage tree: Start on the left with a square: "survey or not". The "no survey" branch leads to another square with three branches, Large, Medium and Small, each ending in a circle with three chance branches (high 0.3, medium 0.5, low 0.2) and payoffs at the tips. The "survey" branch leads first to a circle (good 0.51, bad 0.49), and each result leads to its own square with the same three building choices, but now with the updated probabilities on the final circles. Drawing it carefully, left to right in time order, is half the work; the arithmetic is then just averages and maximums.

Decision trees: Real decisions often come in sequences: first decide whether to do a survey, then see its result, then decide what to build. A decision tree draws this in time order. Squares are decision nodes (you choose), circles are chance nodes (nature chooses, with probabilities), and the ends carry payoffs. You solve it by rolling back from the right: at a chance node take the expected value, at a decision node take the best branch. It is the same backward thinking as dynamic programming in lesson 17.

A survey in the tree: A market survey reports "good" or "bad". From past experience, it says good 80% of the time when demand turns out high, 50% when medium, and 10% when low. By Bayes' theorem (Probability & Statistics, deep-cse-2-6), P(good) = 0.3 x 0.8 + 0.5 x 0.5 + 0.2 x 0.1 = 0.24 + 0.25 + 0.02 = 0.51. If good, the updated probabilities are about 0.47, 0.49 and 0.04, and the best choice is Large with expected value about 113.9. If bad (probability 0.49), they are about 0.12, 0.51 and 0.37, and the best choice is Medium with about 44.5.

Value of the survey: Rolling back, the expected payoff with the survey is 0.51 x 113.9 + 0.49 x 44.5, about 79.9 lakh, before the survey's cost. Without it, it is 70. So the expected value of sample information (EVSI) is about 9.9 lakh. If the survey costs 5 lakh, do it: the net gain is about 4.9 lakh. If it costs 12 lakh, skip it. The efficiency of the survey is EVSI / EVPI, about 9.9 / 32, roughly 31%: an imperfect survey captures about a third of what perfect information would be worth.

Risk attitude and utility: EMV treats a sure 70 the same as a gamble averaging 70. Most people and small firms are risk-averse: a loss of 120 lakh might mean bankruptcy. Utility theory replaces money with a utility score that bends to reflect this, and you maximise expected utility instead. Insurance exists because risk-averse people prefer paying a small sure premium to facing a small chance of a huge loss, even though the premium's expected value is negative.

Sensitivity to probabilities: The probabilities are estimates, so check how much they can change before the decision flips. If the chance of high demand rises from 0.3 to 0.4 (taking it from medium), Large becomes 80 + 20 - 24 = 76 and Medium 48 + 32 - 6 = 74: the choice flips to Large. A decision that flips with small changes deserves more information; one that is stable can be made with confidence.

Real-life example 1, a farmer's crop choice: A farmer in the haor region decides whether to plant early Boro rice, which risks flash floods before harvest, or a later, lower-yield variety. With rough probabilities of an early flood and payoffs per bigha, EMV and regret tables make the trade-off explicit, and an accurate flood forecast has a clear value: the EVPI tells the government how much early-warning systems are worth to farmers.

Real-life example 2, launching an app feature: A startup must decide whether to build a big new feature, a small version, or nothing. Market response is uncertain. A quick A/B test on a small group of users is the "survey". The decision tree computes whether the test's expected information value exceeds its cost in time and money, which is how product teams justify running experiments before big builds.

Common mistakes: Mixing up maximin (best of worst) and minimax regret (smallest worst regret). Computing regret row-wise instead of column-wise: regret compares within each state. Forgetting that probabilities must add to 1. Treating EVPI as the value of an imperfect survey: it is only an upper limit. Rolling back a tree from the left instead of the right. Forgetting to subtract information costs.

What exams ask: Build a payoff table and apply maximax, maximin, Laplace, Hurwicz and minimax regret. Compute EMV and choose under risk. Compute EVPI. Draw and roll back a decision tree, possibly with Bayes revision of probabilities, and find the value of sample information. Discuss risk attitude and sensitivity.

Recap: Under uncertainty, maximax picks Large (200), maximin picks Small (10), Laplace picks Medium (56.7), Hurwicz at 0.6 picks Large (72), and minimax regret picks Medium (80). Under risk with probabilities 0.3, 0.5, 0.2, EMV picks Medium at 70 lakh; perfect information is worth 102 - 70 = 32 lakh; a realistic survey is worth about 9.9 lakh. Decision trees roll back from the right, chance nodes averaging and decision nodes choosing. Next, lesson 24 leaves straight lines behind: nonlinear optimisation and metaheuristics for very hard problems.
key_points: Decision analysis chooses among alternatives when the state of nature is unknown; payoff table rows = actions, columns = states.
Maximax (optimist) picks Large 200; maximin (pessimist) picks Small 10; Laplace averages and picks Medium 56.7.
Hurwicz = alpha x best + (1 - alpha) x worst; alpha 0.6 picks Large with 72.
Regret = column best minus payoff; minimax regret picks Medium with maximum regret 80.
EMV with probabilities 0.3, 0.5, 0.2: Large 61, Medium 70, Small 40; choose Medium.
EVPI = expected payoff with perfect information (102) minus best EMV (70) = 32 lakh, the upper limit for any information.
Decision trees: squares decide, circles average, roll back from the right; the survey's EVSI is about 9.9 lakh.
Risk-averse decision makers use expected utility; always test how sensitive the choice is to the probabilities.
lessons.tip: Compute EVPI before discussing any study, survey or consultant. It takes two lines and gives a hard ceiling on what information is worth, which ends many long meetings quickly.
lessons.task: Pick a real choice your family faces with uncertain outcomes (for example, buying a generator before load-shedding season, or which coaching centre to join). Write 3 alternatives, 3 states and rough payoffs. Apply all five uncertainty rules, then guess probabilities, compute EMV and EVPI, and write which answer you would actually follow and why.

quiz.q: Worst payoffs are Large -120, Medium -30, Small 10. Which does maximin choose?
quiz.explain: Maximin picks the best worst case, and 10 is the largest of -120, -30, 10 and 0.

quiz.q: Regret for an action in a state is:
options: The payoff divided by the best payoff
The best payoff in the row minus the payoff
The best payoff in that state's column minus the action's payoff
The probability of the state times the payoff
quiz.explain: Regret compares within each state (column): how much better the best action would have done.

quiz.q: With probabilities 0.3, 0.5, 0.2, what is the EMV of Medium (120, 80, -30)?
Expected payoff with perfect information is 102 and the best EMV is 70. A survey costs 40 lakh. What should you do?
options: Buy it because surveys always help
Refuse: EVPI is 32, so no information can be worth 40
quiz.explain: EVPI = 102 - 70 = 32 lakh, an upper limit on the value of any information.

quiz.q: How do you solve a decision tree?
options: Roll back from the right: average at chance nodes, choose the best at decision nodes
Go left to right choosing the biggest payoff
Pick the branch with the highest probability
quiz.explain: Backward induction, like dynamic programming, computes the value of each node from its future.

lessons.title: Nonlinear Optimisation and Metaheuristics
lessons.content:
Linear programming assumes everything is a straight line: double the production, double the profit. But real life bends. Selling more often needs lower prices, so revenue curves flatten. The area of a field grows with length times width, a product, not a sum. And some problems, like finding the shortest route through 50 delivery stops, are so huge that no exact method finishes in a lifetime. This lesson covers two tools for these cases: nonlinear programming, which handles curved objectives and constraints, and metaheuristics, clever search strategies that find very good answers to very hard problems quickly.

What nonlinear programming is: A nonlinear program (NLP) has the same parts as an LP, decision variables, an objective and constraints, but at least one of them is not linear: squares, products, square roots, exponentials. Examples: the EOQ cost (D / Q) S + (Q / 2) H from lesson 18, portfolio risk which involves products of investment amounts, or the profit of a shop whose demand falls as its price rises.

Why NLP is harder: In an LP, the optimum is always at a corner of the feasible region, which simplex exploits. In an NLP, the optimum can be anywhere: a corner, an edge, or deep inside. Worse, a curved function can have several hills. A local optimum is the best point in its neighbourhood; the global optimum is the best overall. A climber who always walks uphill reaches the top of the nearest hill, which may not be the highest mountain.

Convexity, the good case: If you are minimising a convex function (shaped like a bowl, curving upwards everywhere) over a convex feasible region (no dents or holes), every local minimum is a global minimum. Then simple methods like gradient descent, which steps downhill along the negative gradient, are guaranteed to find the best answer. Many important models are convex: EOQ, least-squares regression, portfolio variance. Machine Learning (deep-cse-6-1) trains models by gradient descent for this reason.

Unconstrained optimisation: Without constraints, set the derivative to zero to find candidates, then check the second derivative: positive means a minimum, negative a maximum. For f(x) = x squared - 6x + 13, f'(x) = 2x - 6 = 0 gives x = 3, f''(x) = 2 > 0, so the minimum is f(3) = 4. With several variables, set all partial derivatives to zero and check the Hessian matrix, which you met in Linear Algebra (deep-cse-2-5).

Gradient descent by hand: Use the same f(x) = x squared - 6x + 13, start at x = 0 and use a step size of 0.25. The rule is: new x = x - 0.25 x f'(x). At x = 0, f'(0) = -6, so x becomes 0 + 1.5 = 1.5. At 1.5, f' = -3, so x becomes 2.25. At 2.25, f' = -1.5, so x becomes 2.625. Each step halves the distance to 3, the true minimum. Too large a step would overshoot and bounce around; too small would crawl. Choosing this step size, the learning rate, is a daily job in machine learning.

Lagrange multipliers for equality constraints: A farmer has 100 metres of fence to enclose a rectangular plot beside a river; the river side needs no fence. Let x be each side perpendicular to the river and y the side parallel to it. Maximise area A = xy subject to 2x + y = 100. Form the Lagrangian L = xy - lambda (2x + y - 100). Set the partial derivatives to zero: y - 2 lambda = 0, x - lambda = 0, and the constraint. So x = lambda, y = 2 lambda, and 2 lambda + 2 lambda = 100, giving lambda = 25, x = 25, y = 50 and area 1,250 square metres.

What lambda means: The Lagrange multiplier is a shadow price, exactly like the dual values in lesson 7. Here lambda = 25 means one extra metre of fence adds about 25 square metres of area. Check: with 101 metres, x = 25.25 and y = 50.5, area 1,275.1, an increase of about 25.1. So if fence costs 200 taka per metre and land in the plot is worth more than 8 taka per square metre, buying more fence pays.

KKT conditions for inequality constraints: When constraints are inequalities (like a budget limit), the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions generalise Lagrange. At an optimum: the gradient of the objective is a combination of the gradients of the active constraints; multipliers are non-negative; and complementary slackness holds: a constraint that is not tight has multiplier zero, exactly as in LP duality. For convex problems, the KKT conditions are sufficient for the global optimum. Support vector machines in machine learning are solved through their KKT conditions.

Hard combinatorial problems: Some problems are not curved but huge. The travelling salesman problem (TSP): visit every city once and return home with the shortest total distance. With 5 cities there are 4! / 2 = 12 distinct tours. With 20 cities there are 19! / 2, about 6 x 10^16 tours: checking a billion per second would take about two years. The TSP is NP-hard (Theory of Computation, deep-cse-3-5), so no known method solves every large instance quickly. Vehicle routing, timetabling, and factory scheduling are similar.

Heuristics: A heuristic is a rule of thumb that finds a good, not necessarily optimal, answer fast. Constructive heuristics build a solution step by step. The nearest neighbour heuristic for TSP: from where you are, always go to the nearest unvisited city. Improvement heuristics start from a solution and make small changes that reduce cost.

Nearest neighbour worked: A delivery van starts at a depot D in Tejgaon and must visit A, B, C and E and return. Distances in km: D-A 4, D-B 9, D-C 11, D-E 5, A-B 13, A-C 10, A-E 8, B-C 5, B-E 4, C-E 10. From D, the nearest is A (4). From A, the nearest unvisited is E (8). From E, B (4). From B, C (5). Then back to D (11). Tour D, A, E, B, C, D, total 4 + 8 + 4 + 5 + 11 = 32 km. The greedy start was fine, but it was forced into the long 11 km return at the end.

2-opt improvement: A 2-opt move removes two edges and reconnects the tour the other way, which reverses the path between them. Remove A-E (8) and C-D (11), total 19, and add A-C (10) and E-D (5), total 15. The new tour D, A, C, B, E, D is 4 + 10 + 5 + 4 + 5 = 28 km, saving 4 km. Checking all 12 tours confirms 28 is the optimum. 2-opt keeps applying improving moves until none remain. It is simple and usually gets within about 5% of optimal on real road problems.

The local optimum trap: Improvement heuristics stop when no small change helps, which may be a local optimum, not the global one. Metaheuristics are higher-level strategies that guide a heuristic to escape such traps. They work on almost any problem, need no derivatives, and are widely used in industry. The price: no guarantee of optimality, and settings that need tuning.

Simulated annealing: Inspired by slowly cooling metal so its atoms settle into a strong structure. At each step, try a random small change. If it is better, accept it. If it is worse by delta, still accept it with probability e^(-delta / T), where T is a temperature that slowly decreases. With T = 20, a move worse by 10 is accepted with probability e^(-0.5), about 0.61. With T = 5, only e^(-2), about 0.14. With T = 1, about 0.00005. Early on, the search wanders freely and escapes local traps; later, it settles down and only improves.

Genetic algorithms: Inspired by evolution. Keep a population of solutions, for example 100 delivery tours. Pick the better ones as parents (selection), combine pieces of two parents into children (crossover), and make small random changes (mutation). Over many generations the population improves. Genetic algorithms suit problems where good solutions share good building blocks, like timetables where good room choices can be combined.

Tabu search: Like a local search that always moves to the best neighbouring solution, even if it is worse, but keeps a short memory list (tabu list) of recent moves that are forbidden for a while. This prevents cycling back to the same local optimum and pushes the search into new regions. Tabu search is popular for scheduling and routing. Other metaheuristics include ant colony optimisation, which mimics how ants find short paths with pheromone trails, and particle swarm optimisation.

Exact versus heuristic, choosing wisely: If the problem is an LP or a convex NLP, use an exact solver: it is fast and optimal. If it is a moderate integer program, try branch and bound (lesson 12) with a modern solver first; they often solve thousands of variables. Use metaheuristics when the problem is huge, very nonlinear, or the objective is a black-box simulation. A common practical combination is to get a quick heuristic answer and give it to an exact solver as a starting point.

Real-life example 1, delivery routing in Dhaka: E-commerce and food delivery companies plan hundreds of drop-offs per van each day, with time windows and traffic. Exact solutions are impossible at that size, so they use construction heuristics plus improvement steps like 2-opt and metaheuristics such as tabu search or simulated annealing, re-optimising as new orders arrive. Saving even 5% of kilometres across a fleet means large fuel savings.

Real-life example 2, university exam timetabling: A university must schedule hundreds of exams into a limited number of slots and rooms so no student has two exams at once and few have two on the same day. This is a graph colouring problem with extra rules, NP-hard. Timetabling software commonly uses simulated annealing or tabu search, starting from a feasible timetable and swapping exams to reduce conflicts and penalties. Advanced Algorithms (deep-cse-7-1) studies approximation guarantees for such problems.

Common mistakes: Using LP for a clearly curved problem. Assuming a local optimum from gradient descent is global on a non-convex problem. Forgetting the second-order check after setting derivatives to zero. In Lagrange problems, dropping the constraint equation. Running a metaheuristic once and trusting the result; run it several times with different seeds. Claiming a heuristic result is optimal without proof.

Recap: NLP handles curved objectives and constraints; convex problems are easy because local equals global. Lagrange multipliers solve equality-constrained problems and act as shadow prices: the riverside fence gives x = 25, y = 50, area 1,250 and lambda = 25 square metres per extra metre. KKT extends this to inequalities. For NP-hard problems like TSP, nearest neighbour gave 32 km and one 2-opt move reached the optimum 28 km. Simulated annealing accepts worse moves with probability e^(-delta / T), while genetic algorithms and tabu search use populations and memory. Next, lesson 25 brings the whole course together in a capstone.
key_points: NLP has a nonlinear objective or constraint; the optimum need not be at a corner, and local optima can trap you.
Convex minimisation over a convex region: every local minimum is global; gradient descent works.
Unconstrained: set derivatives to zero and check the second derivative or Hessian.
Lagrange: riverside fence 2x + y = 100 gives x = 25, y = 50, area 1,250, lambda = 25 (a shadow price).
KKT conditions extend Lagrange to inequalities with non-negative multipliers and complementary slackness.
TSP is NP-hard: 20 cities give about 6 x 10^16 tours.
Nearest neighbour gave 32 km; one 2-opt move gave the optimum 28 km.
Simulated annealing accepts worse moves with probability e^(-delta / T); genetic algorithms and tabu search are other metaheuristics.
lessons.tip: Before reaching for a metaheuristic, ask whether the problem is really linear, convex, or a moderate integer program. Exact solvers are fast and come with a guarantee. Use metaheuristics when size or nonlinearity truly rule exact methods out, and always compare against a simple baseline like nearest neighbour.
lessons.task: Mark 6 places you know on a map (home, school, market, a relative's house, a mosque or temple, a park) and estimate distances between them. Build a tour starting and ending at home with nearest neighbour, then try 2-opt moves by hand until none improve it. Count how many kilometres you saved and how many tours exist in total.

quiz.q: When is a local minimum guaranteed to be the global minimum?
options: When the function is convex over a convex feasible region
quiz.explain: Convexity removes extra valleys, so any local minimum is the global one.

quiz.q: For max xy subject to 2x + y = 100, what is the Lagrange multiplier lambda?
quiz.explain: Conditions give x = lambda and y = 2 lambda, so 4 lambda = 100 and lambda = 25.

quiz.q: What does lambda = 25 mean in the fence problem?
options: One extra metre of fence adds about 25 square metres
quiz.explain: A Lagrange multiplier is a shadow price: the objective's rate of change per unit of the constraint.

quiz.q: Nearest neighbour gives D, A, E, B, C, D = 32 km. Which 2-opt move gives 28 km?
options: Replace A-E and C-D with A-C and E-D
quiz.explain: Removing 8 + 11 = 19 km and adding 10 + 5 = 15 km saves 4 km, giving D, A, C, B, E, D = 28.

quiz.q: In simulated annealing with T = 5, what is the probability of accepting a move that is worse by 10?

lessons.title: Practice and Capstone: Running a Distributor with Operations Research
lessons.content:
You have now learned linear programming, duality, transportation and assignment, integer programming, networks, project scheduling, dynamic programming, inventory, queues, games, decision analysis, and heuristics. In real jobs, problems do not arrive labelled "this is a transportation problem". A manager says "our costs are too high and trucks are always waiting". This capstone follows one invented company, DeshMart, a fast-moving consumer goods distributor, through a planning season, so you can practise spotting which OR model fits each piece of a messy real situation, solving it, and explaining the answer.

The company: DeshMart distributes soap, biscuits and cooking oil to shops across Bangladesh. It has two warehouses, in Dhaka (Tongi) and Chattogram, and serves three sales zones: North, Central and South. It runs a fleet of small trucks, a loading dock at each warehouse, and a sales team that wants to open a new depot in Sylhet. The numbers below are invented but realistic in shape.

Step 1, frame the problem before touching numbers: The OR process from lesson 1 still applies: define the problem, collect data, build a model, solve it, validate it, and implement. Talk to people first. The logistics head worries about transport cost, the warehouse manager about trucks queuing at the dock, finance about money tied up in stock, and sales about growth in Sylhet. Each concern becomes a separate, smaller model, and the models are later checked for consistency with each other.

Step 2, shipping plan as a transportation problem: Each month Dhaka can ship 300 truckloads' worth (in hundreds of cartons) and Chattogram 200. North needs 150, Central 200, South 150, so supply equals demand at 500. Cost per unit in taka (hundreds): Dhaka to North 20, Central 10, South 30; Chattogram to North 40, Central 25, South 12. This is exactly the structure of lessons 9 and 10.

Solving the shipping plan: A naive start would fill the cheapest cell, Dhaka to Central (10), first. It is better to think in opportunity costs, as VAM does. Chattogram is far cheaper for the South (12 versus 30), and Dhaka is far cheaper for the North (20 versus 40). So send Chattogram to South 150, Dhaka to North 150, then split Central: Dhaka sends its remaining 150 and Chattogram its remaining 50. Cost = 150 x 20 + 150 x 10 + 50 x 25 + 150 x 12 = 3,000 + 1,500 + 1,250 + 1,800 = 7,550. A check of every feasible split confirms 7,550 is optimal. With MODI, all unused cells have non-negative reduced costs, which also proves it.

Reading the duals of the shipping plan: The MODI numbers also tell finance something useful. Setting u for Dhaka to 0: from the used cells, v North = 20, v Central = 10, then u Chattogram = 25 - 10 = 15 and v South = 12 - 15 = -3. The unused cells have reduced costs Dhaka to South = 30 - 0 - (-3) = 33 and Chattogram to North = 40 - 15 - 20 = 5. Both are positive, so the plan is optimal and no other plan ties with it. The 5 means that forcing even one unit from Chattogram to North would raise cost by 5. The u and v values act as shadow prices, showing where extra capacity or demand is cheap or expensive to serve, just as in lesson 7.

Step 3, inventory for a top-selling soap: DeshMart sells 24,000 cartons of its best soap a year. Placing an order with the factory costs 1,200 taka (transport booking, paperwork and receiving labour), and holding one carton for a year costs 40 taka. EOQ = square root of (2 x 24,000 x 1,200 / 40) = square root of 1,440,000 = 1,200 cartons, about 20 orders a year. Annual ordering cost = 20 x 1,200 = 24,000 taka and holding cost = 600 x 40 = 24,000 taka, total 48,000. With daily demand of 80 cartons (300 days), a 4-day lead time, and some safety stock, the reorder point is about 320 plus safety stock. The ABC rule tells DeshMart to model the top 20% of products this carefully and use simple rules for the rest.

Step 4, the loading dock queue: At the Dhaka warehouse, trucks arrive for loading at about 6 per hour, and one dock crew loads a truck in 15 minutes on average, 4 per hour. One crew is impossible: rho = 6 / 4 = 1.5, and the line would grow forever. With 2 crews (an M/M/2 queue), rho = 0.75 and the average wait before loading is about 19.3 minutes. With 3 crews, rho = 0.5 and the wait drops to about 2.4 minutes. With 4 crews, about 0.4 minutes.

Choosing the number of crews: A crew costs 800 taka per hour, and a truck with its driver costs 600 taka per hour while it is at the dock (waiting or loading). Total cost per hour: 2 crews: 1,600 + 600 x 3.43 trucks in the system, about 3,657 taka. 3 crews: 2,400 + 600 x 1.74, about 3,442 taka. 4 crews: 3,200 + 600 x 1.54, about 4,127 taka. Three crews is cheapest. The surprise for the manager: adding a third crew saves money, because waiting trucks were the hidden cost.

Step 5, daily delivery routes: Each van in Dhaka visits 15 to 30 shops a day. This is a vehicle routing problem, NP-hard like the TSP. DeshMart starts with a nearest neighbour route for each van, improves it with 2-opt, and runs a metaheuristic overnight when orders are known. Even on a 5-stop example from lesson 24, 2-opt cut the route from 32 to 28 km, a 12.5% saving; on full routes, savings of 5 to 10% are common.

Step 6, should we open Sylhet: Sales estimates that a Sylhet depot would earn 60 lakh taka over three years if demand grows (probability 0.6) and lose 25 lakh if it does not (probability 0.4). EMV of opening = 0.6 x 60 + 0.4 x (-25) = 36 - 10 = 26 lakh, better than 0 for not opening. With perfect information, DeshMart would open only if demand grows: expected 0.6 x 60 = 36. EVPI = 36 - 26 = 10 lakh. A market study costing 3 lakh might be worth it; one costing 15 lakh is not. Finance, being risk-averse, may also check the maximin: not opening guarantees 0, while opening risks -25.

Step 7, scheduling the depot project: If DeshMart opens Sylhet, the project (find land, build racks, hire staff, set up IT, trial run) is planned with CPM and PERT from lessons 15 and 16. The critical path tells management which activities to watch, PERT gives the probability of opening before the peak Eid season, and crashing decides whether paying overtime to finish early is worth it.

Solving with software: Real models have thousands of variables, so OR professionals use solvers. In Python, the free PuLP library lets you write a model almost like mathematics: create a problem with LpProblem, add variables with LpVariable, add the objective and constraints with ordinary + and <=, and call solve(). Google OR-Tools adds routing and scheduling solvers. Excel Solver handles small LPs and is common in offices. Commercial solvers like Gurobi and CPLEX handle very large integer programs. The skill is not typing the model but formulating it correctly.

Validating the model: Before trusting results, test them. Does the shipping plan obey every supply and demand? Does the EOQ make sense next to the warehouse's shelf space? Does the queue model match how long trucks actually waited last month? Run the model on past data and compare with what really happened. Check sensitivity: if fuel prices rise 20%, does the shipping plan change? A model that cannot reproduce the past should not be trusted for the future.

Explaining to managers: Decision makers rarely want formulas. Present the decision, the saving, and the key assumption in one sentence each: "Use three dock crews. It saves about 215 taka per hour, roughly 5 lakh taka a year on one shift. This assumes trucks keep arriving at about 6 per hour; if arrivals drop below 4, go back to two crews." Show one simple chart, and keep the detailed model for questions. Good OR work is half mathematics and half communication.

How the topics connect: Look back at the course as a map. LP (lessons 2 to 8) is the foundation; transportation and assignment (9 to 11) are LPs with special structure; integer programming (12) handles yes/no choices; network models (13 to 16) are graphs with special algorithms; dynamic programming (17) handles stages; inventory (18, 19) and queues (20, 21) handle randomness in stock and service; game theory and decision analysis (22, 23) handle opponents and uncertainty; nonlinear models and metaheuristics (24) handle curves and huge problems. Duality and shadow prices appear again and again.

Where OR leads: OR skills are used in supply chains, airlines, banking, telecom, ride-hailing, e-commerce, hospitals, energy and government planning. Job titles include operations research analyst, supply chain analyst, data scientist, and optimisation engineer. The next courses build on this one: Simulation & Modeling (deep-cse-6-5) for systems too complex for formulas, Software Project Management (deep-cse-6-11) which uses CPM and PERT, Advanced Algorithms (deep-cse-7-1) for approximation and complexity, and Reinforcement Learning (deep-cse-8-4), which grows out of dynamic programming.

Common capstone mistakes: Solving the wrong problem because the real goal was never clarified. Building one giant model when several small ones would be clearer. Trusting data without checking units and outliers. Presenting an "optimal" plan without stating assumptions. Ignoring people: a plan that drivers or warehouse staff cannot follow will fail however optimal it is on paper.

Practice set: Try these on your own, then check with software. 1. Change Chattogram's supply to 250 and add a dummy zone; re-solve the shipping plan. 2. If ordering cost falls to 300 taka with online booking, find the new EOQ (it halves to 600). 3. If trucks arrive at 7 per hour, how many dock crews minimise cost? 4. If the chance of demand growth in Sylhet falls to 0.3, should DeshMart still open? (EMV = 18 - 17.5 = 0.5 lakh, barely positive.) 5. Draw the Sylhet project network with your own activity estimates and find its critical path.

Recap of the capstone: DeshMart's shipping plan costs 7,550 using Dhaka for North and Central and Chattogram for South and part of Central. Its best soap is ordered 1,200 cartons at a time for 48,000 taka a year. Three loading crews minimise dock cost at about 3,442 taka per hour. Routes are improved with 2-opt and metaheuristics. Opening Sylhet has EMV 26 lakh and EVPI 10 lakh. Each answer came from a model you learned in this course, and the real skill is choosing the right model, checking it, and explaining it clearly. Congratulations on finishing Operations Research.
key_points: Real problems arrive unlabelled: split them into smaller models and pick the right OR tool for each.
Shipping plan (transportation): Dhaka to North 150 and Central 150, Chattogram to Central 50 and South 150; cost 7,550.
Soap EOQ = square root of (2 x 24,000 x 1,200 / 40) = 1,200 cartons, 20 orders, 48,000 taka a year.
Loading dock M/M/c: 2 crews give Wq about 19.3 min, 3 crews about 2.4 min; 3 crews minimise cost (about 3,442 taka per hour).
Sylhet depot: EMV = 0.6 x 60 - 0.4 x 25 = 26 lakh; EVPI = 10 lakh caps what a study is worth.
Solvers: PuLP and OR-Tools in Python, Excel Solver, Gurobi or CPLEX for large problems; formulation is the real skill.
Validate models on past data, test sensitivity, and state assumptions plainly.
Explain each decision with the action, the saving and the key assumption in plain language.
lessons.tip: When facing a messy real problem, write three lines before any model: the decision to be made, the objective, and the main limits. Those three lines usually reveal which lesson's model applies, and they keep you from solving the wrong problem beautifully.
lessons.task: Choose a real organisation you can observe, such as your school canteen, a local pharmacy or a neighbourhood courier office. Identify at least three decisions it makes (what to stock, how many counters, which routes). For each, name the OR model from this course that fits, list the data you would need, and make a rough estimate of the answer using that model. Write a one-paragraph recommendation as if presenting to the owner.

quiz.q: DeshMart's dock: trucks arrive at 6 per hour and one crew loads 4 per hour. Why is one crew impossible?
options: Because rho = 1.5 is above 1, so the queue grows forever
Because queues need at least three servers
quiz.explain: A single server needs lambda < mu; here 6 > 4, so no steady state exists.

quiz.q: What is the EOQ for D = 24,000, S = 1,200 taka and H = 40 taka?
quiz.explain: EOQ = square root of (2 x 24,000 x 1,200 / 40) = square root of 1,440,000 = 1,200.

quiz.q: For Sylhet, EMV of opening is 26 lakh and the expected value with perfect information is 36 lakh. What is the most a market study could be worth?
quiz.explain: EVPI = 36 - 26 = 10 lakh, the upper limit for any information.

quiz.q: Why does a third dock crew reduce total cost?
options: Trucks load faster with more crews each
Waiting truck time costs more than the extra crew's wage
quiz.explain: Total cost falls from about 3,657 to about 3,442 taka per hour because truck waiting drops sharply.

quiz.q: Which step should come before building any model?
options: Defining the decision, objective and limits with the people involved
quiz.explain: The OR process starts with understanding the problem; a perfect model of the wrong problem is useless.
